title: Terrain-Aware Thompson Sampling for Multi-Drone Search and Rescue
comment: Accepted to the 18th International Symposium on Distributed Autonomous Robotic Systems (DARS 2026)
summary: In this work, we propose a decentralized terrain-aware multi-drone Thompson Sampling algorithm tailored for search and rescue (SAR) applications. A probability distribution of locating a lost person is informed by terrain data, using established SAR models (displacement ring, elevation, watershed, dispersion angle, and track offset) derived from historical SAR case data on lost person behavior. Exploration is conducted by a team of drones using Thompson Sampling, where candidate actions are selected by drawing samples from this probability distribution, represented by a per-cell Gaussian posterior whose mean and variance are updated through Bayesian inference. This approach balances exploration of uncertain regions with exploitation of high-probability areas to locate a lost person. Observation uncertainty is incorporated through fractional forest coverage, which measures the percentage of an observation occluded by tree coverage and accounts for reduced detection performance in densely vegetated areas. Simulations using real SAR case data (YOSAR) evaluate the proposed method against a coverage planner and a probabilistic active search method in search regions of 1.5 and 3.8 square kilometers, with 5, 10, 15, and 20 agents flying at 50 km/hr. We demonstrate that our method achieves a success rate of approximately 87% within 60 to 247 seconds in the 1.5 square kilometer region, and success rates of approximately 75% to 91% within 161 to 466 seconds in the 3.8 square kilometer region, across different agent configurations.

A probability distribution of locating a lost person is informed by terrain data, using established SAR models (displacement ring, elevation, watershed, dispersion angle, and track offset) derived from historical SAR case data of lost person behavior. This approach enables a balance between exploration of uncertain regions and exploitation of high-probability areas with the goal of locating a lost person. Observation uncertainty is incorporated through fractional forest coverage, measuring the percent of an observation occluded by tree coverage and accounting for reduced detection performance in densely vegetated areas. Simulations are performed using real SAR case data (YOSAR) to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method compared to a coverage planner and probabilistic active search method in a 1.5 and 3.8 search region with 5,10,15, and 20 agents flying at 50 km/hr. We demonstrate that our method is able to successfully locate a lost person at a success rate of within -- ~s for an area of 1.5~ , and at a success rate of within -- ~s for an area of 3.8~ , across configurations. Introduction Wilderness search and rescue (WiSAR) operations are inherently arduous, time-consuming, and resource-intensive, requiring careful planning and efficient execution to maximize the probability of survival of a lost person. In land-based SAR missions, survivability decreases rapidly over time, making timely and informed decision-making critical. To support this process, a variety of models have been developed Koester2008,Doke2012AnalysisOS,mapscore to generate probability maps that estimate the likely locations of a missing individual. These approaches are grounded in mathematical search theory Koopman1980 , which addresses the fundamental challenge of locating an unknown target within a large search space. While such probabilistic approaches significantly improve search efficiency, SAR operations still demand extensive human effort, coordination, and time to achieve successful outcomes. Multi-robot systems, in particular teams of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), offer a promising solution by enabling rapid, parallel exploration of large areas Baxter2007,Drew2021SARReview,SARSurvey . However, the effectiveness of such systems depends critically on their ability to operate autonomously and in a distributed manner. Centralized coordination approaches reduce robustness in SAR scenarios due to limited communication infrastructure, bandwidth constraints, and the risk of single points of failure. To address these challenges, decentralized task allocation methods have been proposed, enabling each agent to independently and cooperatively make decisions while contributing to a shared objective trajenpy_book,TANG2018132,disttask . Thompson Sampling (TS), a Bayesian decision-making framework increasingly used in search and rescue thompsonsearch,activethompson,distthompson , provides a natural basis for decentralized decision-making under uncertainty. TS maintains a probabilistic belief over unknown quantities via a prior probability distribution that is updated as observations are collected (posterior). Agents sample from this posterior to select actions with the highest sampled reward, naturally balancing exploration and exploitation. When each agent maintains its own posterior and shares observations with agents within communication range, this enables a scalable, parallel decision-making process without a central coordinator. We propose a decentralized, terrain-aware Thompson sampling framework for multi-drone SAR applications that incorporates key terrain characteristics such as linear features, elevation, and watershed structures to inform prior probability distributions based on established models of lost person behavior. Each UAV maintains a local belief over the search space and selects actions by sampling from this distribution over candidate actions. The proposed framework is evaluated in simulation using real-world SAR case data (YOSAR https://hub.arcgis.com/maps/620a96d2429249a187bdc4a7cc058cf5/about ), with the objective of locating a missing individual in large, remote environments. Overall, this work aims to improve the scalability, robustness, and efficiency of multi-drone SAR operations. In summary, our major contributions are: A decentralized terrain-aware Thompson sampling algorithm that leverages existing search and rescue models to assign informed priors for search of lost persons in large, remote environments. Object detection uncertainty based on fractional forest coverage. Experimental simulations analyzing the performance of the proposed method using real search and rescue cases. Related Works Decentralized methods for multi-agent search and rescue (SAR) offer several desirable properties, including robustness, scalability, flexibility, and reduced communication requirements~ MRTA . By eliminating reliance on a central coordinator, these approaches can effectively operate over large areas with large teams while avoiding single points of failure. A significant portion of work in multi-drone SAR has focused on coverage-based planning, which aims to ensure complete and exhaustive exploration of the search area~ spantree,rlcover,coopplan,linuav , typically generating trajectories that evenly distribute agents across the environment. Grøntved et al.~ grontved2022icar proposed a decentralized task allocation framework based on the consensus-based bundle algorithm (CBBA), enabling drones to coordinate trajectory assignments for coverage path planning. While such approaches achieve performance comparable to centralized methods, they primarily emphasize area coverage and do not explicitly optimize for rapid target discovery. In contrast, our approach prioritizes high-probability regions through terrain-informed priors, enabling faster target localization rather than uniform exploration. To improve search efficiency for search and rescue applications, probabilistic methods have been explored. Ewers et al. introduced predictive probability mapping techniques that model the likely behavior of missing persons using real-world SAR data ~ Ewers_2025,Ewers_2023 . These methods generate probability distributions over the search space to guide human responders; however, they do not incorporate active search by autonomous agents. Our method builds on these probabilistic priors but integrates them directly into multi-robot decision-making framework, enabling a team of autonomous agents to actively explore large remote areas efficiently. Active search strategies based on Thompson sampling have demonstrated strong performance in balancing exploration and exploitation when locating objects of interest under uncertainty~ ghods2021,nats . Bakshi et al. proposed the GUTS framework, which leverages uncertainty-aware Thompson sampling for multi-agent coordination ~ guts . Their method allocates tasks to heterogeneous agents by sampling from a sparse posterior distribution, enforced through a zero-mean prior. While effective in promoting exploration, this approach does not incorporate domain-specific priors, such as typical missing person behaviors, which can be critical in SAR applications. In contrast, our framework incorporates terrain-informed priors to prioritize high-probability regions in the search area while incorporating inter-agent repulsion to reduce redundant exploration for efficient and coordinated search in realistic SAR environments. title: Learning Low-Latency Action Verification for Frozen Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have made significant progress in general-purpose robotic manipulation. However, sampled action sequences can be ineffective, while evaluating alternatives with computationally expensive verifiers adds latency at each policy query. In this work, we propose HDH, a lightweight framework that uses hindsight from a frozen VLA's own deployments to improve action verification. The framework has three stages. First, we deploy the policy and collect its autonomous rollouts. We then train a compact action verifier to assign each action chunk a predicted task-success score. Finally, the frozen VLA generates action candidates, and the verifier selects the candidate with the highest score for execution. Across four LIBERO-10 tasks, HDH achieves an average success rate of 82.3\% and on three real-world manipulation tasks, HDH improves average success over the baseline policy by 22.6\%.
full_text: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have made significant progress in general-purpose robotic manipulation. However, sampled action sequences can be ineffective, while evaluating alternatives with computationally expensive verifiers adds latency at each policy query. In this work, we propose , a lightweight framework that uses hindsight from a frozen VLA's own deployments to improve action verification. The framework has three stages. First, we deploy the policy and collect its autonomous rollouts. We then train a compact action verifier to assign each action chunk a predicted task-success score. Finally, the frozen VLA generates action candidates, and the verifier selects the candidate with the highest score for execution. Across four LIBERO-10 tasks, achieves an average success rate of 82.3 and on three real-world manipulation tasks, improves average success over the baseline policy by 22.6 . Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved state-of-the-art performance on general-purpose manipulation, mapping visual observations and language instructions into robot actions~ rt2,openvla,pi0,pi05 . In deployment, however, the common practice is to sample a single action from the VLA, and execute it on the robot. Existing deployments, thus, do not exploit a fundamental property of generative policies, where the same observation and instruction can yield a full distribution of candidates with substantial variation in execution quality. To exploit this distributional generation capability, a simple test-time solution is to sample multiple candidate action chunks and select the candidate with the highest estimated quality. The question of how to select that action is, however, an open problem. Existing work has considered several heuristic selection strategies, including random selection and candidate evaluation using large vision-language models~ vgps,robomonkey,forewarn,rover . However, we believe that instead of relying on very large external models, the policy's own deployment experience can provide explicit supervision for this choice. We therefore investigate whether terminal success and failure provide sufficient supervision for candidate ranking and whether a compact verifier can achieve selection performance comparable to that of substantially larger verifiers. To address these questions, we introduce Hindsight Decision Model with History ( ), a lightweight verifier trained on terminal outcomes from autonomous policy rollouts, without expert comparisons, synthetic preferences, or predicted futures. Each training example consists of the current observation, the executed action prefix, and the episode's terminal outcome. To provide context about task progress, the verifier additionally receives recent observations and executed actions. At deployment, assigns a predicted eventual task-success score to each candidate sampled from the frozen VLA, and the robot executes the highest-scoring prefix. We evaluate in simulation and in the real-world in four dimensions. First, does a verifier trained only from terminal outcomes improve the closed-loop success of a frozen VLA? Second, does it produce candidate rankings that improve selection performance, beyond randomly selecting from the same set? Third, does history-conditioned scoring improve candidate discrimination by revealing task progress? Finally, how does such a compact verifier compare with verifiers based on large vision-language models on task success and inference latency? We find that hindsight supervision alone substantially improves closed-loop manipulation. Across four LIBERO-10 tasks, achieves an average success rate of 82.3 , outperforming both the frozen policy and random selection from the same candidate set. On three real-world manipulation tasks, it raises average success from 44.7 to 67.3 within a real-time control budget. Furthermore, history-conditioned scoring improves candidate ranking, and the compact verifier achieves selection performance comparable to that of much larger verifiers with substantially lower inference cost. Our contributions are thus threefold: Problem setting. We frame VLA deployment as real-time candidate selection supervised only by the frozen policy's own rollout outcomes. Verifier and selection. We introduce a lightweight, history-conditioned verifier for ranking native VLA candidates without updating the policy. Evaluation. We show in both simulation and real-world experiments that hindsight-supervised selection improves closed-loop manipulation with substantially lower inference cost than large verifiers. Related Work Generative Robot Policies and Test-Time Sampling Large-scale robot datasets have enabled policies that can generalize across diverse tasks, environments, and embodiments~ oxe,bridge,droid . Recent vision-language-action models further combine visual and language representations with expressive action generators~ rt2,openvla,octo,cogact . Diffusion Policy models multimodal action distributions through iterative denoising~ diffusionpolicy , while the family uses flow matching to generate continuous action chunks~ pi0,pi05 . Because these policies represent distributions over actions, repeated sampling can produce different behaviors for the same observation and instruction. Similar test-time sampling strategies have improved language-model inference by generating multiple candidate responses and selecting among them~ cobbe,monkeys,snell . In robot control, however, additional samples are useful only when the system can identify which candidate is most likely to advance the task. Our work keeps a fine-tuned policy fixed and learns to select among its sampled action chunks using outcomes from prior policy rollouts. Action Verification and Policy Steering Several approaches improve robot behavior by evaluating multiple candidate actions before execution. V-GPS reranks actions using a value function learned through offline reinforcement learning, without modifying the original policy~ vgps . IDQL similarly combines expressive diffusion behavior models with critic-based policy extraction~ idql . RoboMonkey generates synthetic action preferences from expert demonstrations and trains a vision-language model to select among policy candidates~ robomonkey , while RoVer and CoVer-VLA learn evaluators that assess candidate quality and consistency with the current observation and instruction~ rover,cover . Other methods explicitly estimate the consequences of an action: FOREWARN predicts future latent states with a world model and evaluates them using a vision-language model~ forewarn , whereas inference-time policy steering can incorporate human guidance into generative sampling~ itps . DSRL instead learns to steer the latent noise supplied to a frozen generative policy~ dsrl . These methods establish that inference-time evaluation can improve pre-trained policies, but differ in how candidates are produced, how supervision is obtained, and how much computation is required. In contrast, scores the frozen VLA's native action candidates with a compact verifier trained directly from terminal outcomes of its own rollouts. Learning from Policy Rollouts Policy rollouts can also improve behavior after initial policy training. Autonomous improvement systems collect additional interactions beyond expert demonstrations~ autonomous ; RECAP uses this experience to estimate action values and fine-tune the VLA toward more successful behavior~ recap . Policy-optimization methods adapt diffusion policies using reward feedback~ ddpo,dppo , while GRAPE, SafeVLA, and RL Token provide alternative interfaces for preference alignment, constrained adaptation, or compact actor--critic refinement~ grape,safevla,rltoken . These approaches primarily use policy rollouts to update or steer the policy. A related line of work uses execution data for failure detection rather than policy improvement. Sentinel monitors temporal action consistency and semantic task progress~ sentinel , and SAFE detects failures from internal VLA representations~ safe . Such monitors can predict when execution is likely to fail, but do not necessarily determine which alternative action should be executed. In contrast, uses terminal rollout outcomes to train a verifier that ranks the frozen policy's candidate actions and directly determines which action is executed. Learning Action Verification from Policy Rollouts sec:method An overview of our method is shown in Fig.~ fig:vsa-action-selection . First, we collect rollouts from a frozen VLA and use their terminal outcomes to supervise the recorded actions. We train a Hindsight Decision Model (HDM) to score candidate actions using the current observation and proprioceptive state. Our full model, the Hindsight Decision Model with History (HDH), additionally incorporates recent observations and executed actions. During closed-loop control, the frozen VLA samples multiple action candidates, and the verifier selects the candidate with the highest predicted task-success score. Action Chunk Success Estimation Let contain the camera observations and proprioception at decision , and let denote the instruction. A chunk is generated by sampling from the frozen policy using these inputs and flow-matching noise (the frozen policy's action-generation noise). The robot executes only , after which the system samples a new plan using the resulting observation. The verifier context is defined to include the current observation and, for the history-conditioned configuration, information from prior observations and executed actions recorded before decision . The quantity of interest is the probability of eventual task success after is executed and subsequent actions are generated by the baseline policy: where denotes terminal episode success. We approximate this quantity as , where is a failure logit. Thus, represents the predicted eventual task-success score learned from observed rollout outcomes. Learning from Terminal Outcomes Each retained example consists of a decision context, its actually executed prefix, and the terminal outcome of that episode. With failure label , the simulation objective is The same episode return is assigned to all retained queries from that episode. The dataset is partitioned at the episode level, rather than by randomly assigning queries from the same trajectory across splits. Under the current preprocessing convention, queries whose recorded executed length is below are excluded. This convention prevents supervision from being applied to action rows that were not executed, especially at terminal queries. Action Verifier Architecture The core attention-based scoring path is shown in Fig.~ fig:vsa-action-selection . In HDM, frozen backbone features are extracted from two image views (early-layer outputs of the backbone's SigLIP image pathway)~ siglip,pi05 . After region pooling, the representation contains an grid for each view, yielding 128 visual tokens of feature dimension 2048. These features are projected to width 128, with spatial and view embeddings. An eight-dimensional proprioceptive state is projected into one additional token. A separate verifier is used for each task, with a constant task token. The scorer input does not include language-prompt tokens, although the policy remains instruction-conditioned. The scorer input includes the executed prefix, typically from a length- predicted chunk. Action tokens are formed using a linear action projection and learned temporal embeddings. The architecture applies four-head action self-attention, followed by cross-attention from the action tokens to the observation tokens~ attention , with residual connections, normalization, and a feed-forward network. The failure logit is computed by mean pooling over the action tokens followed by an MLP of widths . We convert this logit into the task-success score for candidate selection. title: Scaling VLA Serving Under Robotic Execution Constraints
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation. In our production setting, hundreds of VLA-powered robots are already operating in real-world environments, creating an immediate need for efficient fleet serving. We present XInfer, a production-deployed VLA serving system designed to reduce the inference infrastructure cost of large-scale robotic deployments. XInfer jointly coordinates heterogeneous VLA computation with the evolving response requirements of robotic execution. By exploiting computational parallelism while managing interference, XInfer improves GPU efficiency while protecting time-critical robotic feedback. We evaluate XInfer across three VLA models using production-derived workloads, achieving 1.26-3.75 times the effective robot capacity (ERC) of state-of-the-art systems under physical-execution constraints. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/X-Square-Robot/xinfer.
full_text: \@captype figure Production parcel handling. A carton (top) and a soft parcel (bottom) are reoriented and pushed onto the conveyor. Each row follows the same parcel from left to right. fig:production-sequences ] Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models are bringing general-purpose robotic manipulation into logistics and manufacturing, where multiple robots can share GPU infrastructure to reduce serving cost. Figure~ fig:production-sequences shows representative parcel-handling operations from our production deployment. Recent inference engines improve the efficiency of individual VLA queries flashrt,embodiedcpp,flashvla . However, higher inference throughput does not necessarily translate into greater physical productivity, as delayed feedback can disrupt robotic execution. We use effective robot capacity (ERC), the maximum number of concurrent robots a GPU can serve while meeting specified latency and reliability requirements, as the serving objective. Shared VLA serving requires exploiting concurrency without compromising time-critical feedback. VLA requests traverse heterogeneous stages with distinct computational demands, creating opportunities to overlap independent work across robots. However, concurrent GPU execution also introduces interference: admitting a new stage may delay stages already in progress. Since these stages are non-preemptive, prioritizing urgent requests alone cannot prevent deadline violations caused by previously admitted work. Effective fleet serving therefore requires two coordinated decisions: which requests should be prioritized, and which stages can be admitted without jeopardizing the deadlines of current and forthcoming requests. The cost of this interference is not uniform across requests. Robots continue executing previously predicted actions while awaiting new responses, and the consequences of delayed feedback depend on their ongoing physical execution. As a result, requests with similar computational demands may have substantially different response-time requirements, which evolve throughout task execution. Moreover, response timing influences subsequent request arrivals, coupling scheduling decisions with future workload dynamics. Fleet serving must therefore balance concurrency against interference under changing per-request deadlines, rather than optimize inference throughput or average latency alone. Prior systems adapt action horizons and request priorities to execution context kairos,armory , coordinate serving for factory productivity rosa , or overlap encoding and diffusion in lockstep rounds robion . Yet effective fleet serving must reconcile the time-varying urgency of robotic feedback with the distinct computational demands of VLA stages. This calls for fine-grained scheduling that matches stage execution to available GPU capacity while controlling interference with time-critical requests. We present , a VLA serving system that couples asynchronous execution with fine-grained, execution-aware scheduling. Its dependency-driven engine exposes parallelism across requests and heterogeneous VLA stages, allowing computation to progress as dependencies resolve. The scheduler coordinates these execution opportunities with the time-varying urgency of robotic feedback by decoupling request prioritization from stage admission. At stage boundaries, it combines per-request response-time budgets, remaining computation, and predicted interference to admit ordinary work only when protected requests remain predicted feasible. It further accounts for anticipated earlier-deadline arrivals using request history, balancing immediate concurrency gains against future scheduling demands. We evaluate VLA-2B, , and Wall-OSS-0.5 using production-derived closed-loop workloads and controlled experiments. With error-free responses, achieves ERCs of 18 VLA-2B and 24 robots, versus 10 and 15 for vLLM-Omni; Robion serves 19 robots. In a separate VLA-2B evaluation with heterogeneous response-time budgets, all policies share the same backend and execution resources. Under the same real-time feasibility criterion, achieves an ERC of 18 robots, compared with 15 for Slack-Gate, 14 for FIFO, and 12 for EDF ( sec:eval ). Mechanism ablations isolate the effects of asynchronous execution and scheduling decisions. Our contributions are: An asynchronous VLA serving engine that exposes cross-request and cross-stage parallelism by advancing work as its dependencies complete. Execution-aware cross-stage scheduling that coordinates shared GPU computation by separating request priority from stage admission, accounting for interference on current and anticipated urgent requests. Production deployment and empirical evaluation. is deployed in production. We characterize closed-loop workloads, compare ERC across three VLA backends, and evaluate heterogeneous-budget scheduling and its mechanisms. Background sec:workload Heterogeneous VLA Computation sec:bg:vla Vision-language-action (VLA) models map observations and instructions to robot actions. We study models coupling a vision-language backbone to an action expert that generates continuous actions through flow matching or diffusion flowmatching,diffusionpolicy,pi05,walloss05,walloss . As Figure~ fig:bg (a) shows, the backbone computes conditioning keys and values once; the expert reuses them over denoising steps to generate an action chunk of future keyframes act . We distinguish three computational stages: ViT encodes visual observations, Prefill performs language-model computation after visual encoding, and Action generates actions through denoising. title: Fast Inference-Time Policy Refinement via Action-Affine World Models
summary: Imitation policies can perform complex manipulation, yet small execution errors can accumulate and cause failure. Refinement can correct these errors, but existing approaches often require additional on-policy learning or costly online planning. Our key insight is that a pretrained policy already supplies a useful nominal behavior: refinement can focus on predicting how small action corrections change its outcome. We therefore learn this local response in a form that is cheap to optimize. Our \textit{action-affine world model} (A\textsuperscript{2}WM) learns local action sensitivities offline from action-perturbed policy rollouts. Given interaction history and a policy proposal, it predicts task-relevant geometry as a nominal trajectory plus a linear response to corrections. It predicts the full planning horizon directly, avoiding the propagation of intermediate errors through recursive model evaluations. Quadratic penalties on predicted task errors and linear correction constraints then yield a cheap convex quadratic program (QP). Online refinement requires one model evaluation and one QP solve, while both policy and model weights remain frozen. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, our framework achieves the highest success rate among evaluated baselines, adding only 3.8 ms of mean refinement overhead per control step, excluding base-policy sampling.
full_text: Imitation policies can perform complex manipulation, yet small execution errors can accumulate and cause failure. Refinement can correct these errors, but existing approaches often require additional on-policy learning or costly online planning. Our key insight is that a pretrained policy already supplies a useful nominal behavior: refinement can focus on predicting how small action corrections change its outcome. We therefore learn this local response in a form that is cheap to optimize. Our action-affine world model (A WM) learns local action sensitivities offline from action-perturbed policy rollouts. Given interaction history and a policy proposal, it predicts task-relevant geometry as a nominal trajectory plus a linear response to corrections. It predicts the full planning horizon directly, avoiding the propagation of intermediate errors through recursive model evaluations. Quadratic penalties on predicted task errors and linear correction constraints then yield a cheap convex quadratic program (QP). Online refinement requires one model evaluation and one QP solve, while both policy and model weights remain frozen. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, our framework achieves the highest success rate among evaluated baselines, adding only 3.8 ms of mean refinement overhead per control step, excluding base-policy sampling. Introduction Behavior cloning (BC) enables robots to acquire manipulation skills from expert demonstrations. Diffusion policies represent multimodal action sequences and provide useful proposals for reaching, grasping, and assembly~ chi2023diffusion,ho2020ddpm . At deployment, however, execution errors can drive the robot outside the demonstrated state distribution, where further errors can accumulate and lead to failure~ ross2011dagger . Refining a pretrained policy through feedback offers a way to recover from such deviations without relearning the task. For precision-demanding manipulation, this refinement must anticipate the consequences of corrections while remaining fast enough to respond to new observations. The central challenge is to structure a world model so that it supports accurate prediction and cheap optimization of policy corrections. Related Work One route to policy refinement learns an additional correction policy through environment interaction. Residual policy learning follows this route, augmenting an existing controller with learned corrections~ silver2018residual,johannink2018residual . ResiP applies residual reinforcement learning (RL) to precise assembly~ ankile2024refinement , Policy Decorator refines pretrained imitation policies through online interactions~ yuan2024decorator , and KoRR conditions a residual policy on Koopman-predicted states~ gong2025korr . Another route selects or optimizes actions at inference time using fixed learned models. V-GPS ranks samples with an offline-learned value function~ nakamoto2024vgps , while LPB guides diffusion sampling toward the expert state distribution~ sun2025lpb . Within this second route, a learned world model can instead predict the consequences of proposed actions and support their optimization against a task objective. Our work follows this predictive refinement route. World models support policy learning in imagined trajectories~ hafner2023dreamer and online action optimization~ chua2018pets,hansen2024tdmpc2 , including manipulation planning with predicted images or visual features~ finn2017foresight,zhou2024dinowm . Sampling and gradient-based planning can require many model evaluations. Local linearization offers another approach through quadratic programming within nonlinear model predictive control (MPC), but forming the local problem still requires model derivatives~ diehl2005rti . More directly related to our setting, LaDi-WM and GPC use world models to refine diffusion-policy proposals~ huang2025ladi,qi2025gpc . GPC ranks sampled proposals or optimizes them through model gradients. Although the frozen policy supplies a useful starting point, refinement still incurs candidate-evaluation or repeated differentiation costs. This motivates learning the action-response coefficients needed for optimization directly, so that deployment requires neither candidate search nor differentiation of a nonlinear rollout. State representation matters because task objectives often depend on nonlinear geometry. For example, assembly requires controlling the relative pose between two parts, a nonlinear function of their individual poses. Making raw-state predictions affine in action corrections therefore does not automatically make the task cost quadratic. Learned control representations offer ways to address this issue. Embed to Control (E2C) learns locally linear latent dynamics~ watter2015e2c , while Koopman approaches augment the state with nonlinear functions, called observables, and approximate their evolution using fixed or learned dictionaries~ williams2015edmd,lusch2018deep . These representations have been used for robot control and diffusion-based imitation~ abraham2017koopman,bi2025koap . In lifted MPC, observables can explicitly include geometric quantities used by the objective~ korda2018koopman , allowing them to be predicted rather than recomputed nonlinearly inside the optimizer. Such augmentation does not guarantee exact linear dynamics; finite-dimensional linear representations remain structurally restrictive~ brunton2016invariant . Our setting calls for a local approximation of how task-relevant geometry responds to corrections around a policy proposal. A separate design choice is how to predict over the control horizon. MPC evaluates action sequences over multiple future steps~ mayne2000mpc . Recursive one-step prediction feeds intermediate predictions back into the model, propagating their errors through subsequent evaluations~ venkatraman2015multistep and requiring repeated model calls. Direct multi-step prediction learns the finite-horizon mapping instead, as studied in receding-horizon control~ terzi2018multistep and Koopman-based MPC~ wu2026multistep . Since refinement ultimately requires a trajectory over the full horizon, learning that trajectory directly removes this source of error propagation and reduces sequential online model evaluations. We therefore evaluate whether this structural advantage translates into improved prediction accuracy and lower computation time over the same control horizon. Proposed Approach We propose an action-affine world model (A WM) for fast inference-time refinement of frozen imitation policies, using measured robot and object states and specified geometric task objectives ( ). A useful policy proposal supplies the nominal behavior, allowing the model to focus on bounded corrections around that behavior. Our key insight is to learn trajectory predictions that are explicitly affine in these corrections, so that the corrections can be optimized efficiently. Conditioned on interaction history and the proposal, the model predicts a nominal trajectory and a matrix mapping the full correction sequence to changes in future task quantities. During each optimization, the predicted trajectory is the fixed nominal forecast plus the fixed response matrix multiplied by the correction sequence. We retain measured states, include task-relevant geometry in the prediction space, and append learned nonlinear features to represent context-dependent behavior. We train A WM offline on action-perturbed rollouts of the frozen policy, supervising the full predicted trajectory. At each control step, the trained model generates a new nominal forecast and response matrix from the current context, instead of computing the response through online differentiation. All horizon steps are predicted directly in one model evaluation, without feeding intermediate predictions back into the model. This aligns supervision with the controller's prediction horizon. Quadratic penalties on the predicted task errors and linear correction constraints define a convex quadratic program (QP). Each control update requires one model evaluation followed by a QP solve. The controller executes the first corrected action and replans from new observations, with both policy and model weights frozen. Together, the action-affine structure and direct horizon prediction make repeated feedback correction cheap without candidate search or world-model differentiation. Contributions Our contributions are: Action-affine world modeling. We learn a local action-response model conditioned on interaction history and a frozen policy's proposal. By predicting task-relevant geometry explicitly, the model makes the predicted task errors affine in action corrections. Direct multi-step action-response prediction. We formulate direct finite-horizon action-response prediction, producing the affine response in one model evaluation without feeding intermediate predictions back into the model. We assess its accuracy and computational cost against recursive alternatives that retain QP-compatible planning. Fast closed-loop policy refinement. We integrate the predictor with constrained QP-based correction and evaluate the complete framework on four simulated manipulation tasks, demonstrating improved task-averaged success with millisecond-scale refinement overhead and no on-policy residual-policy training. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, our framework improves task-averaged success from 27.2 for the frozen policies to 59.5 ( ). It exceeds the evaluated GPC-based refiners in task-averaged success while requiring only 3.4--4.0\,ms of refinement overhead per control step ( ). A frozen policy provides nominal actions ; a correction gives the executed command , where adds position corrections and composes rotation corrections. Over a horizon of steps, uppercase letters denote stacked vectors: , , and . The history contains states and intervening executed actions. Given a general one-step world model with parameters , refinement takes the receding-horizon MPC form~ mayne2000mpc : Here hats denote predictions, is the stage cost, and collects stage constraints. The measured history supplies model context. The model, cost, and constraints can all be nonlinear. Below, denotes the summed cost and stacks the stage constraints. Task-relevant state lifting. Task errors and constraints often involve nonlinear geometry, such as an object's pose relative to its assembly target. Following the use of observables to express control objectives in lifted coordinates~ korda2018koopman , we include these quantities among the predicted states instead of recomputing them inside the optimizer. Let retain the raw state and the required geometric quantities, and let stack them over the horizon. For squared task errors and constraints with affine dependence on corrections, suitable observables give Here stacks task targets, weights task errors, and encode affine inequalities. The correction regularizer is , with and linear coefficient , omitting constant terms. These quantities are set from the current state and task stage and held fixed during each solve. Nonlinear geometry is now absorbed into the observable dynamics. Action-affine world model. We augment the physical observables with a learned nonlinear dictionary and condition prediction coefficients on history and proposal (Sec.~ sec:world-model ). The goal is a local affine approximation of the response to action corrections, not globally linear physical dynamics. title: RSLiveBench-UAV: A Continually Evolving Vision-Language Benchmark for Aerial Spatial Intelligence
summary: Aerial spatial intelligence (ASI) requires models to understand objects and spatial relationships across changing viewpoints and scales. Evaluating these abilities as models evolve calls for fresh physical observations, yet producing new aerial spatial questions requires repeatedly establishing entity identities, geometric references, and cross-view correspondences. We introduce \textbf{RSLiveBench-UAV}, a continually evolving vision-language benchmark driven by recurring acquisition of real UAV imagery. Its update protocol admits images captured after the preceding release and delays answer disclosure. An entity-centered production workflow uses geometry-assisted association to link repeated observations of physical vehicles, reuse human-verified attributes, and combine them with view-specific annotations and spatial references for traceable question generation. All tasks use deterministic scoring without model judges. We evaluate 30 general-purpose, remote-sensing, and embodied models on 35,491 question records from ten scenes, covering 17 tasks across 2D perception, 3D perception, cross-view perception, and reasoning. All 18 tested embodied models outperform the three selected remote-sensing comparators in Overall, although the strongest embodied model scores 43.29 versus 59.88 for GPT-6-Astra. Fine-grained vehicle recognition remains challenging, and performance varies across heights and camera pitches. Retrospective scene-group comparisons and rolling-window replay characterize score-pattern consistency under scene renewal. RSLiveBench-UAV connects fresh physical observations, entity-centered answer production, and systematic model evaluation to support continual assessment of ASI. Benchmark will release at https://rslivebench.space
full_text: Aerial spatial intelligence (ASI) requires models to understand objects and spatial relationships across changing viewpoints and scales. Evaluating these abilities as models evolve calls for fresh physical observations, yet producing new aerial spatial questions requires repeatedly establishing entity identities, geometric references, and cross-view correspondences. We introduce RSLiveBench-UAV, a continually evolving vision-language benchmark driven by recurring acquisition of real UAV imagery. Its update protocol admits images captured after the preceding release and delays answer disclosure. An entity-centered production workflow uses geometry-assisted association to link repeated observations of physical vehicles, reuse human-verified attributes, and combine them with view-specific annotations and spatial references for traceable question generation. All tasks use deterministic scoring without model judges. We evaluate 30 general-purpose, remote-sensing, and embodied models on 35,491 question records from ten scenes, covering 17 tasks across 2D perception, 3D perception, cross-view perception, and reasoning. All 18 tested embodied models outperform the three selected remote-sensing comparators in Overall, although the strongest embodied model scores 43.29 versus 59.88 for GPT-6-Astra. Fine-grained vehicle recognition remains challenging, and performance varies across heights and camera pitches. Retrospective scene-group comparisons and rolling-window replay characterize score-pattern consistency under scene renewal. RSLiveBench-UAV connects fresh physical observations, entity-centered answer production, and systematic model evaluation to support continual assessment of ASI. Benchmark will release at https://rslivebench.space Introduction sec:introduction Spatial intelligence is the ability to perceive, represent, and reason about objects, their physical properties, and their relationships in space. For embodied models, these capabilities support the spatial understanding needed for navigation and interaction. Recent benchmarks have advanced their evaluation through visual perception, spatial reasoning, and multi-image understanding~ fu2024blink,yang2025thinking,yang2026mmsibench . A central question is how well this spatial understanding extends to observation conditions that differ substantially in viewpoint and scale. Aerial spatial intelligence (ASI) provides an important setting for examining this question. Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) observe the world across varying altitudes and camera orientations, which change object scale, visible surfaces, occlusion, and projected spatial relationships. Models must distinguish objects from overhead views, estimate physical quantities from perspective-dependent evidence, associate instances across images, and reason between camera-centered and object-centered reference frames. Keeping this evaluation current as models evolve requires a continuing supply of fresh physical observations and the spatial references needed to assess them. This introduces two challenges. First, producing new spatial questions requires recurring field acquisition and renewed verification of object identities, physical attributes, camera geometry, and cross-view correspondences. Second, replacing scenes changes the composition and difficulty of the evaluation set. Sustainable ASI evaluation therefore requires both a reusable answer-production workflow and an explicit renewal protocol supported by consistency analysis. We introduce RSLiveBench-UAV, a continually evolving vision-language benchmark driven by recurring field acquisition of real UAV imagery, with an inventory of 102 collected scenes. Focusing initially on vehicles, our entity-centered answer-production workflow uses geometry-assisted association to link observations of the same vehicle within each capture batch and reuses verified make/model attributes to provide specification-based references across views. Templates combine entity records, view-specific annotations, and spatial references to generate traceable answers under human review. The live protocol replaces one scene monthly within a four-scene window, admitting only images captured after the preceding leaderboard release. A capture-ordered retrospective replay assesses task--model score-pattern consistency under scene renewal. As shown in Figure fig:tasks , using ten scenes from this inventory, we construct Start-10 full, comprising 35,491 question records across 17 tasks spanning 2D perception, 3D perception, cross-view perception, and reasoning. A 928-question minival supports task examples and reasoning diagnostics. We evaluate 30 general-purpose, remote-sensing, and embodied models. All 18 tested embodied models outperform the three selected remote-sensing comparators in Overall; the strongest embodied model scores 43.29, compared with 59.88 for GPT-6-Astra. Fine-grained vehicle recognition remains challenging, and performance varies across observation heights and pitches. Our contributions are threefold: Fresh physical observations for continual aerial evaluation. We introduce a live benchmark driven by recurring acquisition of real UAV imagery, with capture-time admission, scene-wise renewal, delayed answer disclosure, and versioned scoring. Entity-centered spatial answer production. We develop a geometry-assisted workflow that associates repeated observations with physical vehicles, reuses human-verified attributes, and preserves answer provenance for objectively scored spatial questions. Systematic ASI evaluation across model families. We evaluate 30 general-purpose, remote-sensing, and embodied models across 17 tasks, characterizing their profiles, fine-grained recognition difficulties, and performance under varying aerial observation conditions. Related Work sec:related_work Live Benchmarks Live benchmarks refresh evaluation data to mitigate test-set contamination and maintain meaningful comparisons as models evolve. LiveBench and LiveCodeBench periodically introduce questions with objectively verifiable answers from recent information sources and programming contests, respectively~ white2025livebench,jain2025livecodebench . LiveXiv and MMBench-Live extend continual evaluation to scientific documents and multimodal understanding through recurring acquisition and verifiable question generation~ shabtay2025livexiv,mmbench_live . Extending this paradigm to ASI requires physically acquiring new observations and reconstructing and verifying geometric references and cross-view identities. RSLiveBench-UAV addresses these challenges through recurring UAV acquisition, geometry-assisted entity association, human-verified spatial references, and versioned evaluation. Aerial Spatial Intelligence ASI encompasses object semantics, physical properties, and spatial relationships from aerial viewpoints. General-purpose benchmarks such as BLINK, VSI-Bench, and MMSI-Bench evaluate visual perception, spatial reasoning, and multi-image understanding~ fu2024blink,yang2025thinking,yang2026mmsibench . Complementary work on embodied world models connects environmental prediction with action planning: DAWN jointly refines world and action predictions, while RISE adaptively allocates future rollout computation for autonomous driving~ lu2026dawn,lu2026rise . In aerial settings, SpatialSky-Bench, SpatialUAV, and Geo3DVQA evaluate UAV scene understanding, aerial spatial reasoning, and geospatial perception~ zhang2025skyready,zhang2026spatialuav,tsujimoto2026geo3dvqa . AVI-Math and AirSpatialBot further explore vehicle-centered mathematical reasoning and fine-grained spatial attributes in aerial imagery~ zhou2025avimath,zhou2025airspatialbot . These efforts advance spatial evaluation and embodied modeling. RSLiveBench-UAV extends this work with live ASI evaluation driven by continuously acquired UAV observations. Remote-Sensing Vision-Language Benchmarks Remote-sensing vision-language benchmarks have expanded in task diversity, grounding, data quality, and evaluation coverage~ zhou2026datadriven . RSVQA and RSVG establish visual question answering and referring-expression grounding~ lobry2020rsvqa,zhan2023rsvg , while VRSBench and XLRS-Bench broaden coverage to comprehensive image understanding, grounding, and extremely high-resolution imagery~ li2024vrsbench,wang2025xlrsbench . CHOICE provides hierarchical capability evaluation, whereas ChatEarthBench emphasizes independently collected Earth-observation imagery~ an2025choice,yuan2026chatearthbench . Many remote-sensing benchmarks use static test sets. RSLiveBench-UAV complements them with newly captured aerial imagery and delayed answer disclosure, supporting recurring evaluation while mitigating contamination risk. RSLiveBench-UAV sec:method RSLiveBench-UAV connects scene renewal, entity-centered ground-truth production, and model evaluation. Scenes define the update unit, physical vehicle instances organize reusable attributes, and questions provide the inputs and references for evaluation. Acquisition-Constrained Live Protocol sec:live_protocol To tie benchmark renewal to fresh UAV observations, we define a scene as a timestamped field-acquisition batch. Building on continual evaluation~ white2025livebench , we maintain a four-scene first-in, first-out (FIFO) window. Let index benchmark versions, with denoting the release time of version and its active scene roster, where . After initialization, each update admits a newly acquired scene and retires the earliest-admitted active scene : Here, is the capture time of image , and is the incoming image set. Each monthly update retains three scenes and replaces one; four consecutive replacements retire the entire initial roster. This 25 renewal rate applies to scenes, while question counts and within-component score contributions may vary by scene. Before release , questions and references must be reviewed, and every declared task component must be covered. Each release records its scene roster, capture dates, component counts, answer/scorer versions, and model runs, allowing results to be traced to their scene composition and scoring configuration. Full answers for a scene remain confidential until retirement and expiry of the minimum embargo from first admission: Here, , , and denote first admission, retirement, and full-answer disclosure, respectively. The minimum embargo is four calendar months. Across the 102 collected scenes, acquiring UAV imagery took an average of 14.48 minutes per scene, with the acquisition-time distribution reported in Appendix~ app:capture_time . These records provide an empirical estimate of the acquisition effort required to add a new scene and support the feasibility of recurring field acquisition for monthly benchmark renewal. Geometry-Assisted Ground-Truth Production sec:production Continual benchmark renewal requires efficient ground-truth production. Historical image-by-image annotation averaged 136.31 minutes per scene, whereas the mean recorded with our entity-centered workflow was 29.52 minutes per active scene--month in September 2026, 78.3 below the historical mean (Table~ tab:production_cost ). The workflow reuses verified entity attributes across views while preserving observation-specific references and answer provenance. Figure~ fig:pipeline summarizes collection, association, attribute curation, and question generation. Spatial mapping. Each batch contains multi-height, multi-view images with timestamps, GPS coordinates, height/pitch metadata, and field-verification records. Oriented bounding box (OBB) detection~ zhou2022mmrotate and COLMAP-based structure-from-motion (SfM) provide vehicle observations and sparse scene geometry. We align the reconstruction to a metric east--north--up (ENU) frame through a similarity transform based on XMP geolocation and relative altitude. title: Decide Before You Move: Diffusion-Generated Search Reference for Zero-Shot Open-Vocabulary Object Navigation in Semi-Static Environments
summary: Open-world navigation requires a robot to locate a user-specified target in an indoor scene under open-vocabulary queries. Realistic indoor environments are semi-static: walls and furniture largely persist while smaller objects move, relocate, or vanish between visits. Prior-map systems answer queries from object poses recorded at reconstruction time, which expire as soon as objects move, whereas online methods re-derive where to look from current observations every few steps, often through expensive calls to a vision--language model. Assuming that walls and large furniture do not move, we keep their map to plan paths, but use a target--furniture co-occurrence prior to decide where to search. We present PreNav, an ObjectNav framework on semi-static environments. Rather than invoking a vision-language model at each step, PreNav generates a single global search reference before the robot moves: an LLM converts target--furniture co-occurrence into a spatial prior, a conditional diffusion model turns that prior and the persistent structure into an ordered centerline with a band around it, and the robot approaches the target once it is detected online. Experiments on a Gibson ObjectNav benchmark show that PreNav outperforms a strong online baseline under matched structural priors, using a generator trained only on room-level ScanNet++ scenes and applied to floor-level Gibson without fine-tuning. Real-world experiments under object relocation and open-vocabulary queries further validate the approach.
full_text: Open-world navigation requires a robot to locate a user-specified target in an indoor scene under open-vocabulary queries. Realistic indoor environments are semi-static: walls and furniture largely persist while smaller objects move, relocate, or vanish between visits. Prior-map systems answer queries from object poses recorded at reconstruction time, which expire as soon as objects move, whereas online methods re-derive where to look from current observations every few steps, often through expensive calls to a vision--language model. Assuming that walls and large furniture do not move, we keep their map to plan paths, but use a target--furniture co-occurrence prior to decide where to search. We present , an ObjectNav framework on semi-static environments. Rather than invoking a vision-language model at each step, generates a single global search reference before the robot moves: an LLM converts target--furniture co-occurrence into a spatial prior, a conditional diffusion model turns that prior and the persistent structure into an ordered centerline with a band around it, and the robot approaches the target once it is detected online. Experiments on a Gibson ObjectNav benchmark show that outperforms a strong online baseline under matched structural priors, using a generator trained only on room-level ScanNet++ scenes and applied to floor-level Gibson without fine-tuning. Real-world experiments under object relocation and open-vocabulary queries further validate the approach. Introduction Object navigation requires a robot to move through an indoor environment and find a target specified only by a user query~ batra2020objectnav,anderson2018evaluation . Existing methods keep either too much of the building or too little. Prior-map systems answer queries from dense object-level maps~ werby2024hovsg,gu2023conceptgraphs , whose object poses expire as soon as objects move. Map-free methods use no prior knowledge of the building and decide where to look online, re-deriving candidate regions from current observations every few steps, often through expensive calls to a vision--language model~ yokoyama2024vlfm,padilla2026openfrontier . Real buildings are semi-static: walls and large furniture such as wardrobes and tables barely move, whereas objects such as keys and cups change position between visits. Between these extremes, two lines of work handle the semi-static building differently. One follows what changes: systems for changing scenes keep a semantic map of objects and update it online as they move, adding and removing voxels~ liu2024dynamem or tracking whether each object instance is still in place~ bogenberger2026glasses , yet their search still runs over the whole maintained map, movable objects included. The other builds on what persists: osmAG~ feng2023osmag , a lightweight, text-based hierarchical map of areas such as rooms and corridors, supports localization~ xie2024agloc and LLM-based map understanding and navigation~ xie2024osmagcomp,xie2025copilot even when incomplete, and osmAG-LLM~ xie2026osmag uses it to reliably identify the room that holds a moved or never-mapped target. Within that room, however, the robot can only check candidate locations recorded during mapping, namely viewpoints along the mapping trajectory and past object positions, which need not cover where the target now lies. With the search already narrowed to a room, and tracking every object as it moves requiring continual map maintenance, we ask whether the part of the room that barely changes, its walls and large furniture, suffices to plan where to look, and in what order, before the robot moves. We argue that it does. Real buildings are semi-static: walls and large furniture persist across missions, while movable objects, including the target, may change location. Therefore, instead of continually updating object locations, or treating the environment as a completely unknown scene, we treat only the objects as unknown and rely on the layout of walls and furniture to infer where the target may be. Thus, even if the target has moved, we do not rely on previously recorded target locations. Instead, we use semantic scores between the target and furniture to guide the search: a cup may be near a dining table, whereas a television is unlikely to be near a toilet. We propose , which uses this prior knowledge of a scene to pre-plan an informed object search for a given query whenever a query arrives. An LLM scores target--furniture co-occurrence once, offline, and the scores are projected onto the mapped furniture as a spatial prior. A conditional diffusion model then turns this prior, the wall raster, and the start pose into what we call the search reference: a globally planned reference path that optimizes the order of where to search in a floor or room. The reference is thus both an order to follow and a region to sweep. Trained on references from a solver for the traveling salesman problem (TSP), the generator produces one in about a second rather than tens of seconds. The robot then follows the reference, detects the target online, and approaches it, without repeated foundation-model calls or query-conditioned global replanning. We evaluate on an expanded Gibson xia2018gibson ObjectNav benchmark, asking three questions: whether it outperforms online baselines under matched structural priors; how generation efficiency trades against navigation quality when compared with its TSP teacher; and whether it transfers to real-world robots under open-vocabulary queries. As a summary, our main contributions are: We propose , an ObjectNav framework for semi-static environments: it guides online search through a search reference that is globally optimized with respect to the known room layout and semantic areas. We introduce an open-vocabulary interface that projects any user query onto the persistent furniture through LLM-generated co-occurrence scores between the query and each furniture category. As the generator's only query-dependent input, these scores let a conditional diffusion model plan a search reference for any query without retraining. We demonstrate zero-shot transfer from room-level ScanNet++ training to floor-level Gibson scenes, without fine-tuning the generator on Gibson. On the six-category benchmark, our method outperforms SGM under matched structural priors and achieves navigation performance comparable to its TSP teacher with an order of magnitude less generation time. We further demonstrate deployment on a real mobile robot with open-vocabulary queries. Related Work Navigation with Prior Maps Prior-map systems organize a scanned building into persistent semantic representations and answer queries directly from this memory, without re-exploring. HOV-SG~ werby2024hovsg and ConceptGraphs~ gu2023conceptgraphs structure open-vocabulary 3D features into hierarchical scene graphs that support language queries over a pre-scanned building, and osmAG-LLM~ xie2026osmag tolerates such changes by searching online, but still draws its candidates from objects and views recorded during mapping. Their answers, however, depend on object poses recorded at reconstruction time---once objects move, the memory returns expired answers. likewise assumes a familiar building, but deliberately retains only walls and large-furniture regions; the current pose of the queried object is never provided. Navigation without Prior Maps Knowledge about the scene has to come from somewhere when no prior is given. Existing methods fall into three families. The first family decides on an online semantic map: SemExp~ chaplot2020semexp predicts exploration goals on the map it builds, PONI~ ramakrishnan2022poni learns potential functions that prioritize promising regions, and SGM~ zhang2024sgm extends this map into unseen regions with a self-supervised generative model, selecting goals on the completed map. The second family explores through frontier scoring: CoWs~ gadre2023cows scores frontiers with CLIP, VLFM~ yokoyama2024vlfm builds a vision--language value map, and OpenFrontier~ padilla2026openfrontier treats visually grounded frontiers as sparse semantic anchors. The third family follows route instructions end-to-end: recent VLN methods such as NaVILA~ cheng2025navila fine-tune a vision--language model to map natural-language route descriptions and RGB observations to navigation actions. The first two families require no persistent map, since the scene is entirely unknown when the task starts. They build a temporary map from observations and use the goal's semantics to decide the next action, and every few steps the robot re-decides through semantic reasoning, sometimes through expensive calls to a vision--language model. The third family builds no map; instead, each instruction already implies the scene it describes. The instruction itself is the prior---scene-specific, human-given. Of these, only the first family decides on a top-down semantic map into which known walls and furniture can be written before the episode starts; we therefore compare against its most recent member, SGM, under the same priors. Semi-Static Environments DynaMem~ liu2024dynamem adds and removes voxels as objects move, treating stable and movable parts of the scene alike. OpenIN~ wang2025openin and Where Did I Leave My Glasses?~ bogenberger2026glasses separate the two, through static carriers or per-instance stationarity, and let an LLM rank where to search. All three, however, maintain a map that includes the movable objects and choose their next goal during navigation. keeps only walls and furniture, which need no maintenance, and plans the whole search before the robot moves. Diffusion Models for Planning Diffusion models learn to generate outputs from a training distribution by iterative denoising~ ho2020ddpm . In robot planning they serve at three levels: at the trajectory level, Diffuser~ janner2022diffuser generates long-horizon state--action sequences; at the policy level, NoMaD~ sridhar2024nomad navigates on topological memory with a single diffusion policy; and at the level of combinatorial solving, TSPDiffuser~ yonetani2025tspdiffuser casts TSP as a denoising process over solution space, showing that diffusion can act as a learned sampler for combinatorial path planning. The last is closest to ours: the training labels likewise come from a combinatorial solver---TSP, the traveling salesman problem with neighborhoods, supplies the ground-truth path points---and we additionally learn a width at every path point, forming a band that marks where the target is likely to appear. This output is trained on room-level scenes, infers on floor-level scenes, and is validated on a real robot, with zero-shot and open-vocabulary queries supported by construction. Methodology sec:method separates search-reference generation from online perception. When a query comes, the search reference is generated in two steps. First, the furniture-conditioned search prior (Sec.~ sec:prior ) computes a spatial prior that encodes where the target is likely to be found relative to known furniture. Second, the diffusion-based global search generator (Sec.~ sec:diffusion ) takes this prior, the persistent wall raster, and the start pose as inputs and generates a single search reference. The robot follows this reference, detects the target online, and then approaches it; subsequent execution requires neither repeated high-level foundation-model calls nor query-conditioned global replanning. Furniture-Conditioned Search Prior sec:prior In a semi-static environment, the target's current location is unknown, but its co-occurrence with persistent furniture provides a stable search prior. title: PolyMorphWBC: Whole-Body Control from End-Effector Trajectories for Quadrupedal Mobile Manipulation across Arm Morphologies with Extended Reach
summary: Quadrupedal mobile manipulators can extend their manipulation workspace by coordinating the mounted arm with the mobile base. At the task level, short-horizon end-effector (EE) trajectories provide an interface for specifying the desired manipulation motion without prescribing how it should be realized by the arm and base. However, executing such trajectories remains challenging because the controller must determine when and how the base should move, and this decision depends on the mounted-arm morphology. We therefore present PolyMorphWBC, a hierarchical controller that takes an EE trajectory as the sole task-level motion command and generates coordinated arm--base motions across four families of 6-DoF mounted arms, with extended-reach trajectories beyond the initial fixed-base reach. Within PolyMorphWBC, a trajectory-conditioned coordinator determines the base motion from previewed EE targets, while arm-specific Inverse Kinematics (IK) tracks the current target, and a frozen locomotion backend executes the resulting motion. Cross-arm reuse is enabled by a Unified Robot Description Format (URDF)-derived morphology conditioning, together with online residual-wrench feedback. We train PolyMorphWBC on procedurally generated arms and structured trajectories within and beyond fixed-base reach. In IsaacLab, it achieves 93.95% completion with 2.30cm position error and 4.81° orientation error on held-out trajectories and arm morphologies. In MuJoCo evaluation against UMI-on-Legs, PolyMorphWBC reduces EE position error by 69--72% and orientation error by 91--97% across four within- and extended-reach trajectories. On a physical Go2--ARX5 system, we demonstrate language-conditioned extended-reach pick-and-place using EE trajectories from pi_0 without vision-language-action (VLA)-generated base commands.

title: Test-Time Selective Adaptation for Cross-Modal UAV Object Tracking with Token Shift
summary: Cross-modal unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) object tracking faces modality-induced appearance discrepancies and abrupt target-position shifts that can arise from modality switching, UAV motion, and inter-sensor offsets. Although existing methods model modality and spatial variations, they primarily rely on offline representation learning and offer limited localization-oriented adaptation during testing. To address these challenges, we propose Test-Time Selective Adaptation with Token Shift (TSAT), which derives spatial and temporal adaptation signals from unlabeled test sequences for online optimization. Specifically, we design a controllable token shift auxiliary task, which imposes explicit spatial correspondence between predefined token translations and resultant localization offsets, generating stable annotation-free spatial adaptation signals. Furthermore, we introduce a temporal backward prediction auxiliary task to exploit frame-wise temporal dependencies, effectively mitigating cumulative localization errors in continuous tracking. To suppress interference from unreliable tracking samples, we develop a reliability-aware update gating strategy to screen valid adaptation signals and stabilize online parameter updates. Experiments on CM-UOT demonstrate that TSAT achieves state-of-the-art performance against existing test-time adaptation methods, exhibiting superior robustness under frequent modality switching and severe spatial displacement. Experiments across tracking frameworks and datasets further validate the effectiveness and generalization capability of TSAT.
