Although existing methods model modality and spatial variations, they primarily rely on offline representation learning and offer limited localization-oriented adaptation during testing. To address these challenges, we propose Test-Time Selective Adaptation with Token Shift (TSAT), which derives spatial and temporal adaptation signals from unlabeled test sequences for online optimization. Specifically, we design a controllable token shift auxiliary task, which imposes explicit spatial correspondence between predefined token translations and resultant localization offsets, generating stable annotation-free spatial adaptation signals. Furthermore, we introduce a temporal backward prediction auxiliary task to exploit frame-wise temporal dependencies, effectively mitigating cumulative localization errors in continuous tracking. To suppress interference from unreliable tracking samples, we develop a reliability-aware update gating strategy to screen valid adaptation signals and stabilize online parameter updates. Experiments on CM-UOT demonstrate that TSAT achieves state-of-the-art performance against existing test-time adaptation methods, exhibiting superior robustness under frequent modality switching and severe spatial displacement. Experiments across tracking frameworks and datasets further validate the effectiveness and generalization capability of TSAT. Cross-modal object tracking, unmanned aerial vehicles, test-time adaptation, token shift. Introduction Visual object tracking estimates a target's state in subsequent frames from its initial location in the first frame~ bertinetto2016siamfc, danelljan2019atom,bhat2019dimp,yan2021stark . Deployed on UAV platforms, it benefits from flexible mobility, adjustable aerial viewpoints, and wide-area coverage, supporting applications such as intelligent surveillance, emergency rescue, low-altitude aerial inspection, and UAV reconnaissance. However, single-modal UAV tracking is limited by modality-specific weaknesses. Visible images provide rich appearance details but are sensitive to low illumination, whereas thermal infrared images are less affected by illumination changes but lack fine-grained texture information. Multimodal UAV tracking exploits their complementarity to improve robustness in complex environments~ li2019rgbtbenchmark,zhang2022vtuav , but continuous acquisition and joint processing increase communication, computation, and power costs. To balance adaptability and efficiency, cross-modal UAV object tracking processes one modality at a time and switches between visible and thermal infrared as needed, offering a practical solution for resource-constrained UAV platforms~ xiao2026sarla . However, modality switching also poses two major challenges for cross-modal UAV object tracking. On the one hand, differences in imaging mechanisms and appearance distributions across modalities can lead to inconsistent feature representations during switching. On the other hand, when compounded by UAV viewpoint movement, target scale variations, and inter-sensor offsets, modality switching can further exacerbate target-position shifts between frames, making accurate localization more difficult and increasing the risk of target drift and tracking failure. Existing methods mitigate modality discrepancies through multimodal feature fusion~ xiao2022apfnet, liu2024challenge , cross-modal feature interaction~ hui2023tbsi, zhu2023vipt,cao2024bat,hou2024sdstrack , modality-adaptive representation learning, knowledge distillation, and prototype learning~ li2022crossmodal, liu2024modalityfusion,li2024multiteacher,liu2025prototype . Recent cross-modal UAV object tracking research further models modality and spatial state variations to improve robustness in dynamic aerial scenarios~ xiao2026sarla . Despite these advances, current methods remain primarily focused on offline representation learning and provide limited online correction when modality switching or target-position shifts cause localization errors. Consequently, localization errors in individual frames may propagate and accumulate through subsequent search-region initialization, eventually causing tracking drift.As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:tracking_motivation , SARLA may still localize the target at the modality-switch frame, but its localization can deteriorate during subsequent tracking as errors propagate and accumulate. These observations motivate the introduction of reliable spatial and temporal constraints during testing to stabilize localization responses and improve tracking performance after modality switching. Test-time adaptation has emerged as an effective solution to address domain distribution shift by online fine-tuning with unlabeled test data~ sun2020ttt,wang2021tent,wang2022cotta . Different from static offline models, TTA enables continuous model adaptation to dynamic test environments, which naturally matches the iterative and time-varying characteristics of cross-modal UAV object tracking. Nevertheless, existing TTA paradigms have inherent limitations for tracking tasks. Most TTA methods are designed for classification and segmentation, optimizing models via entropy minimization, confidence estimation or parameter recovery~ wang2021tent,niu2022eata,niu2023sar,shao2025pura . They prioritize prediction certainty and parameter stability but ignore the spatial-temporal structural properties of tracking responses, failing to model localization offset correlations and suppress cumulative tracking errors. To address the above gaps, we propose Test-Time Selective Adaptation with Token Shift (TSAT), a TTA framework for cross-modal UAV object tracking. Specifically, TSAT constructs two complementary self-supervised auxiliary tasks, Token Shift Equivariance (TSE) and Temporal Backward Prediction (TBP), from unlabeled test sequences to provide reliable spatial and temporal signals for online adaptation. First, TSE establishes verifiable spatial correspondence between controllable token translations and response offsets, thereby enhancing localization stability under spatial perturbations. Second, TBP uses adjacent-frame backward prediction to exploit temporal dependencies and provide a temporal constraint for online adaptation. Third, we propose Reliability-aware Update Gating (RUG), which hierarchically filters noisy samples and abnormal adaptation signals, reducing the risk of unreliable online updates amplifying localization errors during continuous tracking. As shown in Fig.~ fig:tse_motivation , the actual response becomes more closely aligned with the expected response as the adaptation loss decreases, indicating more accurate spatial adaptation. Extensive experiments on CM-UOT~ xiao2026sarla validate that TSAT achieves consistent performance gains over state-of-the-art trackers and TTA methods, especially under modality switching and large spatial displacement conditions. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: We propose Test-Time Selective Adaptation with Token Shift (TSAT), which constructs spatial and temporal self-supervised auxiliary tasks from unlabeled test sequences to address spatial response shifts and cumulative localization errors in cross-modal UAV object tracking. We design Token Shift Equivariance (TSE) as a spatial auxiliary task that derives annotation-free spatial supervision from the correspondence between controllable token shifts and localization response offsets. We further introduce a temporal constraint through the temporal auxiliary task Temporal Backward Prediction (TBP), which exploits backward prediction across adjacent frames to complement the spatial supervision and reduce error propagation. We develop Reliability-aware Update Gating (RUG), which filters unreliable samples and abnormal adaptation signals at multiple levels, enabling stable and effective online adaptation. Evaluations across datasets and tracking frameworks validate the effectiveness and generalization capability of TSAT. The results demonstrate performance gains over the corresponding baselines in different tracking settings, together with improved localization robustness under modality switching and spatial displacement. Related Work Cross-modal Object Tracking Cross-modal object tracking exploits complementary information from different imaging modalities to improve tracking robustness in challenging scenarios, with the key objective of mitigating target-representation discrepancies caused by modality switching. Li et al.~ li2022crossmodal constructed an RGB/NIR cross-modal tracking benchmark and proposed a modality-aware dual-branch model. Subsequent studies further enhanced the adaptability of target representations to modality variations through modality-aware feature fusion~ liu2024modalityfusion , knowledge distillation~ li2024multiteacher , and prototype learning~ liu2025prototype . Compared with fixed-view settings, cross-modal UAV object tracking is further affected by platform motion, viewpoint changes, and target-scale variations, resulting in more challenging tracking conditions and considerable practical significance. To facilitate research on this task, Xiao et al.~ xiao2026sarla established the CM-UOT benchmark and proposed state-aware representation learning to jointly model modality and spatial states, thereby improving tracking robustness in dynamic UAV scenarios. However, existing methods still largely rely on offline representation learning and focus primarily on enhancing cross-modal target representations, leaving limited capability to adapt online to dynamic spatial states during testing. Test-time Adaptation Test-time adaptation (TTA) updates a pretrained model online using unlabeled test samples to reduce the distribution mismatch between source and target domains. Wang et al.~ wang2021tent proposed TENT, which adapts normalization-layer parameters by minimizing prediction entropy. To handle continually changing test distributions, Wang et al.~ wang2022cotta proposed CoTTA, which combines prediction averaging with stochastic weight restoration to mitigate error accumulation during long-term adaptation. Niu et al.~ niu2022eata further proposed EATA to suppress noisy gradients by selecting reliable samples, while SAR~ niu2023sar integrates reliability estimation and sharpness-aware optimization to improve update stability. Recently, Shao et al.~ shao2025pura introduced TTA to RGB-T tracking, combining fast updates and parameter decomposition recovery to balance adaptation and stability. Despite their effectiveness under distribution shifts, most existing TTA approaches are designed for classification or segmentation and primarily focus on prediction confidence and parameter stability. Although PURA extends TTA to RGB-T tracking, it mainly addresses update efficiency and parameter stability. In addition, Segu et al.~ segu2023darth propose DARTH, which uses detection consistency and patch contrastive learning to adapt object detection and instance appearance representations in multiple object tracking at test time. Bertrand et al.~ bertrand2023testtime explore test-time training based on mask cycle consistency for matching-based video object segmentation. Cross-modal UAV object tracking also involves modality- and motion-induced spatial drift and recursively accumulated localization errors. However, these methods primarily construct adaptation objectives around prediction confidence, parameter stability, detection consistency, or mask cycle consistency, while spatial localization changes and inter-frame localization relationships in cross-modal UAV tracking call for more targeted adaptation constraints. title: DroneDiffusion: Uncertainty-Guided Diffusion Path Planner for UAV Navigation
summary: We present DroneDiffusion, a perception-aware diffusion planner for local 3-D UAV trajectory generation that explicitly models and avoids failure zones caused by lens flare, overexposure, and reflective surfaces. A vision-language perceptual safety estimator produces a pixel-aligned reliability map that highlights regions of degraded sensing. A denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) is conditioned on this map together with the onboard RGB image, goal point, and initial velocity to generate egocentric 3-D trajectories. To enforce obstacle avoidance at inference time without retraining, we apply training-free CHOMP guidance over a 3-D Euclidean signed distance field. The model is trained entirely in simulation and deployed zero-shot on a real drone. Reliability conditioning raises the mean perceptual reliability along generated trajectories to 0.71, compared with 0.63 for a geometric baseline, while guidance halves the collision rate of the learned prior from 14.7% to 7.8%. Perceptual safety conditioning and geometric guidance are therefore complementary: treating sensor reliability as a first-class signal reduces incursions into unreliable regions while maintaining competitive navigation performance.

Introduction Autonomous UAV navigation in cluttered indoor environments exposes onboard sensors to perceptual hazards that geometric planners routinely ignore: overexposed corridors, lens flare, transparent walls, and specular surfaces. A planner unaware of such failures may route a drone confidently through a region where the sensor stream cannot be trusted. Diffusion models have recently emerged as expressive trajectory generators for navigation and manipulation, offering flexible multimodal conditioning and strong generalization from data~ c8,c9,c15 . Yet existing diffusion planners condition only on geometric and semantic cues such as RGB images, goal specifications, or occupancy maps. They provide no mechanism to reason about input reliability when the image is saturated or the depth measurements are invalid. Vision-language tools such as CLIPSeg~ c34 and AnyTraverse~ c35 can detect such failure zones, but have not been integrated into trajectory-level planning. We present a diffusion planner for 3-D UAV trajectory generation that treats a perceptual safety map as a first-class conditioning signal alongside the RGB image, goal point, and initial velocity. A CLIPSeg-based estimator produces a pixel-aligned reliability map that penalizes overexposure, lens flare, and transparent surfaces. A DDPM denoiser generates egocentric 4-DoF paths ( ) of 24 waypoints at 10\,Hz conditioned on this map, naturally steering away from unreliable regions. Training-free CHOMP guidance on a 3-D ESDF enforces geometric obstacle avoidance at inference time. The model trains in simulation and transfers to real drone flights without fine-tuning. The main contributions are: A perceptual safety map formulation that encodes sensor failure zones as a spatial reliability prior for diffusion trajectory planning. A conditional DDPM planner for 3-D UAV navigation jointly conditioned on visual context and perceptual reliability, with sim-to-real transfer validation. A training-free guidance module enforcing obstacle avoidance and goal reaching without retraining. Related Work UAV Trajectory Planning Local trajectory planning for UAVs has been addressed through gradient-based optimization~ zhou2019fastplanner , sampling-based methods~ c18 , and Model Predictive Control~ c19 . These approaches generate smooth, collision-free trajectories from explicit geometric representations such as a signed distance field, but each query returns a single solution rather than a distribution over feasible behaviors. Diffusion Models for Robot Navigation Diffusion models have demonstrated strong performance as trajectory generators for robot navigation. Diffuser~ c9 shows that diffusion policies can plan over long horizons from offline data. NoMaD~ c15 extends this to goal-conditioned exploration using a masked diffusion policy over image observations. DTG~ c12 applies diffusion to mapless outdoor navigation with traversability-aware losses. For UAVs specifically, CGD~ c27 incorporates constraint guidance into a diffusion planner for obstacle avoidance, while related guidance schemes have been applied to other platforms, such as autonomous racing~ c41 . More recently, aerial diffusion planners have been extended along further conditioning axes, including swarm path generation with generative impedance control~ batool2026impedance , an agentic reasoning layer above the planner~ batool2026agentic , and goals inferred from a detected person for search and rescue~ batool2026human . Across all of this work, the visual input itself is treated as trustworthy. Our work shares the guidance-based inference paradigm of these methods but introduces perceptual reliability as a conditioning modality, which none of them address. Traversability and Safety-Aware Navigation Traversability estimation has long been studied as a precondition for safe robot motion in unstructured environments. Recent work has shown that coupling traversability directly into the diffusion generation process, rather than treating it as a post-hoc filter, yields more robust and consistent trajectories. EmbodiedDiffusion~ c46 demonstrates that safety awareness through traversability conditioning plays a vital role in navigation: jointly generating traversability maps and trajectories from a single RGB image achieves strong sim-to-real transfer across heterogeneous platforms. Our work extends this direction in two respects. Rather than encoding terrain-level traversability, we model sensor-level perceptual failures as the source of risk. Additionally, trajectory generation and guidance operate in full 3-D space, addressing the geometric limitations of image-space planning for aerial platforms. Perceptual Failure Detection Detecting regions of degraded sensing has been studied in the context of robust perception pipelines. Vision-language models enable open-vocabulary scene understanding~ c33 , and CLIPSeg~ c34 extends this to dense pixel-level segmentation from text prompts. AnyTraverse~ c35 leverages CLIPSeg to produce prompt-driven traversability maps for ground robots, covering concepts such as glass surfaces and overexposed regions. These tools have not previously been used to condition trajectory-level planning. We repurpose the AnyTraverse framework specifically to identify sensor failure zones and encode them as a spatial prior for a diffusion-based 3-D planner. It consists of three blocks: a perceptual safety estimator that predicts reliable regions from onboard observations; a conditional diffusion planner that generates trajectories based on the current UAV state, observation, and estimated safety map; and a cost-guidance module that enforces collision avoidance. Each state therefore has four degrees of freedom, , stored as five values because the heading is encoded as the unit vector instead of a raw angle, which avoids angle wrapping and preserves the smoothness of the training data. Perceptual Safety Certain scene conditions degrade the RGB and depth streams: overexposure and lens flare saturate the image and corrupt depth returns, while transparent surfaces stay invisible to the depth sensor and specular ones produce phantom geometry from reflected scene content. Because the onboard camera is the primary sensing modality for the UAV, such degradation propagates directly into planning. A planner that reads such observations at face value may confidently route the UAV through regions where the sensor data cannot be trusted. Since these failures are visible in the image itself, we exploit the ability of diffusion models to handle multimodal conditioning and feed the planner a pixel-aligned reliability map alongside the RGB observation. title: APG-Planner: Learning Vision-Based High-Speed Trajectory Planning via Analytic Policy Gradient
summary: Vision-based high-speed navigation requires a trajectory planner that can reactively generate smooth, collision-free trajectories from onboard visual observations. Deep reinforcement learning offers a promising approach to vision-based trajectory planning, as it enables the optimization of sequential decision-making policies in complex environments. However, model-free policy gradient methods rely on sample-based policy gradient estimation, which yields noisy gradient estimates and inefficient training. To this end, we propose a framework for learning trajectory planning policies using the analytic policy gradient (APG) method and use it to train APG-Planner, a vision-based high-speed trajectory planner. The proposed framework leverages differential flatness to analytically reconstruct vehicle states from planned trajectories, thereby enabling differentiable trajectory-level state transitions without requiring an explicit low-level dynamics model. By iteratively performing trajectory planning and differentiable state transitions, we construct a differentiable episode rollout and analytically compute policy gradients from episode-level losses, improving both training efficiency and policy performance. After approximately 30 minutes of training on a single GPU, APG-Planner demonstrates comparable or superior performance to existing baseline methods in simulation and achieves speeds of up to 11\,m/s in real-world flight experiments. We further validate the proposed framework on a skid-steer ground robot, demonstrating its applicability to differentially flat robotic systems beyond quadrotors.

The proposed framework leverages differential flatness to analytically reconstruct vehicle states from planned trajectories, thereby enabling differentiable trajectory-level state transitions without requiring an explicit low-level dynamics model. By iteratively performing trajectory planning and differentiable state transitions, we construct a differentiable episode rollout and analytically compute policy gradients from episode-level losses, improving both training efficiency and policy performance. After approximately 30 minutes of training on a single GPU, APG-Planner demonstrates comparable or superior performance to existing baseline methods in simulation and achieves speeds of up to 11\,m/s in real-world flight experiments. We further validate the proposed framework on a skid-steer ground robot, demonstrating its applicability to differentially flat robotic systems beyond quadrotors. Aerial robotics, analytic policy gradient, autonomous navigation, differential flatness, trajectory planning. Introduction Vision-based high-speed flight has been widely studied to fully exploit the agility of quadrotors. The central challenge is to plan collision-free trajectories online from visual observations under limited onboard computation. Conventional systems reconstruct a geometric representation of the environment and then perform a trajectory search or optimization~ ego,wang2022gcopter,9592663 . Although effective, these approaches introduce computational latency that may limit rapid replanning for obstacle avoidance. To address this limitation, recent studies have proposed learning-based planners that directly generate trajectories from depth observations~ loquercio2021highspeed,rapid,lpnet,10528860 . Recent works on learning-based trajectory planning have adopted training paradigms such as imitation learning~ and guidance learning~ 10528860 . Imitation learning can offer advantages in sample efficiency but is limited by the availability and quality of expert trajectories. Guidance-based learning removes the need for expert demonstrations by exploiting gradients from a predefined planning-cost landscape, but such guidance remains local to each planning decision. In high-speed flight, each planned trajectory affects future states and decisions, influencing overall flight performance. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising approach to this problem, as it optimizes sequential decisions with respect to task-level objectives. However, training model-free RL policies for high-speed flight remains challenging, as model-free policy gradient methods rely on sampled rollouts to estimate policy gradients. These estimates can exhibit high variance, making training sample-intensive and slowing convergence~ newton . An alternative should enable task-level optimization while providing more accurate policy gradients. Analytic policy gradient (APG) methods provide such an alternative by constructing a differentiable episode rollout and backpropagating task-loss through it~ apg_controller,brax . Previous studies have employed APG to learn control policies, typically by propagating system states through differentiable dynamics. Recent work has successfully applied this approach to learn an end-to-end control policy for vision-based high-speed drone flight~ newton . However, this approach required a differentiable dynamics simulator calibrated using real-world flight data, necessitating recalibration of parameters such as aerodynamic drag across vehicles, while its end-to-end formulation limits interpretability. Therefore, learning high-speed trajectory planners remains a distinct and important research direction, providing explicit trajectories that facilitate interpretation and fallback design while integrating with existing low-level controllers to reduce reliance on low-level dynamics modeling. In this work, we propose a learning framework that uses APG to train APG-Planner, a vision-based high-speed trajectory planner. The proposed policy outputs trajectory segments in the flat-output space, while an existing low-level controller tracks the planned trajectories. Training a trajectory planning policy with APG requires differentiable state transitions between successive planning steps. We construct these transitions directly from planned trajectories using differential flatness, instead of explicitly simulating low-level vehicle dynamics. Differential flatness enables quadrotor states to be represented in terms of position, heading, and a finite number of their derivatives~ mellinger2011minsnap , and has been widely exploited for trajectory optimization~ wang2022gcopter,9592663 . We take this idea a step further by using differential flatness not only to parameterize trajectories, but also to define the state transition between successive planning decisions. Following a receding-horizon scheme, we analytically evaluate the planned trajectory at each replanning instant and reconstruct the corresponding vehicle state through the flatness map for the subsequent planning decision. This enables differentiable trajectory-level state transitions without explicitly modeling or unrolling low-level vehicle dynamics. By iteratively performing trajectory planning and differentiable state transitions, we construct differentiable episode rollouts and directly compute policy gradients from episode-level losses. This allows the planner to account for the downstream effects of sequential planning decisions during policy optimization while avoiding sampling-based policy-gradient estimation. Furthermore, by leveraging the flatness map of the target system, our framework enables the training of trajectory planners without requiring platform-specific low-level dynamics models. Moreover, the proposed framework is not limited to quadrotors and can be extended to other differentially flat robotic systems. The main contributions of this work are as follows: We formulate differentiable trajectory-level state transitions using differential flatness, without explicitly modeling low-level system dynamics. Based on this formulation, we propose an APG-based framework for training trajectory planning policies. Using this framework, we train APG-Planner in just 30 minutes on a single GPU. We demonstrate the performance of APG-Planner through extensive experiments, achieving competitive results in simulation and peak flight speeds of 11\,m/s in real-world quadrotor flights. Further experiments on a skid-steer ground robot validate its applicability beyond quadrotors. title: BiPOP: Partial-Order Planning for Long-Horizon Bimanual Robotic Manipulation
summary: Bimanual robotic manipulation is versatile, yet its central challenge lies not only in executing dexterous motion with each hand, but also in coordinating the two arms for long-horizon manipulation under coupled spatial and temporal constraints. Prior work has largely focused on endowing robots with human-level manipulation skills, paying less attention to the structure of bimanual behaviour itself: many practical tasks are a coordinated composition of reusable unimanual skills and a small set of synchronous bimanual skills. This makes high-level spatio-temporal coordination, rather than skill acquisition alone, a key bottleneck for efficient bimanual execution. We propose BiPOP, a framework that couples Large Language Models (LLMs) with Temporal Partial-Order Planning for long-horizon bimanual manipulation. At its core is an explicit spatio-temporal model that partitions the workspace by arm reachability and captures inter-arm dependencies, arm assignment, synchronization requirements, and opportunities for safe concurrent execution. Building on this model, an LLM translates natural-language instructions into a formal PDDL specification, while a temporal planner enforces the constraints and schedules actions, yielding plans that are logically consistent at the symbolic level and efficient through parallel execution. On simulated long-horizon tasks of varying complexity, BiPOP outperforms open-loop planning with strong reasoning models and closed-loop ReAct-style planning in success rate, planning time, and plan efficiency, and the full pipeline runs end to end on the real bimanual robot NICOL. A failure analysis further shows that LLM-only planners mainly violate spatial and temporal coordination constraints, which motivates delegating these constraints to a symbolic planner. Code: https://github.com/Kchu/BiPOP
full_text: Bimanual robotic manipulation offers substantial versatility, yet its central challenge lies not only in executing dexterous motion with each hand, but also in coordinating the two arms for long-horizon manipulation under coupled spatial and temporal constraints. Prior work has largely focused on endowing robots with human-level manipulation skills, paying comparatively less attention to the structure of bimanual behaviour itself: many practical tasks are best understood as a coordinated composition of reusable unimanual skills together with a small set of synchronous bimanual skills. This makes high-level spatio-temporal coordination, rather than skill acquisition alone, a key bottleneck for efficient bimanual execution. Therefore, we propose BiPOP, a framework that couples Large Language Models (LLMs) with Temporal Partial-Order Planning for long-horizon bimanual manipulation. At its core is an explicit spatio-temporal model that partitions the workspace by arm reachability and captures inter-arm dependencies, arm assignment, synchronization requirements, and opportunities for safe concurrent execution. Building on this model, an LLM translates natural-language instructions into a formal PDDL specification, while a temporal planner enforces the constraints and schedules actions, yielding plans that are logically consistent at the symbolic level and efficient through parallel execution. On simulated long-horizon tasks of varying complexity, BiPOP outperforms open-loop planning with strong reasoning models and closed-loop ReAct-style planning in success rate, planning time, and plan efficiency, and the full pipeline runs end-to-end on a real bimanual robot NICOL. A failure analysis further shows that LLM-only planners mainly violate spatial and temporal coordination constraints, which motivates delegating these constraints to a symbolic planner. Our implementation is publicly available at . Introduction Humans effortlessly perform bimanual tasks, from tying shoelaces to flipping book pages while holding a coffee cup, orchestrating complex spatial and temporal synchronization without conscious thought. Robots, in contrast, struggle even with apparently simple bimanual tasks, which demand planning, synchronization, and coordination. Bridging this gap remains an inherent challenge in robotics Krebs2022, Drolet2024 . Deep learning techniques ease the acquisition of dexterous bimanual manipulation, such as folding shirts shawbimanual , cutting vegetables Grannen2023 , and scooping food Grannen2023a . However, most approaches focus on learning human-level skills as a whole and overlook high-level task planning, which demands task decomposition, subtask assignment between the arms, execution sequencing and parallelization over long horizons. Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong reasoning and planning abilities across domains zhao2023survey , and recent work applies them to robotic task planning Ahn2022, liang2023code, Chu2024, gao2024dag . Yet generating embodiment-aware, executable plans is difficult for complex manipulation, where LLMs remain prone to long-horizon reasoning errors and hallucinations wang2024survey, stechly2024self , especially in spatially constrained scenarios. To mitigate these limitations, LLMs have been combined with classical symbolic planners liu2023 : by translating natural-language instructions into declarative representations such as PDDL mcdermott1998pddl , LLMs enable plans with logical-correctness guarantees. However, these approaches generally do not address the spatio-temporal coordination intrinsic to bimanual manipulation, in particular inter-arm dependencies, task allocation, synchronization, and parallelization. Our research question is therefore: how can LLMs be integrated with symbolic planning to achieve efficient spatial and temporal coordination for long-horizon bimanual robotic tasks? To address this, we propose BiPOP (Bimanual Partial-Order Planning), a framework (Fig. fig:method ) for long-horizon bimanual task planning that integrates semantic reasoning with explicit spatio-temporal coordination. Our contributions are threefold. First, we introduce a spatio-temporal model that partitions the workspace by arm reachability and encodes inter-arm dependencies, synchronization, and safe concurrency as durative PDDL actions with mutual-exclusion predicates. Second, we couple LLM-based problem generation with temporal planning: an LLM translates the task description and scene information into a PDDL problem, and a temporal planner computes a validated partial-order plan with a short symbolic makespan. Third, we evaluate BiPOP against open-loop and closed-loop LLM planners on three simulated bimanual task domains and deploy it on a real bimanual robot NICOL~ Matthias2023 . The results show that BiPOP outperforms open-loop planning with recent OpenAI and DeepSeek reasoning models and closed-loop ReAct-style planning in success rate, planning time, and plan efficiency. Related Work sec:related Task Planning in Robotics with Symbolic Planners. Task planning generates action sequences that achieve specified goals gerevini2020introduction, jiang2019task . Classical planners formalize domains and problems in declarative languages, most prominently PDDL mcdermott1998pddl , and generate plans with guaranteed logical correctness through domain-independent search helmert2006fast, Eyerich2009 . Task and motion planning couples such a symbolic planner in discrete space with a motion planner in continuous space Ding2020, kaelbling2013integrated, jiao2021efficient . These planners provide formal validity guarantees but require expert effort to author the symbolic representations, motivating the use of LLMs to automate this step. with LLMs. Prompting LLMs to generate robot behaviour directly is now a common technique Ahn2022, Chu2024, huang2022language, ding2023task . SayCan Ahn2022 lets an LLM propose feasible skills and grounds them to the current scenario through learned value functions, while language-to-code methods ground language more directly in executable robot behaviour: Code as Policies liang2023code writes policy code over perception and control primitives, and VoxPoser huang2023voxposer composes LLM/VLM-generated 3D value maps for zero-shot trajectory synthesis. These methods turn short-horizon instructions into executable, mostly single-arm motion, but presuppose a short or given task-level sequence and execute the LLM output unverified. Although iteratively querying LLMs with feedback or error messages mitigates these issues Chu2024, Wang2023, Rana2024 , such strategies still offer no formal guarantee of plan validity and rely on hand-crafted, domain-specific feedback with considerable expert effort. To pair language understanding with formal guarantees, a growing line of work uses LLMs not as planners but as translators of natural-language tasks into PDDL solved by classical planners. LLM+P liu2023 established this paradigm; ViLaIn shirai2024vision adds visual grounding, DELTA liu2025delta decomposes long-horizon goals into sub-goals, and AutoGPT+P birr2024autogptp handles incomplete information via affordance-based scene representations. However, these methods plan for a single agent and produce strictly sequential plans. Although AutoGPT+P is validated on bimanual humanoid platforms, it models neither the two arms as coordinated agents nor the action durations and concurrency constraints required for bimanual manipulation. LLM+MAP~ chu2025llmmap combines LLM reasoning with PDDL-based multi-agent planning for bimanual manipulation. Although it also produces partial-order plans, it frames coordination primarily as task and resource allocation between the two arm agents, rather than explicitly optimizing makespan through temporal planning. Bimanual Manipulation and Planning Manipulation. Deep learning has enabled dexterous bimanual skills Drolet2024 with parallel grippers Grannen2023 or anthropomorphic hands Chen2022 , from scooping food Grannen2023a to folding clothes avigal2022speedfolding and zipping zippers Grannen2023 . As these works focus on skill acquisition, they do not address planning for complex, long-horizon tasks; the diversity of coordination patterns they exhibit suggests that high-level planning should be considered jointly in an integrated control-system design Krebs2022, Smith2012 . Planning. Recent bimanual planning methods fall into two main categories. (i) Multi-agent formulations Zhao2024, zhao2025dual model each arm as an autonomous agent and use LLMs to decompose and allocate subtasks. This design is flexible, but typically lacks explicit concurrency scheduling, so coordination rests on heuristic LLM reasoning rather than verified constraints. (ii) Graph-centric pipelines gao2024dag, duan2026robopara induce a task-dependency graph with an LLM and dispatch its nodes to the two arms, exploiting parallelism where precedence permits. DAG-Plan gao2024dag assigns nodes to arms reactively at run-time via heuristic feasibility and cost estimates, leaving the LLM-generated dependencies unverified. RoboPARA duan2026robopara validates its graph only against a few hand-crafted structural error patterns and schedules it greedily with deadlock rollback, without a correctness guarantee or an explicit makespan objective. In both, the dependency semantics depend substantially on LLM assertions. In contrast, we ground concurrency in a verified symbolic model: the workspace partition and skills are formalized as temporal PDDL, and a temporal planner determines which actions may remain partially ordered and which require coordination, minimizing makespan with correctness guaranteed at the symbolic level. Method sec:method Given a task description in natural language, we aim to generate a valid and efficient plan for a bimanual robot based on the initial scene configurations, e.g., spatial information about the objects with respect to the robot. To this end, this section introduces the three elements of BiPOP: (A) Spatio-temporal modelling, (B) Bimanual PDDL definition with the LLM, and (C) ~Partial-Order Planning with the temporal planner. Spatio-temporal Modelling To enable efficient bimanual manipulation, we first develop a spatio-temporal model that characterizes the reachable workspace of each arm and the coordination relations between them, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:category . The workspace is partitioned into two uncoordinated regions, each reachable by a single arm, and one coordinated region (the overlap area) reachable by both. Arms operating in separate uncoordinated regions on distinct objects are spatially independent and can execute concurrently as parallel unimanual skills. Within the coordinated region, the arms become spatially and temporally coupled, requiring either asynchronous coordination, in which one arm establishes the preconditions for the other, or synchronous coordination, in which both arms execute a tightly coupled bimanual action. This workspace partitioning operates at the task-planning level: it determines whether two actions may proceed concurrently based on the arms, objects, and regions they involve, rather than on the geometric feasibility of the underlying trajectories. Two actions are scheduled concurrently only when they share no symbolic resource (neither arm, object, nor region), while all remaining cases are serialized through explicit coordination (ordering) constraints. Consequently, the resulting schedules are sound at the task level. Collision-free execution of concurrent motions, including cross-arm trajectory interference near the coordinated region, is delegated to the downstream motion planner. When a concurrent assignment proves geometrically infeasible, the motion planner may serialize it without affecting the validity of the produced plan. title: Bind-WAM: Binding-Uncertainty-Guided Selective Future Imagination in World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) can improve robot learning by jointly predicting future visual states and actions, but generating a visual future at every replanning step is expensive and sometimes unnecessary. This raises a critical question: when should a robot policy imagine the future? In this paper, we propose Bind-WAM, a binding-uncertainty-guided WAM for selective future imagination. Bind-WAM introduces language-object binding uncertainty, selectively invoking joint future-action generation when the current observation does not support stable task-relevant action generation. An offline labeling pipeline uses complete demonstrations and action context to identify task-relevant objects and detect reference mismatch, invisibility, and identity drift. The resulting pseudo-labels supervise a lightweight router that predicts binding uncertainty from the current observation and language instruction. At inference, a shared WAM policy invokes selective future imagination according to the predicted uncertainty and its change between consecutive replanning steps. Simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate that Bind-WAM can establish binding uncertainty as a strong, interpretable signal for selective future imagination.
full_text: World Action Models (WAMs) can improve robot learning by jointly predicting future visual states and actions, but generating a visual future at every replanning step is expensive and sometimes unnecessary. This raises a critical question: when should a robot policy imagine the future? In this paper, we propose Bind-WAM, a binding-uncertainty-guided WAM for selective future imagination. Bind-WAM introduces language-object binding uncertainty, selectively invoking joint future-action generation when the current observation does not support stable task-relevant action generation. An offline labeling pipeline uses complete demonstrations and action context to identify task-relevant objects and detect reference mismatch, invisibility, and identity drift. The resulting pseudo-labels supervise a lightweight router that predicts binding uncertainty from the current observation and language instruction. At inference, a shared WAM policy invokes selective future imagination according to the predicted uncertainty and its change between consecutive replanning steps. Simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate that Bind-WAM can establish binding uncertainty as a strong, interpretable signal for selective future imagination. Introduction World Action Models (WAMs) improve robot policies with the ability to imagine how a scene may evolve. By jointly predicting future visual states and actions, they can exploit temporal and physical structure that is absent from a purely reactive observation-to-action interface~ ye2026dreamzero . Yet traditional WAMs always make an implicit assumption: future imagination should be triggered at every replanning step. This uniform strategy ignores a basic property of policy execution: the value of dreaming ahead is state dependent. In many states the current observation already specifies the relevant objects and action, whereas in others the policy must resolve missing, ambiguous, or unstable visual evidence before acting. This leads to the central question of this paper: when should a robot policy imagine the future? Existing work like Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwam shows that video co-training can benefit action prediction even when future imagination is totally removed at deployment, and Faster-WAM~ zhao2026fasterwam finds that future representations can improve robustness under visual distribution shift. The important distinction is therefore not whether future prediction is globally useful, but whether its additional information is useful for the current state. Recent methods such as AdaWAM~ tang2026adawam enable adaptive inference by routing among action-only, visual, and textual reasoning according to the execution context. However, this identifies the need for future prediction mainly through execution phases, but when imagination is truly necessary for the current state remains unclear. Selective future imagination requires an interpretable signal to determine whether joint future-action prediction should be invoked. We choose language-object binding uncertainty as such a signal. A language instruction assigns semantic roles to objects in the scene. For example, in ``place the bowl on the plate,'' the bowl is the affected object and the plate is the relational reference. The policy's decision is fragile when a required object is invisible, when similar instances compete for the same role, or when an object's tracked identity changes during execution. These cases are jointly defined by language and vision, arise before low-level action generation, and directly threaten task completion, therefore requiring future imagination to provide additional guidance. Stable language-object bindings, in contrast, provide a clear setting for policies to skip future generation and predict correct actions. In this paper, we propose Bind-WAM, a binding-uncertainty-guided WAM for selective future imagination. Bind-WAM introduces an offline labeling pipeline that leverages Qwen3-VL~ bai2025qwen3vl , SAM~3.1~ carion2026sam3 and DINOv3~ simeoni2025dinov3 to generate uncertainty labels representing role mismatch, invisibility, and identity drift, which are used for training a 6.65M-parameter lightweight predictor. At deployment, the predicted uncertainty value switches one shared WAM between direct action prediction and joint future-action denoising. Our contributions are threefold. First, we formulate selective future imagination in World Action Models as a state-dependent problem, and introduce language-object binding uncertainty as an interpretable signal for deciding when joint future-action prediction should be invoked. Second, we develop Bind-WAM, which constructs binding uncertainty supervision from an offline labeling pipeline, and predicts uncertainty with a lightweight predictor to route a shared WAM between direct and joint inference. Third, simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate that binding uncertainty can identify the states where future imagination is useful. Related Work Future Imagination in World--Action Models World Action Models (WAMs) integrate visual world modeling with action generation, allowing robot policies to exploit representations of how a scene may evolve. A common design retains future prediction at inference, either deriving actions from predictive future representations or jointly generating futures and actions~ ye2026dreamzero,hu2024vpp,kim2026cosmos,zhou2026tau0wm . Other methods remove explicit future generation or replace dense video prediction with more compact inference mechanisms. Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwam retains video co-training but skips future prediction at deployment, showing that video modeling can benefit action generation through training alone. ImageWAM~ zhang2026imagewam replaces video generation with an image-editing prior and conditions its action expert on editing-derived key-value caches, without decoding a target image at inference. Faster-WAM~ zhao2026fasterwam preserves future-conditioned representations through a single video-expert pass, then reuses them through sparse video-action interaction during action denoising. These approaches offer different choices about whether and how to retain future information. Between always invoking future imagination and removing it entirely, adaptive inference allows a WAM to decide when to imagine. AdaWAM~ tang2026adawam uses execution-phase supervision to selectively activate visual future reasoning and textual subtask reasoning alongside action prediction. RISE~ lu2026rise adapts latent rollout depth for autonomous driving by balancing expected planning gains against computation cost, including zero rollout when the observed context suffices. Bind-WAM uses language-object binding uncertainty to route a shared WAM between direct action prediction and joint future-action generation. Its routing signal assesses whether task-relevant object roles are reliably grounded in the current observation, tying selective imagination to reference mismatch, invisibility, and identity drift. Language-Object Binding and Object-Centric Perception Language-object binding associates the entities and relational roles named in an instruction with physical objects in the scene. Object-centric semantic-spatial reasoning supports this association by selecting task-relevant objects before predicting manipulation affordances~ luo2023grounding . For world modeling, SlotFormer~ wu2023slotformer learns temporal interactions among object slots and predicts their future states, providing a structured alternative to holistic scene representations. Object-Centric World Model~ jeong2025ocwm extends object-centric prediction to language-guided manipulation by forecasting future slot representations conditioned on the instruction. OA-WAM~ liu2026oawam instead makes object identity explicitly addressable by separating each slot into a persistent identity address and time-varying content. Bind-WAM uses object-centric information for uncertainty supervision rather than as the state space of its world model. We construct labels from the consistency of instruction-role assignments to observed objects. These labels train a predictor to recognize unstable bindings from the current observation and instruction, without requiring object-slot extraction in the control loop. Bind-WAM uses this uncertainty supervision to decide when future imagination should be invoked. Method Figure~ fig:overview summarizes the overall architecture of Bind-WAM, showing how our approach connects offline binding supervision to online selective future imagination. The uncertainty predictor evaluates the current observation and instruction before WAM execution, and its output determines which inference path the shared policy uses. Problem Formulation Given a current visual observation , proprioceptive state , and language instruction , we aim to learn a policy that predicts an executable action chunk : Offline Uncertainty Labeling Pipeline Manual frame-level annotation of language roles and visual entities is costly, so we construct pseudo-labels from demonstrations in an automated pipeline. Given a demonstration trajectory and its language instruction, we first identify task-relevant entities, including the manipulated object and relational anchors using Qwen3-VL-32B. To determine which candidate corresponds to each task role, Qwen examines mask overlays from multiple temporal context frames, including interaction-relevant frames. SAM~3.1 then generates candidate instance masks from entity-specific text prompts and propagates them across the trajectory. DINOv3 ViT-L/16 features are then pooled inside each mask to measure identity consistency. The complete annotation flow is illustrated in Fig.~ fig:binding-annotation-pipeline . We uniformly sample 32 frames from each complete demonstration for labeling. For role , let be the overlap between the Qwen-verified reference mask and the original candidate track at the reference frame, the current visibility, and the cosine similarity between current and reference DINO features. The role-level uncertainty label is defined as which means a role is labeled uncertain at frame if its reference mask is unreliable, the tracked object is not visible, or its DINO feature similarity to the verified reference is relatively low. The frame-level label takes the most uncertain task-relevant role: This label captures three concrete binding failures: reference mismatch, invisibility, and identity drift. These binary labels supervise the uncertainty predictor using only the current RGB observation and language instruction. Qwen, SAM, DINO, action signals, and trajectory context are used exclusively during offline annotation and are not required at inference time. Binding Uncertainty Predictor The predictor is trained on offline labeled data to predict frame-level binding uncertainty from the current observation and language instruction : where high denotes unstable binding between instruction roles and objects in the scene. The predictor follows a lightweight ViT-like architecture~ dosovitskiy2021vit , and training loss combines class-weighted binary cross entropy with a Brier term~ brier1950verification : Binding-Uncertainty-Guided WAM Routing Bind-WAM realizes two inference paths. The direct path uses first-frame-only action-to-video attention, where action tokens can attend to the observed frame but not to denoised future-video tokens. The joint path uses full action-to-video attention, which jointly denoises future visual latents and the action chunk. We implement both paths within a single parameter-sharing WAM rather than maintaining separate policies for the two paths. Both paths share the video expert, action expert, and mixed transformer, and differ only in their action-to-video attention masks. title: Low-Cost Mobile Bimanual Manipulation for Long-Horizon Toilet Cleaning
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising capabilities for robot manipulation, but their performance on accessible mobile bimanual platforms remains underexplored. We present a low-cost and reproducible mobile bimanual platform integrating two LeRobot SO-101 manipulators with a TurtleBot 4 and a LeRobot-ROS 2 software stack. Using long-horizon toilet cleaning as a case study, we collect 250 real-world demonstrations and evaluate $π_0$, $π_{0.5}$, SmolVLA, and GR00T under the same embodiment and task conditions. We further evaluate variants using SARM-derived task-progress signals and short-term MEM observation history. Among the evaluated models, $π_0$ performs best, achieving 60% strict and 70% relaxed autonomous success, increasing to 90% with limited human intervention. In contrast, the evaluated progress- and memory-augmented variants do not improve their corresponding baselines. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of long-horizon mobile bimanual manipulation on accessible hardware while highlighting remaining challenges in reliable VLA deployment. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising capabilities for robot manipulation, but their performance on accessible mobile bimanual platforms remains underexplored. We present a low-cost and reproducible mobile bimanual platform integrating two LeRobot SO-101 manipulators with a TurtleBot~4 and a LeRobot--ROS~2 software stack. Using long-horizon toilet cleaning as a case study, we collect 250 real-world demonstrations and evaluate , , SmolVLA, and GR00T under the same embodiment and task conditions. We further evaluate variants using SARM-derived task-progress signals and short-term MEM observation history. Among the evaluated models, performs best, achieving 60 strict and 70 relaxed autonomous success, increasing to 90 with limited human intervention. In contrast, the evaluated progress- and memory-augmented variants do not improve their corresponding baselines. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of long-horizon mobile bimanual manipulation on accessible hardware while highlighting remaining challenges in reliable VLA deployment. Project website: . Hardware-Software Integration in Robotics, Mobile Manipulation, Bimanual Manipulation, Vision-language-action Models, Robot Learning, Long-horizon Manipulation Introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have rapidly advanced from task-specific manipulation toward generalist robot policies capable of dexterous, bimanual, and increasingly long-horizon behaviors~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2025pi0,black2025pi05 . However, translating these advances into reproducible real-world systems remains challenging~ li2024evaluating . Existing models are typically evaluated on different robot embodiments, datasets, and task settings, making it difficult to understand how they compare when deployed under the same physical conditions~ li2024evaluating,guruprasad2024benchmarking . This challenge is particularly pronounced for mobile bimanual manipulation, where locomotion, dual-arm coordination, perception, and contact-rich manipulation must operate reliably over extended task sequences~ fu2024mobile . In this work, we present a low-cost mobile bimanual platform for studying VLA policies in such settings, as shown in Fig. FigRobot . The platform combines two LeRobot SO-101 manipulators with a TurtleBot~4 mobile base, custom 3D-printable mechanical structures, and a multi-camera perception system. A modular LeRobot--ROS~2 software stack supports whole-robot teleoperation, data collection, human-in-the-loop correction, policy training, and deployment. The system is designed to provide an accessible and reproducible testbed for physical evaluation of modern VLA policies. We evaluate the platform through a long-horizon toilet-cleaning case study that requires mobile navigation, bimanual coordination, tool manipulation, contact-rich cleaning, and sequential task execution. Using 250 real-world demonstrations collected on the same platform, we fine-tune and physically evaluate representative open VLA models, including ~ black2025pi0 , ~ black2025pi05 , SmolVLA~ shukor2025smolvla , and GR00T N1.7~ bjorck2025gr00tn1,nvidia2026gr00tn17 . We additionally evaluate two temporal variants based on SARM-derived task-progress signals~ chen2026sarm and short-horizon MEM observation history~ torne2026mem . Our experiments reveal substantial differences between VLA configurations under identical physical conditions. Among the evaluated models, achieves the strongest autonomous performance, whereas the evaluated SARM- and memory-augmented variants do not improve task success in our setting. The experiments further expose recurring failure modes in embodiment adaptation, stage transitions, and long-horizon execution, while showing that limited human intervention can recover a substantial fraction of otherwise unsuccessful rollouts. These results highlight the remaining gap between the capabilities demonstrated by modern VLA models and reliable deployment on accessible mobile bimanual hardware. The main contributions of this work are: We present a low-cost and reproducible mobile bimanual platform based on dual LeRobot SO-101 manipulators and TurtleBot~4, with custom 3D-printable structures, multi-camera perception, and an integrated LeRobot--ROS~2 software stack. We establish a real-world long-horizon toilet-cleaning case study with 250 demonstrations and five sequential task stages, requiring mobility, bimanual coordination, and contact-rich tool manipulation. We provide a controlled physical evaluation of representative open VLA models and temporal variants on the same embodiment and dataset, and analyze their task performance and characteristic failure modes. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Models for Generalist Manipulation Large-scale robot learning has increasingly shifted from task-specific policies toward generalist models that jointly leverage visual observations, language instructions, and robot actions. RT-1 demonstrated that Transformer-based policies can acquire a broad repertoire of real-world manipulation skills~ brohan2022rt1 , while RT-2 further showed that semantic knowledge acquired through vision-language pretraining can be transferred to robotic control~ zitkovich2023rt2 . Open X-Embodiment subsequently introduced large-scale cross-embodiment robot datasets and policies~ o2024open , motivating open generalist models such as Octo~ ghosh2024octo and OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla . Together, these works established the feasibility of training reusable robot policies across diverse tasks, environments, and embodiments. More recent VLA models have increasingly targeted dexterous, bimanual, and long-horizon manipulation. RDT-1B introduced a diffusion foundation model specifically designed for bimanual manipulation~ liu2025rdt . The model employs flow matching for continuous action generation and demonstrates diverse dexterous manipulation behaviors across multiple robot embodiments~ black2025pi0 . Its successor, , further targets open-world generalization through heterogeneous co-training and high-level semantic prediction, demonstrating multi-stage mobile manipulation in previously unseen household environments~ black2025pi05 . SmolVLA explores a complementary direction toward compact and computationally efficient VLA models, with a particular emphasis on affordable robotic hardware and community-collected datasets~ shukor2025smolvla . The GR00T family instead develops generalist foundation models for humanoid and bimanual robotic embodiments~ bjorck2025gr00tn1 . Although these models report strong results on their respective platforms and benchmarks, their evaluations differ substantially in robot embodiment, training data, task definition, and experimental protocol. Consequently, reported performance across individual studies does not directly characterize how different VLA families behave when adapted to the same low-cost mobile bimanual embodiment and trained on the same real-world demonstrations. In this work, we use a common physical platform, dataset, and long-horizon task to provide a controlled case study of several representative VLA families, including , , SmolVLA, and GR00T. Low-Cost Bimanual and Mobile Manipulation In parallel with advances in learning algorithms, accessible robotic hardware has substantially lowered the barrier to collecting large-scale manipulation data and evaluating learned policies. ALOHA introduced a low-cost and open-source bimanual teleoperation system for fine-grained manipulation zhao2023learning , while ALOHA 2 subsequently improved the robustness, ergonomics, and maintainability of the platform aldaco2024aloha . ALOHA Unleashed further demonstrated that large-scale imitation learning on accessible bimanual hardware can produce dexterous behaviors involving deformable objects and complex contact interactions zhao2024aloha . Mobile ALOHA extended this paradigm from tabletop manipulation to whole-body mobile bimanual operation by combining an ALOHA-based bimanual system with a mobile base and whole-body teleoperation interface fu2024mobile . The platform demonstrated autonomous household behaviors involving coordinated locomotion and manipulation, including cooking, cabinet interaction, elevator operation, and rinsing cookware. These results established that relatively accessible hardware can support complex mobile bimanual learning and provided an important foundation for studying whole-body policies outside fixed-base workspaces. The LeRobot ecosystem has recently provided another route toward accessible robot learning by integrating standardized datasets, teleoperation, policy training, and deployment within an open-source framework cadene2026lerobot . Low-cost serial manipulators such as the SO-100 and SO-101 further reduce the hardware requirements for collecting real-world demonstrations and evaluating learned policies Knight_Standard_Open_SO-100 . However, most existing LeRobot-based platforms and datasets focus on fixed-base manipulation, while mobile bimanual configurations remain less extensively characterized as physical testbeds for generalist VLA policies. Our platform follows the broader direction established by ALOHA and Mobile ALOHA, but targets a complementary design point centered on the LeRobot ecosystem. We integrate two SO-101 manipulators with a TurtleBot~4 mobile base and a multi-camera perception system, together with custom 3D-printable mechanical structures and a modular LeRobot--ROS~2 software stack. The resulting system is intended as an accessible and reproducible experimental platform for data collection, human-in-the-loop correction, and physical evaluation of VLA policies under mobile and bimanual task requirements. Long-Horizon Manipulation, Progress Estimation, and Memory Long-horizon manipulation introduces additional challenges beyond generating locally appropriate actions. During multi-stage execution, a robot must maintain consistency across successive behaviors, transition between subtasks, and account for information that may no longer be evident from the current observation. Recent work has therefore investigated mechanisms for representing task progress and maintaining temporal context during robot execution. One direction explicitly models progress through a task. Stage-Aware Reward Modeling (SARM) learns a video-based reward model that jointly estimates high-level task stages and fine-grained progress within each stage chen2026sarm . By deriving supervision from natural-language subtask annotations, SARM provides a structured representation of task progress that can be used to evaluate demonstrations and improve policy learning through Reward-Aligned Behavior Cloning. Long-VLA approaches have similarly investigated phase-aware representations and subtask structure to improve execution over extended manipulation sequences fan2025long . A complementary direction incorporates observation or interaction history directly into the policy. MemoryVLA introduces explicit memory mechanisms for retrieving task-relevant historical information during action generation

title: AFTER: A World Model with Adaptive Fast--Slow Timescales for Error-Driven Retention
summary: In robotics and embodied AI, a core challenge for world models is adapting to sudden, persistent, yet initially unknown changes in robot dynamics during interaction. For instance, when a robotic arm grasps an object with an unknown payload, the robot dynamics change suddenly. If the world model fails to adapt, its prediction errors accumulate over the open-loop rollout and ultimately mislead the robot's actions. Existing world models, however, struggle to simultaneously satisfy three critical requirements for dynamics adaptation: responsiveness, reacting promptly to sudden changes to curb prediction error accumulation; stability, distinguishing persistent changes from transient disturbances to prevent incorrect updates; and persistence, retaining the adapted dynamics without new observations so that later predictions do not revert to the old dynamics. Inspired by predictive coding in the human brain with multi-timescale adaptation, we propose AFTER-WM, a world model with Adaptive Fast-slow Timescales for Error-driven Retention, whose prediction errors drive a fast correction that fades and a slow correction that persists, while dynamically adjusting the combination weights of pre-trained experts without altering them, to overcome the trade-offs among responsiveness, stability and persistence. On five simulated robot datasets and real UAV data, AFTER-WM has a lower multi-step mean error than all ten compared models and the highest mean return in a joint-failure control task. In simulation, its multistep mean error is 16%-34% below the strongest compared model's and is also the lowest 1-4 steps after a change and under transient disturbances alone, and its step-40 error is the lowest as well, reflecting responsiveness, stability and persistence. All code (method, baselines, experiments) and datasets will be released online.

Introduction sec:intro A world model predicts how a robot's state responds to actions, for planning and control~ ha2018world,chua2018pets,hafner2025dreamerv3,hansen2024tdmpc2 . In robotics and embodied AI, a core challenge for world models is adapting to sudden, persistent, yet initially unknown changes in robot dynamics during interaction. For instance, the robot dynamics change when a robotic arm grasps an unknown payload, or when a joint or engine fails~ nagabandi2019grbal,keipour2021alfa . Such unknown dynamics mainly comprise sudden and persistent changes~ alegre2021mbcd,luo2022escp , so the world model must adapt online from its prediction errors~ nagabandi2019grbal,nagabandi2019mole . Otherwise, prediction errors accumulate over the open-loop rollout and mislead the robot's actions. Existing world models, however, struggle to simultaneously satisfy three critical requirements for dynamics adaptation. (1)~Responsiveness is needed because the change is sudden and, in the open-loop rollout, each prediction is fed back as input, so prediction errors accumulate~ venkatraman2015improving,janner2019mbpo . (2)~Stability is needed because a transient disturbance is equally sudden and initially hard to distinguish from a persistent change~ widmer1996learning,gama2014survey . (3)~Persistence is needed because the change persists, yet no new observations arrive during the open-loop rollout, so if adaptation fades, later predictions revert to the old dynamics. Satisfying all three at once is hard. The faster adaptation reacts, the more easily a transient disturbance misleads it~ widrow1976stationary,haykin2002adaptive , and adaptation that fades quickly enough to drop a transient disturbance cannot persist. General-purpose world models~ hafner2025dreamerv3,hansen2024tdmpc2 serve many tasks but lack dedicated dynamics adaptation. Online-adaptive world models~ nagabandi2019grbal,nagabandi2019mole adapt each model at one timescale and face this trade-off. Multi-timescale world models~ shaj2023mts3 infer slow variables only at fixed intervals and respond late. Humans adapt well to such changes. Neuroscience explains this by predictive coding~ rao1999predictive,friston2010free,keller2018predictive , shown in a for lifting a cup heavier than expected. In the motor dynamics row, the lift is a persistent change and the bump a transient disturbance. The brain compares predicted and sensed arm motion, and their difference, the prediction error, peaks at the lift and the bump and drives adaptation~ wolpert1995internal,tseng2007sensory,shadmehr2010error . This mechanism has three features, numbered on the right, meeting the requirements in the boxes: responsive, stable and persistent. (1)~Being error-driven, adaptation starts once a prediction fails, providing responsiveness. (2)~It runs through neural pathways that adapt at multiple timescales~ smith2006interacting,kording2007dynamics . Some act at once and fade, others build up and persist, so the response to the bump fades but that to the lift persists, providing stability and persistence. (3)~Modules are reweighted by their prediction errors and learn in proportion to their weights~ wolpert1998multiple,haruno2001mosaic . In the module weights row, the weight moves from empty hand to full cup, providing persistence, and the empty hand module stays intact. Inspired by this, we propose ( ), whose three designs carry over these features (arrows in a). (1)~Predictive correction mainly serves responsiveness. Pre-trained dynamics models, called experts, act as internal models, and their one-step prediction errors update online memories at each observed step without gradients. (2)~Dual-timescale adaptation mainly serves stability and persistence. Its fast correction acts at once and fades, while its slow correction builds up and persists. (3)~Multiple internal models mainly serve persistence. Prediction errors adjust the combination weights via a routing memory and never alter the experts. We evaluate on two datasets with established change protocols, three new simulated datasets and one real UAV dataset. On all six, it has a lower multi-step mean error than all ten compared models. b lists how much lower this error is than the closest compared model's, by steps since the latest change. It is lower in every cell, even 1--4 steps after a change. In simulation, shows that the fast correction acts at once (responsiveness), transient disturbances move the slow state no more than usual (stability), and the routing memory and slow correction still remove error at step 40 (persistence). Our contributions are: We identify adapting to unknown dynamics as a core challenge for world models, with three requirements. Inspired by predictive coding, we propose , whose three designs target all three requirements. We build three simulated robot datasets with changes in robot dynamics. In simulation, 's multi-step mean error is 16 --34 below the strongest compared model's. Related Work sec:related -purpose world models. They serve online planning or policy learning in imagined trajectories~ ha2018world,hafner2019planet,hafner2025dreamerv3,hansen2024tdmpc2,chua2018pets,janner2019mbpo . TD-MPC2, PETS and others predict only from the current state and cannot detect changes. Recurrent models such as DreamerV3 and RKN~ becker2019rkn update a latent state with new observations, RKN by Kalman updates. But they lack dedicated dynamics adaptation, so their multi-step predictions worsen after a change. 's predictive correction adds error-driven corrections to a pre-trained base as errors grow. -adaptive world models. They adapt to recent data at test time, in four main ways. GrBAL and MOLe update parameters by gradient steps, and MOLe also adds models for new situations~ nagabandi2019grbal,nagabandi2019mole . ReBAL, CaDM and HiP-RSSM~ nagabandi2019grbal,lee2020cadm,shaj2022hiprssm encode recent history into a context variable for the current dynamics, as adaptive policies do~ yu2017uposi,luo2022escp,kumar2021rma . MBCD and GPMM~ alegre2021mbcd,xu2020gpmm detect the change or infer the current dynamics, then switch models. Others, as in adaptive control, freeze learned features and fit only the last linear layer online, with Kalman-style or least-squares rules~ oconnell2022neuralfly,ingebrand2024zeroshot,levy2025metalearning . Recent methods make low-rank second-order weight updates~ altawaitan2026adapting , reweight world models by prototype similarity~ jang2026tmow or correct predictions with one feedback state~ an2026feedback . Yet each adapts at a single timescale, set by a step size, history length, detection threshold, filter noise or feedback gain, so it trades responsiveness against stability. 's dual-timescale adaptation writes each error into a fast state that fades and a slow one that persists, avoiding this trade-off. Its multiple internal models never alter the pre-trained experts, so noise cannot corrupt them. -timescale world models. They split latent states into fast and slow timescales. Clockwork VAE updates higher layers more slowly for video prediction~ saxena2021clockwork , and THICK updates part of its state only now and then for planning~ gumbsch2024thick . MTS3~ shaj2023mts3 updates a fast latent state every step but infers its slow variable only at fixed intervals from a window of observations, not from errors. So after a change, its multi-step predictions follow the old dynamics until the next inference, and prediction errors accumulate. 's predictive correction feeds every error to the slow state at once.
