title: MatrixSplat: Matrix-Parallel and Feature-Scalable 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering on GPUs
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a mainstream representation for real-time novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction. However, existing 3DGS rendering pipelines are poorly aligned with modern GPU architectures: depth-sorted alpha compositing introduces strong per-pixel sequential dependencies, limiting parallelism and resulting in scalar FMA-dominated execution that underutilizes high-throughput matrix units such as Tensor Cores. This mismatch becomes more severe for multimodal and semantically enriched 3DGS, where high-dimensional features must be accumulated from millions of Gaussians, leading to rapidly increasing computation and memory costs. We propose MatrixSplat, a matrix-parallel rendering framework for feature-scalable 3DGS on modern GPUs. We first identify the sequential dependency of alpha compositing as a key obstacle to efficient high-dimensional feature rendering, and adopt an order-independent weighted accumulation formulation that transforms feature rendering into matrix-oriented computation. Our framework features three key designs: (i) a tile-based splatting pipeline that maps feature accumulation to warp-level matrix-multiply-accumulate execution on Tensor Cores; (ii) a warp-granularity Gaussian packing strategy that mitigates visibility irregularity and improves feature reuse; and (iii) a lazy channel-batched feature-fetching pipeline that reduces shared-memory pressure, maintains high warp occupancy, and overlaps memory access with matrix execution for high-dimensional features. On Mip-NeRF 360, LERF, and 3D-OVS, MatrixSplat achieves up to 3.8$\times$ speedup over 3DGS and 2$\times$ over TC-GS while maintaining rendering quality and semantic accuracy, and further reduces render-kernel time by up to 36.7$\times$ for high-dimensional features. Integrated into existing fast renderers, it provides an additional 1.69-2.84$\times$ speedup.
full_text: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a mainstream representation for real-time novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction. However, existing 3DGS rendering pipelines are poorly aligned with modern GPU architectures: depth-sorted alpha compositing introduces strong per-pixel sequential dependencies, limiting parallelism and resulting in scalar Fused Multiply-Add (FMA)-dominated execution that underutilizes high-throughput matrix units such as Tensor Cores. This mismatch becomes more severe for multimodal and semantically enriched 3DGS, where high-dimensional features must be accumulated from millions of Gaussians, leading to rapidly increasing computation and memory costs. To address these challenges, we propose MatrixSplat, a matrix-parallel rendering framework for feature-scalable 3DGS on modern GPUs. We first identify the sequential dependency of alpha compositing as a key obstacle to efficient high-dimensional feature rendering, and adopt an order-independent weighted accumulation formulation that transforms feature rendering into matrix-oriented computation. Our framework features three key designs: i) a tile-based splatting pipeline that maps feature accumulation to warp-level matrix-multiply-accumulate execution on Tensor Cores; ii) a warp-granularity Gaussian packing strategy that mitigates visibility irregularity and improves feature reuse; and iii) a lazy channel-batched feature-fetching pipeline that reduces shared-memory pressure, maintains high warp occupancy, and overlaps memory access with matrix execution for high-dimensional features. Experiments on Mip-NeRF 360, LERF, and 3D-OVS demonstrate both high performance and strong scalability for feature-rich 3DGS rendering. Particularly, our method achieves up to 3.8 speedup over 3DGS and 2 over TC-GS while maintaining rendering quality and semantic accuracy, and further reduces render-kernel time by up to 36.7 for high-dimensional features. Integrated into existing fast renderers, it provides an additional 1.69--2.84 speedup. Introduction sec:introduction Modern GPU architectures are increasingly optimized for high-throughput matrix computation, yet many emerging graphics and vision workloads fail to fully exploit these capabilities. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233d has recently emerged as a mainstream paradigm for novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction~ chen2024survey,hanson2025speedy,jia2026splaxel . It represents a scene as a set of 3D Gaussian primitives, each parameterized by spatial position, scale, opacity, rotation, and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients, enabling differentiable rendering with high visual quality and real-time performance~ bagdasarian20243dgs . However, the standard 3DGS pipeline relies on depth-sorted alpha compositing, where Gaussian contributions are accumulated in a strict front-to-back order. This design introduces strong per-pixel sequential dependencies, limiting parallelism and causing frequent instruction stalls, with execution dominated by scalar Fused Multiply-Add (FMA) operations~ liao2025tc,feng2024flashgs,du2026mobile . Consequently, the rendering pipeline is poorly aligned with modern matrix-computation-oriented GPU architectures, leaving high-throughput matrix units largely underutilized. As shown in Fig.~ fig:sm-utilization , profiling of Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) utilization reveals that rendering is dominated by Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) and FP32 FMA operations, while Tensor Cores remain entirely unused despite offering up to 4 higher peak throughput. This mismatch exposes a between the dependency structure of current 3DGS rendering algorithms and the computing patterns of modern GPUs. This challenge becomes significantly more severe as 3DGS evolves toward multimodal and semantically enriched representations. Recent advances extend 3DGS beyond photorealistic reconstruction by integrating high-dimensional features, enabling support for emerging applications such as world models in robotics, embodied AI, and autonomous driving~ liu2026palm,shen2025fine . For example, prior works~ qin2024langsplat,li2025semanticsplat,jiang2024vr embed high-dimensional language features into Gaussian primitives, enabling semantically aligned 3D understanding without relying on expensive and often low-quality 3D annotations. However, existing 3DGS rendering pipelines are not designed for such workloads, and the algorithm-hardware mismatch is therefore further magnified. As feature dimensionality increases, the accumulation workload over millions of Gaussians grows rapidly, resulting in substantially higher memory traffic and computational cost~ huang2025seele . As shown in Fig.~ fig:sweep-plot , the original 3DGS can no longer stage the full feature vector in shared memory when the dimension is greater than 128, so features are fetched from global memory. Rendering performance degrades dramatically with increasing feature dimensionality~ li2025semanticsplat,zhou2024feature , especially once features exceed the shared-memory capacity. Prior works~ deng2024efficient,fan2023lightgaussian,mallick2024taming,lee2024compact,zhang2024gaussianspa,ou2026flicker have attempted to address this mismatch from both algorithmic and hardware perspectives, but they accelerate different stages of the pipeline. Pipeline-level accelerators such as FlashGS~ feng2024flashgs , Speedy-Splat~ hanson2025speedy , and AdR-Gaussian~ wang2024adrgaussian reduce the work around blending through tighter culling, scheduling, and sorting, yet still accumulate each pixel with a serial scalar loop. Sorting-free methods~ hou2024sort,kheradmand2025stochasticsplats,liu2026duplex replace sorted alpha compositing with weighted-sum or stochastic rendering to remove depth sorting, but execute the resulting accumulation with the same scalar FMAs. Tensor-Core approaches such as TC-GS~ liao2025tc and GEMM-GS~ li2026gemmgs map the alpha computation onto matrix units, while the blending loop itself remains order-dependent. Therefore, a gap remains: no existing method uses order independence to express the feature accumulation itself as matrix multiplication, even though this is the part whose cost grows with feature dimensionality~ ha2026langgs . To bridge this algorithm-hardware gap, we propose MatrixSplat, a matrix-parallel framework for feature-scalable 3DGS rendering on modern GPUs. Our key insight is that the sequential dependency introduced by alpha compositing is what prevents feature accumulation from being executed as matrix operations. By revisiting the rendering pipeline, we derive an order-independent weighted accumulation formulation that removes this dependency and transforms scalable feature rendering into matrix-oriented computation. Building on this formulation, we design a scalable tile-based splatting pipeline that maps feature accumulation to warp-level packed matrix-multiply-accumulate (MMA) execution. To further support high-dimensional semantic features, we introduce a lazy channel-batched feature-fetching strategy that preserves data reuse, reduces shared-memory pressure, and maintains high execution efficiency as feature dimensionality grows. Together, these designs enable efficient and scalable 3DGS rendering by leveraging high-throughput matrix units on modern GPUs. Because our method changes how blending is executed rather than how much work reaches it, it is complementary to pipeline-level accelerators and can be combined with them. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We analyze the 3DGS rendering pipeline and identify the sequential dependency of alpha compositing as a key bottleneck for feature-embedded Gaussian rendering on modern GPUs. Inspired by prior order-independent rendering ideas, we tailor weighted accumulation to semantic feature rendering and reorganize the resulting dependency-free computation into a hardware-aligned, matrix-oriented execution pattern. We propose a warp-level, matrix-oriented design that enables efficient mapping of feature-scalable rendering to Tensor Core MMA execution. By packing valid Gaussians at warp level, our method enables efficient matrix-computation-friendly feature accumulation while reducing visibility irregularity. This design improves the reuse of Gaussian features. We develop a scalable, lazy, channel-batched feature-fetching pipeline. This lazy loading reduces shared-memory pressure as feature dimensionality grows, preserves higher active warps per SM, and hides latency by overlapping memory loading and MMA execution, thereby supporting efficient rendering of high-dimensional features. We evaluate our method on Mip-NeRF 360, LERF, and 3D-OVS. Experiments show that our method achieves up to 3.8 end-to-end speedup over 3DGS and 2 over TC-GS while maintaining visual quality and semantic accuracy, and further reduces render-kernel time by up to 36.7 for high-dimensional semantic features. It is also 2.2--3.5 faster than Sort-Free rendering and provides an additional 1.69--2.84 speedup when integrated into existing fast renderers. title: ActionCodec2: A Streaming Action Tokenizer
summary: Most action tokenizers for autoregressive vision language action (VLA) models compress motion into chunks that must be decoded in full before their actions become executable. We introduce ActionCodec2, a non-neural streaming tokenizer that releases actions incrementally while keeping trajectory reconstruction error within a prescribed tolerance. Its encoder quantizes each step relative to the decoder's reconstructed state, so the selected motion primitive corrects residual error rather than allowing errors from independently quantized increments to accumulate. Finding the smallest such primitive set is a geometric covering problem; we derive the exact minimum for translation and constant-factor-tight bounds for rotation. Set-BPE then losslessly merges co-occurring primitive symbols across coordinates and neighboring steps, without a fixed coordinate ordering. A universal version fitted on 20k hours of data from 24 embodiments averages 8.8 tokens per second for 15 Hz end-effector motion on this corpus. With the same VLA backbone, ActionCodec2 outperforms the compared tokenizers on three simulation benchmarks and in zero-shot real-robot evaluation. Its streaming representation allows policies to incorporate state feedback within an action chunk, substantially improving performance over open-loop execution under randomized dynamics, external disturbances, and moving objects. The same tokens also can serve as a direct control interface for VLM agents, which compose successful action sequences into reusable macros. These agent-built macros reduce control decisions and thinking-token usage across attempts and transfer to a held-out task. More results are available at https://zibindong.github.io/actioncodec2-page/

Most existing action tokenizers encode one to two seconds of motion as a chunk (Figure~ fig:teaser , left), following a formulation widely used in diffusion policies chi2023diffusionpolicy, zhao2023aloha, bharadhwaj2024roboagent . For example, FAST fast exploits temporal correlations by compressing DCT coefficients with BPE, while VQ-VAE-based tokenizers mete2024quest, vq-vla, oat, x-tokenizer, dong2026actioncodec learn compact latent representations of action chunks. With chunkwise tokenization, the robot can react to new observations only at chunk boundaries, and an erroneous token may affect multiple actions within a chunk. Real-time chunking black2025real allows earlier reactions by replanning before a chunk ends, but reacting at every control step would require repeatedly predicting overlapping chunks. A streaming tokenizer instead releases actions as their symbols become available, allowing the policy to incorporate new observations at each control step without regenerating entire chunks. The simplest streaming tokenizer is per-dimension binning, as in OpenVLA openvla , which assigns one token to each action dimension. For 7-dimensional actions at , this requires 105 tokens per second, substantially increasing autoregressive decoding latency. An alternative is to shorten the chunks of learned VQ-based tokenizers to one or two steps mete2024quest, vq-vla, liu2026faster, oat . However, their fixed codebooks concentrate reconstruction accuracy on the training distribution, with no guarantee for unfamiliar motions (Figure~ fig:teaser , right). More importantly, accurate reconstruction of individual actions does not guarantee accurate trajectories, as small errors in incremental actions accumulate over time. In a replay test on LIBERO (Figure~ fig:replay-audit ), FAST reconstructs individual actions to within but accumulates about of drift per episode, achieving only replay success. The other chunkwise baselines reach at most , whereas ActionCodec2 keeps the drift below and achieves replay success. ActionCodec2 addresses trajectory drift by accounting for the quantization error left by previous steps. The encoder maintains the same reconstructed state as the decoder and uses it to select the next motion primitive, keeping the reconstructed trajectory within a prescribed tolerance of the original. Rather than allowing small errors to accumulate, each step corrects the error remaining from earlier steps. This reduces the range that needs to be quantized to the possible one-step motions and the residual tracking error, rather than the robot's entire workspace. We derive the minimum number of discrete motion symbols required to guarantee this error bound. The motion primitives guarantee bounded tracking error, but representing every possible combination of primitives with a separate VLA token would require an enormous vocabulary. Representing each coordinate separately avoids this problem but produces long token sequences. We therefore compress these symbols without changing the reconstructed actions. Standard BPE bpe, fast merges only adjacent symbols under a fixed coordinate ordering, limiting its ability to capture correlations across dimensions. We introduce Set-BPE, which losslessly merges co-occurring symbols across coordinates and neighboring steps, regardless of coordinate order. At , ActionCodec2 requires only tokens per second for end-effector control and for joint control. ActionCodec2 is fitted without gradient-based optimization: its primitive sets are determined by the motion bounds and prescribed tolerances, while Set-BPE learns its merges by counting symbol co-occurrences. In addition to benchmark-specific tokenizers fitted on each dataset's training corpus, we fit universal variants on about k hours of data from embodiments for plug-and-play use across robots and tasks. Our contributions are: [topsep=0pt, itemsep=2pt, leftmargin=1.1em, labelsep=0.5em, labelwidth=0.6em, align=left] We formulate bounded-error streaming action tokenization as a covering problem and prove the optimality of fixed motion primitives among one-symbol-per-step decoders, with an exact solution for translation and constant-factor-tight bounds for rotation. We introduce Set-BPE, which losslessly merges co-occurring primitive symbols across coordinates and neighboring steps, without relying on a fixed coordinate ordering. This allows merged tokens to capture coordinated motion patterns that standard BPE may miss, while reducing token count by -- on held-out data. Using the same G0.5 VLA g05 , ActionCodec2 achieves on LIBERO, on SimplerEnv, and on LIBERO-Plus, outperforming FAST, OAT, X-Tokenizer, and ActionCodec. It also achieves task progress across four zero-shot Franka tasks. We show that ActionCodec2 tokens can serve as a direct control interface for VLM agents, which store successful token sequences as reusable macros that carry over across attempts and to new tasks. title: What Makes a VLA Reactive? A Study of Execution Strategies for Dynamic Manipulation
comment: 13 pages, 7 figures, Efficient Foundation Models for Real-Time Embodied AI, CoRL 2026 Workshop
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models predict chunks of future actions, and when objects move, those chunks go stale before they are executed. We study what makes a pretrained VLA reactive, using \pihalf{} on two dynamic simulation benchmarks and three real-robot tasks. We vary the prediction and execution horizons, compare synchronous and asynchronous inference, test methods that deliver actions sooner or keep successive chunks continuous, and adapt the policy with motion cues and latent-space reinforcement learning. The best prediction horizon is about one second, and the best execution horizon depends on the checkpoint. Short horizons help more with asynchronous execution, and methods that keep the trajectory continuous outperform those that only reduce latency. Adapting the policy repairs targeted failures, but on the conveyor task changing the execution horizon gained as much. Reactivity depends on the execution pipeline as much as on the policy, so both should be evaluated together.
full_text: Study Design Problem Setup Given visual observations , language instruction , and proprioceptive state , the policy predicts an action chunk , where is the prediction horizon. The execution horizon specifies how many actions are executed from a predicted chunk. Thus, prediction length and execution commitment can be varied separately~ black2025rtc,lu2026fasterrethinkingrealtimeflow . In synchronous execution, the controller executes the selected actions, then waits for the next prediction. Asynchronous execution overlaps inference with ongoing motion, reducing this waiting time. Inference latency corresponds to a delay of action steps. Asynchronous execution must account for motion during this delay when selecting or conditioning the next chunk. Switching between independently generated chunks can also introduce discontinuities in the commanded trajectory~ black2025rtc . We therefore study execution horizons, inference scheduling, and continuity, and whether temporal information or policy adaptation can compensate for these effects. Experimental Setup We evaluate -based configurations on DOM~ xie2026dynamicvla and DOMINO~ fang2026domino simulation tasks and three real-robot tasks using a Franka Panda: moving-cup placement, rolling-can grasping, and conveyor-belt picking. The conveyor task uses three cubes with a red target cube under stationary, slow ( ), and fast ( ) belt conditions. Left, Middle, and Right denote the target's position along the stationary belt or its relative position within the moving three-cube sequence. Training, hardware, control rates, task configurations, and evaluation protocols are detailed in the appendix. Intervention Selection and Implementation We select approaches that address complementary limitations of dynamic manipulation: temporal commitment, delayed or discontinuous execution, and insufficient motion information or behavioral adaptation. We implement these interventions within a common framework. summarizes their intervention points. These configurations adapt selected mechanisms from the original methods rather than reproduce every original system. r 0.6 Intervention levels and goal of evaluated methods. tab:method_overview 3pt 1.0 @ lccccl@ Method & Model & Inference & Execution & Action Rep. & Target \\ RTC & & & & & Chunk transition \\ FASTER & & & & & Action generation \\ DynamicVLA & & & & & Execution alignment \\ ABPolicy & & & & & Chunk continuity \\ PUMA & & & & & Motion information \\ AAC & & & & & Execution horizon \\ DSRL & & & & & Latent steering \\ Temporal Horizons and Replanning The prediction horizon sets how far ahead the policy plans, and the execution horizon sets how much of that plan is carried out before the policy looks again. Together they decide how old the observation behind each executed action can be. We vary during fine-tuning and at deployment with a fixed policy. A fixed treats every moment the same, so we also test whether the policy can choose itself with Adaptive Action Chunking (AAC)~ liang2026aac . AAC samples several candidate chunks, measures the entropy of the predicted actions, and ends a chunk early when the entropy is high, subject to a minimum action-magnitude constraint in Cartesian space. Scheduling and Continuity Interventions A shorter only helps if new actions arrive in time and join the old ones smoothly. We therefore compare synchronous and asynchronous execution across execution horizons, and evaluate methods that address each requirement as separate configurations: FASTER and DynamicVLA make actions available sooner, RTC and ABPolicy keep the trajectory continuous across chunks. Our DynamicVLA adaptation uses continuous inference and latency-aware action skipping, adding a minimum execution window while retaining the architecture and inputs~ xie2026dynamicvla . With FASTER, we get near-term actions earlier through horizon-aware sampling, action streaming, and early stopping~ lu2026fasterrethinkingrealtimeflow . To test whether continuity-aware chunk transitions improve dynamic performance, we evaluate RTC and ABPolicy. RTC uses inference-time inpainting to align new predictions with overlapping actions from the previous chunk without additional policy training~ black2025rtc . ABPolicy combines bidirectional prediction with continuity-constrained spline refitting. We adapt it to Cartesian actions and train the policy to predict spline control points~ yang2026abpolicyasynchronousbsplineflow . Motion Information and Policy Adaptation The interventions above change how the policy is executed, the last two change the policy itself. PUMA gives it information about how the object moves, and DSRL adjusts what it does with that information. PUMA incorporates historical optical flow and future object-centric feature supervision during training~ fang2026domino . DSRL trains a latent-space actor and critic while keeping the underlying VLA frozen~ wagenmaker2025steering . We use DSRL-SAC with a short visual history aggregated by a temporal convolution for the actor and critic, while the VLA retains its current-observation input.

title: EMS-Nav: Embodied Multi-Scale Navigation
summary: Industrial inspection robots must reach work areas and specific equipment. These destinations span spatial scales from regions to objects, so robots must relate each target to its surroundings to interpret the task and determine where to go. Existing methods support multi-scale navigation through rich environment representations, but at substantial computational and storage cost. These costs limit deployment where wireless coverage is incomplete and robots must rely on onboard computation to keep navigating. We introduce EMS-Nav, a biologically inspired multi-scale navigation framework for online, on-device operation. Its core innovation is to organize perception, spatial understanding, and navigation around regions, making local spaces the basic units of both environmental understanding and computation. EMS-Nav groups objects and their relationships into functionally meaningful spaces and builds a hierarchy from local areas to the broader environment. This organization supports efficient map construction alongside the interpretation and execution of language goals at different scales. In multi-scale navigation experiments, EMS-Nav achieves the highest success rates across all four target categories: objects, rooms, regions, and specific instances. It outperforms state-of-the-art open-vocabulary mapping and navigation methods, improving overall first-attempt success by 9.39 percentage points over the strongest baseline while reducing mapping overhead and language-model input size. Local deployment in real indoor environments further demonstrates its applicability to on-device embodied navigation. By establishing regions as the organizing basis for perception, spatial understanding, and language-guided action, EMS-Nav provides a system that combines multi-scale understanding with computational efficiency to support diverse language goals on resource-constrained robots.
full_text: Applications such as industrial inspection require robots to autonomously reach different work areas and specific pieces of equipment. These destinations span spatial scales from regions to objects, so robots must relate each target to its surroundings to interpret the task and determine where to go. Existing methods support multi-scale navigation through rich environment representations, but at substantial computational and storage cost. These costs limit deployment where wireless coverage is incomplete and robots must rely on onboard computation to keep navigating. We introduce EMS-Nav, a biologically inspired multi-scale navigation framework for online, on-device operation. Its core innovation is to organize perception, spatial understanding, and navigation around regions, making local spaces the basic units of both environmental understanding and computation. EMS-Nav groups objects and their relationships into functionally meaningful spaces and builds a hierarchy from local areas to the broader environment. This organization supports efficient map construction alongside the interpretation and execution of language goals at different scales. In multi-scale navigation experiments, EMS-Nav achieves the highest success rates across all four target categories: objects, rooms, regions, and specific instances. It outperforms representative state-of-the-art open-vocabulary mapping and navigation methods, improving overall first-attempt success by 9.39 percentage points over the strongest baseline while reducing mapping overhead and language-model input size. Local deployment in real indoor environments further demonstrates its applicability to on-device embodied navigation. By establishing regions as the organizing basis for perception, spatial understanding, and language-guided action, EMS-Nav provides a system that combines multi-scale understanding with computational efficiency to support diverse language goals on resource-constrained robots. Introduction sec:intro Navigation is a fundamental capability of embodied robots, connecting perception of the physical world to action within it. Mobile robots support warehouse logistics~ amazon2022navigation , hospital deliveries~ toyota2026potaro , industrial inspections~ anybotics2025deployment , and so on. These tasks require robots to identify destinations and navigate to them. When tasks are specified in natural language, destinations may be described at different spatial scales. A user may ask a robot to reach a room, a functional region, or an object, or combine these scales in one instruction. For example, ``Find the laptop on the mint-green computer desk in the office'' identifies the target through its room, desk attributes, and spatial relationship to the desk. Recognizing the laptop alone is insufficient: multi-scale semantic navigation requires connecting object details with their surrounding spaces~ hovsg,miao2026langmap . Existing studies support such multi-scale semantic navigation through hierarchical representations and spatial context. HOV-SG~ hovsg organizes floors, rooms, and objects to localize language goals, while SG-Nav~ yin2024sgnav uses relationships among objects, object groups, and rooms for object-goal search. LangMap~ miao2026langmap evaluates goals at the scene, room, region, and instance levels. However, constructing rich environment representations can incur substantial computation and storage costs~ conceptgraphs,hovsg . Where wireless coverage is incomplete, as in industrial inspection~ anybotics2023connectivity , robots must continue navigating with limited onboard compute and memory, constraining the deployment of these methods. To reduce these costs, other work explores more efficient map construction and use. Clio~ clio builds compact online scene graphs by retaining task-relevant objects and regions. OneMap~ onemap reuses semantic maps for successive object searches on embedded hardware, while FindAnything~ findanything improves object semantic map construction and storage efficiency. Despite these advances in semantic representation and efficiency, the object-level scene graph methods above largely follow an object-first paradigm: they first reconstruct individual objects, then use those representations to infer spatial relationships and higher-level structure. Separating object reconstruction from spatial organization creates two limitations for on-device multi-scale navigation: the cost of processing a growing body of object information, and the difficulty of recovering functional spaces from object representations. Building and interpreting an environment around objects places increasing computational demands on the system as the scene grows~ conceptgraphs,hovsg . As exploration extends, the map accumulates more objects and relationships. If a local change triggers reprocessing across a wider area, map maintenance and spatial interpretation repeatedly revisit unrelated object details. This mismatch consumes scarce on-device resources and limits efficient online mapping and spatial understanding as coverage expands. Object reconstruction may leave navigation-relevant spatial structure implicit. A laboratory's preparation, storage, and measurement areas can occupy the same room and contain similar object categories. Their differences depend on local layouts, boundaries, and arrangements of objects. Room boundaries alone cannot distinguish these areas, and object labels alone cannot determine their extent~ hydra,yin2024sgnav . The same function can also occur in different layouts, limiting the usefulness of fixed spatial partitions. Thus, even when a target object is already mapped, a robot may be unable to determine whether it lies in the functional space named by the instruction. Resolving this ambiguity requires a map that connects objects to the functional spaces they collectively form and represents hierarchical relationships among those spaces. Addressing these limitations poses three connected challenges for on-device multi-scale navigation. The first is to make sense of local space from partial observations: objects may be recognizable, but which objects form a coherent space, and how they should be organized, are not given. The second is to derive spatial hierarchies that align with everyday understanding and language. Functional relationships need not follow walls or fixed architectural levels, limiting predefined partitions. The third is to retrieve goal-relevant spatial knowledge under limited resources without processing every scale in each decision. When people seek a destination, they connect visible objects to their surroundings and draw on spatial knowledge at the scales relevant to the description. This motivates us to look to biological spatial cognition for design inspiration. Studies of local layout perception~ epstein1998local , hippocampal cognitive maps~ iaria2007maps , and prefrontal goal and contextual control~ koechlin2003control suggest a functional division among local perception, spatial integration, and goal-directed decisions. We draw from this division a design principle: use local spaces to connect object perception with understanding of the broader environment, and access different levels of spatial knowledge according to the navigation goal. This leads us to place regions at the center of perception, understanding, and navigation. We introduce EMS-Nav, a multi-scale language-guided navigation framework designed for online, on-device operation. Its core innovation is a region-centered organization that extends spatial structure beyond an interpretation added after object reconstruction, making it foundational to perception, understanding, and navigation (Figure~ fig:teaser ). EMS-Nav addresses the three challenges within a shared spatial organization. Perceptual structuring inspired by the scene-selective cortex (SSC) forms spatial units from local layouts and object relationships, establishing how the local environment is represented. Hippocampus-inspired spatial parsing constructs a multi-scale hierarchy from functional relationships, supporting spatial understanding beyond fixed room partitions. Goal-directed navigation inspired by the prefrontal cortex (PFC) selects knowledge at the scales relevant to an instruction and uses it to determine the destination. All three modules organize computation around regions: local changes are updated primarily within the relevant spaces, while broader understanding builds on region summaries. Resource constraints thus inform perception, parsing, and navigation throughout the framework. Our contributions are threefold: We introduce EMS-Nav, a multi-scale language-guided navigation framework for online, on-device operation. It connects environmental mapping, spatial understanding, and language-guided goal decisions, enabling robots to use a shared map for navigation instructions at different scales under limited computational resources. We propose a spatial organization that uses regions to connect perception with semantic parsing, making local spaces the basic units of both environmental understanding and computation. By extending object understanding to functional regions and their hierarchical relationships, this organization allows multi-scale spatial understanding and efficient mapping to support one another. Large-scale evaluation and real-world deployment demonstrate improvements in both multi-scale navigation and computational efficiency. Across 18,628 instructions covering object, room, region, and specific-instance targets, EMS-Nav achieves the highest navigation success rates in all four categories, outperforming representative state-of-the-art open-vocabulary mapping and navigation methods while reducing mapping overhead and language-model input size. Real-world deployment on an RTX 4060 Ti reaches a peak on-device processing throughput of 5.19 frames per second (FPS), further demonstrating the framework's practical applicability. We will release the source code for EMS-Nav. Related Work sec:related-work Language Goals and Multi-Scale Semantic Navigation Language-guided navigation requires robots to ground human descriptions in actionable goals in their environment. R2R pairs natural-language route instructions with panoramic trajectories through real indoor environments anderson2018r2r , while RxR extends this setting with multilingual instructions and spatiotemporal alignments ku2020rxr . VLN-CE extends instruction following to low-level actions in continuous environments~ krantz2020vlnce . These tasks primarily assess the ability to follow verbally described routes. Object-goal navigation instead focuses on finding a specified object; GOAT-Bench combines category, language, and image goals in sequential tasks khanna2024goatbench . LangMap's HieraNav further evaluates the understanding of spatial constraints through scene-, room-, region-, and instance-level goals miao2026langmap . Together, these tasks extend navigation requirements from object names to richer spatial contexts. A map must therefore support queries about the space containing a target and its surrounding context, as well as the target itself. Foundation-model navigation systems also differ in how they connect language to action. LM-Nav composes pretrained language, visual-language, and navigation models to ground instructions in a topological map~ shah2023lmnav . NavGPT reasons over textual observations and navigation history~ zhou2024navgpt , while NavGPT-2 combines visually grounded language reasoning with a learned policy~ zhou2025navgpt2 . NaVid instead predicts actions from instruction-conditioned RGB video history~ zhang2024navid . These approaches demonstrate that language-guided behavior can draw on different intermediate representations and observation histories. Our focus is the construction of spatial evidence itself: maintaining an environment representation in which object details remain connected to functional regions and

title: A physics-constrained deep reinforcement learning method for autonomous mission planning of Titan deep space probes
summary: Titan is a compelling target for future deep space exploration, while its extreme Earth-Titan distance and complex environment make continuous ground-in-the-loop planning impractical. Existing planning methods, primarily developed for Earth-observation scenarios, have limited generalizability to uncertain deep space conditions and adaptability to time-varying mission states. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a physics-constrained maskable proximal policy optimization (PCM-PPO) method for Titan autonomous mission planning. A Titan-specific discrete-time Markov decision process is established to characterize mission feasibility and resource constraints. A system dynamics and geometric model is incorporated to enhance physical representation, including central gravity, J2 perturbation, third-body attraction, and downlink occultation. To accommodate opportunity targets under a bounded action dimension, PCM-PPO organizes predefined and opportunity targets through a fixed-capacity target pool and represents the mission state with a target-wise state matrix and a global state vector. A physics-constrained action mask constructs an admissible decision domain from current mission states, guiding policy learning toward physically executable decisions and avoiding infeasible exploration. An integrated training strategy facilitates policy optimization under coupled constraints. Comparative, ablation, and uncertainty experiments validate the effectiveness of PCM-PPO. PCM-PPO provides a feasible and interpretable scheme for autonomous mission planning of Titan deep space probes.
full_text: Introduction 1 Deep space exploration is rapidly advancing toward increasingly distant and complex planetary environments, among which Titan, Saturn’s largest moon, has become a major target of scientific interest horst2017titan . Owing to its dense nitrogen-rich atmosphere, active hydrocarbon cycle, and potential prebiotic chemical environment, Titan is considered one of the most compelling bodies for astrobiological investigation in the solar system hayes2016lakes,raulin2012prebiotic . Its scientific significance has been highlighted by the Cassini-Huygens mission spilker2019cassini and is further reinforced by the ongoing development of NASA’s Dragonfly rotorcraft mission barnes2021science . However, the extreme Earth–Titan distance leads to substantial communication delays, making continuous ground-in-the-loop mission management increasingly impractical nixon2018titan . Therefore, future Titan deep space probes require advanced onboard autonomous mission planning capabilities to generate and adapt observation schedules with limited human intervention. Deep space mission planning is inherently an NP-hard optimization problem lemaitre2002selecting,qi2024mission,junhui2026relaxed , since numerous observation tasks must be coordinated under limited time windows, onboard resources, and multiple constraints zhang2024trajectory,gu2022large . A large number of researchers have proposed various optimization methods, including heuristic, metaheuristic, and multi-objective evolutionary approaches qi2024cooperative . Heuristic methods typically improve planning efficiency by exploiting problem-specific structures or scheduling rules song2022two,chang2023solving,wang2018exact . For example, Rigo et al. rigo2022branch developed a branch-and-price algorithm for nanosatellite task scheduling by combining Dantzig–Wolfe decomposition with dynamic programming-based column generation, thereby improving mission quality of service. Chien et al. chien2015heuristic proposed a greedy constructive onboard rescheduling strategy for an Earth-observing spacecraft, which enables rapid response through model-based constraint handling. Metaheuristic algorithms have also been widely adopted to enhance global search capability in large-scale combinatorial planning problems shang2025joint . Liu et al. liu2017adaptive proposed an adaptive large neighborhood search method for agile satellite scheduling with time-dependent transition times. Similarly, Han et al. han2022simulated designed an improved simulated-annealing-based heuristic to address multiple agile satellite scheduling under cloud coverage uncertainty. Zhang et al. zhang2022improved further formulated an integrated satellite imaging and data transmission scheduling problem and solved it using an improved genetic algorithm. For scenarios involving multiple conflicting objectives, multi-objective evolutionary methods have been introduced wu2022ensemble . Tangpattanakul et al. tangpattanakul2015multi developed an indicator-based multi-objective local search heuristic for agile satellite observation scheduling, and Du et al. du2019moea proposed MOEA-based memetic algorithms for satellite range scheduling to simultaneously optimize competing scheduling objectives. However, autonomous mission planning for Titan exploration is considerably more challenging than conventional satellite scheduling problems. A Titan deep space probe operates in a multi-body dynamical environment and must perform observation and downlink tasks under strict geometric, visibility, and communication constraints. Furthermore, mission execution is complicated by additional uncertainties and operational requirements, including stochastic cloud occlusion, solar avoidance constraints, and time-varying scientific utility of candidate targets. In addition, probes must continuously coordinate strongly coupled onboard resources under mutually exclusive observation and transmission modes. Under such conditions, these traditional methods show clear limitations in highly uncertain and dynamically changing deep space environments. Rule-based heuristic methods usually rely heavily on handcrafted designs, metaheuristic methods are often parameter-sensitive and prone to local optima, and multi-objective evolutionary algorithms still struggle to capture the complex mapping between uncertainty, mission states, and planning decisions. Therefore, they are inadequate for deep space autonomous mission planning that requires rapid response and online adaptation under uncertainty. To address the above limitations of traditional optimization methods, researchers have increasingly introduced reinforcement learning (RL) into mission planning and scheduling problems su2024novel,yang2023impact . RL has shown strong potential for modeling multiple sequential decision processes and resource-constrained operations in spacecraft planning and Earth-observing satellite scheduling zhu2025constrained,qiu2021scheduling . For example, He et al. he2020generic formulated agile Earth observation satellite scheduling as a generic Markov decision process (MDP) and solved it using RL, while Wang et al. wang2022deep developed a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) method for autonomous collaborative mission planning of high- and low-orbit agile Earth-observing satellites. Wen et al. wen2023scheduling further incorporated a hybrid actor-critic framework to jointly schedule observation and transmission tasks. Herrmann et al. herrmann2023reinforcement investigated RL for on-board scheduling of agile Earth-observing satellites, and subsequent studies extended this line toward scalable multi-satellite operations and distributed cooperation. Building on these developments, Liang et al. liang2023fast proposed a DRL approach for rapid satellite range rescheduling. Li et al. li2024mission introduced an attention-based DRL method for distributed mission planning of multiple agile Earth-observing satellites. More recently, DRL has continued to evolve toward more structured and adaptive mission planners. Wang et al. wang2025deep proposed an improved DRL framework for agile Earth observation satellite scheduling with variable image duration. Zhou et al. zhou2025deep developed a two-phase hybrid DRL framework for multi-agile Earth observation satellite scheduling, and Li et al. li2025mission presented a mission sequence model with DRL for dynamic multi-satellite replanning. Meanwhile, Qi et al. qi2024cooperative formulated an MDP model integrating mission planning and proposed the PB-PPO algorithm. Yao et al.~ yao2026meta investigated a meta-reinforcement learning method for dynamic mission scheduling of Earth observation satellites. Li and Dong xuedong2025expert further proposed an expert-guided hierarchical RL framework for collaborative mission planning in low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite clusters, improving policy interpretability and robustness under uncertainty. However, most existing RL-based studies still focus on LEO satellite scenarios, whereas autonomous mission planning for deep space exploration in the Saturnian system remains far less explored. Moreover, many existing methods rely on relatively simplified dynamics and uncertainty patterns and still encounter substantial difficulties in representing high-dimensional mission states, handling strongly constrained and dynamically varying feasible action sets, and optimizing long-horizon sequential decision-making processes. In particular, opportunity targets in deep space missions may become available during mission execution. These limitations restrict their applicability to autonomous Titan mission planning under complex deep space conditions. To address the above issues, we propose a DRL method, termed physics-constrained maskable proximal policy optimization (PCM-PPO), for Titan deep space probes. Specifically, a discrete-time Markov decision process (MDP) is formulated to characterize the coupled physical constraints, resource evolution, dynamic target availability, and uncertainties in Titan mission planning. Within the PCM-PPO framework, a fixed-capacity target pool is introduced to represent predefined targets and dynamically arriving opportunity targets under a bounded action dimension. Based on this representation, the mission state is organized into a target-wise state matrix and a global mission-state vector, which enables target-level attributes and global mission conditions to be represented separately. The actor network generates action logits through a shared target encoder, a context network, and a target-scoring function, so that active targets are evaluated according to their current mission attributes and global planning context. In addition, a physics-constrained action masking mechanism is introduced to construct the admissible decision domain from Titan-specific mission states, including target-slot occupancy, geometric observability, Deep Space Network (DSN) availability, task-completion status, solar safety, cloud visibility, and resource safety. Thus, action sampling and policy updating are restricted to physically executable decisions rather than the full unconstrained action space. An integrated training strategy is further employed to facilitate policy optimization under high-dimensional mission states and strongly coupled constraints. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: (1) A Titan-specific discrete-time MDP is formulated for autonomous Titan mission planning. By incorporating a system dynamics and geometric model with perturbation, third-body attraction, and downlink occultation, the formulation integrates multi-body orbital dynamics, observation and downlink feasibility, onboard resource evolution, dynamic target availability, time-varying target utility, and environmental uncertainties into a unified planning framework. (2) The PCM-PPO method is introduced by integrating target pool-based state representation, target-conditioned policy modeling, and a Titan-specific physics-constrained action mask. A fixed-capacity target pool representation is introduced to accommodate predefined targets and dynamically arriving opportunity targets under a bounded action dimension. Based on this representation, the mission state is organized into a target-wise state matrix and a global mission-state vector, and the actor generates action logits through a shared target encoder, a context network, and a target-scoring function. (3) A Titan-specific physics-constrained action mask is constructed from the current mission state to define the admissible decision domain. By encoding target-slot availability, observation geometry, DSN availability, stochastic visibility, task-completion status, solar safety, and resource safety constraints into a unified feasibility mapping, the mask restricts action sampling and policy updating to physically executable decisions and reduces ineffective exploration over infeasible actions. (4) An integrated training strategy is also incorporated to support policy optimization under high-dimensional mission states and strongly coupled constraints. Comprehensive simulations are conducted under varying target loads, long-horizon evaluation scenarios, ablation settings, and uncertain mission conditions. The experimental results validate the effectiveness of PCM-PPO for autonomous mission planning of Titan deep space probes. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. formulates the Titan autonomous mission planning problem, including the system dynamics and geometric model, environmental uncertainty and resource model, and logical feasibility and operational constraints. introduces the PCM-PPO method, including the Markov decision process formulation, physics-constrained action masking mechanism, network structure, and integrated training process. presents the experimental studies, including training convergence, comparative evaluations under varying target loads, long-horizon tests, ablation and sens

title: Recover, Don't Just Continue: Learning from Feedback for Physical Failure Understanding and Correction
summary: Multimodal large language models are regarded as the cognitive foundation of embodied intelligence, but planning from instructions alone cannot make them reliable. During execution, actions deviate from intended effects, constrained by the embodiment and environment. An embodied brain must understand why execution deviates, identify what can be reliably realized, and revise decisions using interaction experience. These correspond to causal failure localization, capability-constrained adaptation, and experience-driven revision. Current embodied foundation models largely lack these capabilities. To address this, we introduce Embodied-Corrector. We construct failure-recovery data by injecting perturbations at subtask boundaries of successful trajectories, replaying affected subtasks, and keeping failures that are observable from public evidence and recoverable from the current state. We align actions, consequences, failure causes, and recoveries into Judge-Cause-Sub-Fine supervision. Training uses evaluation-first SFT: the model learns Judge and Cause first, then Sub and Fine conditioned on accurate prefixes. Since deployment uses self-generated prefixes, evaluation errors propagate into recovery planning, and response-level rewards are too coarse to locate affected planning tokens. We therefore use OPD to internalize the planning distribution under accurate prefixes into that under self-generated ones: the model generates plans from self-generated prefixes, while a contrastive forward pass with accurate prefixes compares token probabilities to reinforce or suppress planning tokens. At deployment, this branch is removed. Experiments show stronger failure analysis and corrective planning: with a frozen VLA, composite task success improves by 6.1 percentage points; with fixed GPT-5.5 execution, manipulation and navigation tasks improve by 13.9 percentage points.
full_text: Experiments sec:experiments We first evaluate execution understanding and corrective planning on EmbodiedDiag-Bench, followed by transfer to EB-ALFRED. Harness-level experiments then test two mutually exclusive simulated execution settings: code workflows with the VLA function disabled, and VLA-only workflows with all analytic robot functions disabled. We next analyze post-training dynamics and corrective judgments as subtask rewards, and conclude with physical validation on the Piper platform. Brain-Level Evaluation sec:brain_eval Corrective reasoning on EmbodiedDiag-Bench. We first remove the code and action executors and directly test whether the brain can produce a coherent correction from a completed physical execution. EmbodiedDiag-Bench contains held-out navigation and manipulation failures and evaluates four fields. Judge determines whether the current subtask was completed, Cause identifies the failed entity, relation, and outcome, Sub decides whether to advance or complete the current subtask again, and Fine specifies the required actions, grounded arguments, ordering, and intermediate checks. Table~ tab:diagnosis shows that general VLMs can occasionally distinguish success from failure, but their substantially lower Cause and Fine scores indicate that outcome recognition alone does not yield a usable correction. SFT substantially improves consistency among the four fields, while NEPO provides the most balanced performance across navigation and manipulation. It reaches Judge accuracies of 79.6 and 81.2 , Cause accuracies of 58.2 and 54.6 , and at least 63.7 on all four recovery-planning scores. The model therefore learns a relation between a failure cause and the way the interrupted subtask should be executed. Transfer to an external planning benchmark. title: MOSAIC: Modular Obstacle and Spatial-Aware Framework for Manipulation In Cluttered Scenes
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong performance in robotic manipulation, yet most rely primarily on 2D visual observations and language instructions, leaving scene geometry and obstacle relationships to be inferred implicitly. This limitation is particularly problematic in cluttered environments, where small spatial errors can lead to unintended contacts or collisions. We propose MOSAIC, a modular spatial- and obstacle-aware framework that can be integrated with pretrained VLA policies to improve object-level scene understanding and action generation. Our method augments the VLA backbone with an auxiliary semantic grounding task that predicts role-specific masks for the target object, destination region, and surrounding obstacles. We further combine the target and destination masks with depth estimated from 3D scene reconstruction to construct role-specific geometric tokens that are injected directly into the action expert. In addition, we propose obstacle-aware attention supervision that emphasizes obstacles near the robot body during task execution. The resulting attention features are subsequently injected into later action-expert layers to further guide action generation. Together, these components provide explicit semantic, geometric, and obstacle-aware cues while preserving the underlying pretrained VLA architecture. We evaluate our framework on pretrained VLA model using the RoboPRO benchmark, including visual perturbation tests, and further validate it on real-world manipulation tasks. MOSAIC improves the success rate by 5.1% in cluttered scenes, and by 9.7% under visual perturbations, with gains of up to 25.0% in the most challenging environment. We will release our code and dataset upon acceptance at the following Github page: https://mmahdavian.github.io/MOSAIC/
full_text: Methodology Our motivation is to develop modular components that enhance the object-level scene understanding of VLA models and improve their performance in cluttered environments, which is detailed in Fig.~ fig:main . We first describe the general VLA architecture in Section~ sec:vla . Then in Section~ sec:masks , we introduce our semantic mask generation module and explain how the action expert is conditioned on the resulting representations implicitly. In Section~ sec:inject , we describe how object-level depth information is injected into the action expert. Finally, Section~ sec:attn presents our attention-guidance strategy, which directs the action expert toward both the target object and surrounding obstacles. Preliminaries: Vision-Language-Action Model sec:vla A shared vision--language backbone encodes the visual observation and language instruction into a contextual prefix, while a smaller action expert generates a horizon of robot actions as a suffix conditioned on these features. Information flows from the backbone to the action expert through attention, while the backbone representations remain independent of the generated action tokens. Given a multi-view observation \(I=\ I_v\ _ v=1 ^ V \) and a language instruction \( \) (with proprioceptive state embedded as discrete tokens), the vision encoder and language tower produce a sequence. Suffix attention is causal over the action tokens and is allowed to read the entire prefix through a cross-attention block. The attention mask allows action tokens to attend to the contextualized vision--language features while preserving causal attention among actions. The resulting and denote the corresponding hidden representations ( ) with only decoded into an action-space velocity. where \( _t\) is the instantaneous velocity of the action chunk in flow space. Semantic Mask Generation for Objects sec:masks To improve the VLA model's understanding of its environment, we propose auxiliary semantic mask prediction task within the VLM backbone. As Fig.~ fig:main (a) shows, the masks are divided into three task-specific roles: the target object, destination region, and surrounding obstacles. This role-specific representation helps the model preserve their distinct semantics and use them appropriately during action generation. Given the visual observation and the contextual information extracted from the language instruction, the backbone learns to predict these semantic regions jointly with its standard representations. We reserve a dedicated token group for each role, \(e^r\), containing \(K\) tokens, and append it to the VLM prefix. where \( \) denotes the visual encoder's image tokens and \( \) the tokenized prompt. These role tokens participate in bidirectional prefix attention together with the visual and language tokens, therefore each group encodes task-conditioned visual context for its semantic role rather than a generic objectness signal. Following the shared vision--language forward pass, a dedicated mask head uses the role tokens to attend to the primary-camera patch grid. The \(K\) tokens of role \(r\) are then mean-pooled into a single query, and the three queries ( ) independently decode target, destination, and obstacle masks over the same image. A coarse semantic map is first predicted from the visual patch grid and then refined with a shallow RGB residual branch to preserve fine object boundaries. Each valid semantic role is supervised independently using weighted binary cross-entropy, soft Dice, and boundary losses, with the final objective averaged only over valid roles. This avoids penalizing tasks in which a destination or obstacle is absent. The resulting masks preserve clear role distinctions between the target object, destination region, and surrounding obstacles while maintaining accurate boundaries. During action generation, as Fig.~ fig:main (b) demonstrates, each suffix action token attends to the complete VLM prefix, including the role-specific mask tokens: This transfers the disentangled grounding from the VLM backbone to the action expert, so the predicted flow velocity \( _t\) and therefore the executed action chunk can explicitly reason about the object to manipulate, its destination, and the surrounding obstacles. Object Depth Injection into Action Expert sec:inject To improve the action expert's understanding of task-relevant objects, as in Fig.~ fig:main (c), we extract object-level depth information and incorporate it directly into the action-generation process. Specifically, we provide metric depth cues for the target object and destination region according to their semantic roles. A frozen 3D scene reconstruction decoder, \( \), maps the primary-camera image to a scene depth map and confidence map, \((D,C)= (I_ )\). Then the backbone mask head predicts the role-specific masks \(M^ r \). For each role, only pixels with valid depth range and sufficient confidence are retained. The resulting geometric information is processed independently for each semantic role rather than being merged into a single point cloud. Using these masks, we construct two complementary geometric encodings. The first is a compact statistics token: The statistics token captures the masked image centroid, , the bounding region, , and the mean, minimum, and standard deviation of the depth, . While this representation provides the global image location and depth distribution of each semantic role, it does not preserve local geometric variations within the region. To retain this spatial information, we introduce a second encoding by partitioning the same region into a grid (G=4). Each grid cell is represented by its center and mean metric depth . A shared projection module composed of LayerNorm, GELU, and a linear layer maps both the global statistics vector and the local grid features to the action-expert embedding dimension. Finally, a learned role embedding is added to each token, allowing the action expert to distinguish between target and destination representations even when their geometric features are similar. This results in geometry tokens for each semantic role, forming where . These geometry tokens are then added to the noisy action-token sequence before being processed by the action expert. Action queries attend to \( ^ \) only in the final six layers of the action expert. This allows the earlier layers to primarily reason from the VLM prefix, including the semantic mask tokens, while the final layers refine the predicted actions using explicit metric geometry. We found that the same representation is not suitable for surrounding obstacles. Therefore, obstacle information is incorporated using the attention-guidance strategy described in Section~ sec:attn . The obstacle contact mask is multiplied pixel-wise by the aggregated proximity weight map prior to spatial heatmap generation, i.e. , where is initialized as all ones and entry is updated to if object 's segmentation mask occupies pixel . The resulting block is resized and passes through a dedicated AttentionQueryHead, which learns a residual on the attention values in log-space. title: CARE-Drive: Coupled Alternating Refinement for Ego-trajectories
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models bring multimodal understanding and world knowledge to end-to-end autonomous driving. To further improve the quality of predicted trajectories, existing studies introduce candidate refinement, residual denoising, and token correction. However, these methods typically focus on unified refinement of the entire trajectory, paying limited attention to the distinct physical quantities and their interactions. We further investigate physical specialization and coordination in trajectory refinement, centering on position and heading for simpler and more intuitive correction modeling. To this end, we propose CARE-Drive (Coupled Alternating Refinement for Ego-trajectories), which decomposes trajectory refinement into waypoint residual correction and position-conditioned heading generation. Through imitation learning and a future-token auxiliary task, the backbone provides predictive representations and a base trajectory. The position expert predicts bounded metric waypoint residuals, while the heading expert reconstructs vehicle orientation from adjacent angular increments conditioned on the corrected path. With the backbone frozen, the two experts are optimized alternately through supervised initialization and reinforcement fine-tuning. This design simplifies refinement through clear physical specialization while preserving conditional coupling during prediction and optimization. On NAVSIM v1, CARE-Drive achieves 88.8 PDMS, improving by 2.4 points over the unrefined base trajectories generated by the same backbone. Ablation studies further support the effectiveness of specialized experts and staged training.

Introduction Autonomous driving models draw on complementary perception and prediction architectures. Convolutional and Transformer-based encoders extract camera or bird's-eye-view (BEV) features for planning~ uniad , while vision--language models (VLMs) provide pretrained multimodal understanding and a language-generation interface~ autovla,qwen3vl . World models capture temporal structure through video generation~ drivelaw,epona or latent prediction. Joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) methods predict target representations without requiring pixel reconstruction~ vjepa . CoWorld-VLA~ coworld illustrates how predictive representations can complement a VLM backbone. VLMs are particularly attractive because their language interface supports instruction following and visual question answering. Future-feature supervision can additionally train the same backbone to anticipate scene evolution in latent space~ coworld . This provides an architectural basis for combining world-future reasoning with language interaction, while exposing shared features for action planning. Action generation and refinement can use direct trajectory regression, autoregressive physical-action decoding~ autovla , iterative diffusion~ diffusiondrive , or candidate evaluation~ wote . Reinforcement fine-tuning further adapts policies to planning rewards~ autovla . Residual correction offers a complementary approach: adjusting an initial trajectory with targeted updates. For physically interpretable refinement, the key question is how to assign these updates to quantities with distinct roles, such as position and heading. As shown in Figure~ fig:framework , we propose , a future-supervised VLA framework with physically meaningful correction experts. A Qwen3-VL-2B backbone learns predictive representations and an initial trajectory. A position expert predicts bounded XY residuals, and a heading expert reconstructs orientation from adjacent angular increments conditioned on corrected positions and shared features. This gives each expert an explicit physical target and makes heading refinement responsive to position changes. The experts are optimized with the backbone frozen, keeping correction learning modular and the backbone's language-generation interface structurally intact. Deployment produces one trajectory through greedy decoding. Our contributions are twofold: An effective world--action framework. We propose , integrating future-supervised representation learning with staged trajectory refinement for end-to-end driving. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 demonstrate favorable planning performance.
