title: ThermalSplat: Generalizable Pose-Free Gaussian Splatting for Sparse-View Thermal 3D Reconstruction
summary: Thermal infrared imaging is vital for applications like search-and-rescue and autonomous navigation, yet trans- lating it into 3D scene representations remains a critical bottleneck. The low-texture nature and view-dependent emissivity of thermal images cause standard pose estima- tors to fail catastrophically, collapsing standard 3D Gaus- sian Splatting pipelines under sparse-view constraints. Fur- thermore, existing thermal reconstruction methods rely heavily on dense capture and computationally expensive per-scene optimization. Critically, many of these ap- proaches depend on aligned RGB-thermal datasets to ob- tain reliable camera poses and initial point clouds, ren- dering them unusable in purely thermal, unposed envi- ronments. To break this bottleneck, we present Thermal- Splat, the first generalizable, feed-forward Gaussian splat- ting framework that reconstructs 3D scenes directly from sparse thermal images without requiring known camera poses, RGB guidance, or per-scene training. We over- come thermal-specific challenges using a soft census loss for brightness-invariant structural matching and a bound- ary structure loss to explicitly supervise temperature discon- tinuities. Trained on an aggregated multi-source dataset, ThermalSplat synthesizes sharp reconstructions of unseen scenes in a single feed-forward pass. Extensive experi- ments demonstrate that ThermalSplat holds a strict advan- tage over scene-specific thermal splatting methods in the sparse regime. Furthermore, even compared against these baselines operating under their ideal dense capture set- tings, ThermalSplat achieves superior perceptual fidelity. By eliminating the need for computationally expensive per scene optimization, ThermalSplat offers an efficient and generalizable approach to thermal 3D reconstruction.
full_text: Thermal infrared imaging is vital for applications like search-and-rescue and autonomous navigation, yet translating it into 3D scene representations remains a critical bottleneck. The low-texture nature and view-dependent emissivity of thermal images cause standard pose estimators to fail catastrophically, collapsing standard 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines under sparse-view constraints. Furthermore, existing thermal reconstruction methods rely heavily on dense capture and computationally expensive per-scene optimization. Critically, many of these approaches depend on aligned RGB-thermal datasets to obtain reliable camera poses and initial point clouds, rendering them unusable in purely thermal, unposed environments. To break this bottleneck, we present ThermalSplat, the first generalizable, feed-forward Gaussian splatting framework that reconstructs 3D scenes directly from sparse thermal images without requiring known camera poses, RGB guidance, or per-scene training. We overcome thermal-specific challenges using a soft census loss for brightness-invariant structural matching and a boundary structure loss to explicitly supervise temperature discontinuities. Trained on an aggregated multi-source dataset, ThermalSplat synthesizes sharp reconstructions of unseen scenes in a single feed-forward pass. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ThermalSplat holds a strict advantage over scene-specific thermal splatting methods in the sparse regime. Furthermore, even compared against these baselines operating under their ideal dense capture settings, ThermalSplat achieves superior perceptual fidelity. By eliminating the need for computationally expensive per scene optimization, ThermalSplat offers an efficient and generalizable approach to thermal 3D reconstruction. Introduction sec:intro Thermal infrared imaging has become an indispensable sensing modality across a wide range of real-world applications, from search-and-rescue operations and building energy diagnostics to infrastructure inspection and autonomous navigation under adverse lighting and weather conditions. Unlike visible-light cameras, thermal sensors capture emitted radiance rather than reflected light, enabling perception in complete darkness, smoke, and fog. Yet despite this practical utility, translating thermal imaging into robust 3D scene representations remains a largely underexplored and highly challenging bottleneck. The challenge is fundamental. Thermal images are inherently low-texture and low-contrast. Scenes appear as smooth gradients of emitted heat, with object boundaries defined by temperature discontinuities rather than the rich surface texture and colour variation that visible-light reconstruction pipelines rely upon. Spatial resolution is typically lower than RGB cameras, and standard feature detectors and matchers trained on visible imagery transfer poorly to the thermal domain~ usamentiaga2014infrared . As demonstrated in Table~ tab:sfm , due to these properties and the severe view-dependent emissivity, classical Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines like COLMAP~ schonberger2016structure , and even recent feed-forward pose estimators like VGGT~ wang2025vggt , fail catastrophically at extracting reliable camera poses or initial point clouds under sparse capture conditions. Consequently, standard multi-view reconstruction and 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines collapse when applied to sparse thermal inputs. While sparse-view 3D reconstruction has seen remarkable progress in the visible-light domain through feed-forward Gaussian splatting methods~ chen2024mvsplat,charatan2024pixelsplat,huang2026none , these models are trained exclusively on large-scale RGB datasets. Applying them zero-shot to thermal inputs produces perceptually degraded reconstructions that blur critical temperature boundaries and produce inconsistent intensity fields across novel views. Concurrently, the thermal reconstruction literature has successfully modelled emitted radiance through methods such as PhysIR~ gao2026physir , ThermalGaussian~ lu2024thermalgaussian , Thermal3D-GS~ chen2026thermal3d , ThermoNeRF~ hassan2025thermonerf , and Thermal-NeRF~ lin2024thermalnerf . However, a critical limitation unifying all of these thermal methods is their reliance on dense multi-view capture and computationally expensive per-scene optimization. Crucially, to bypass the low-texture nature of thermal images, most of these methods typically depend on aligned RGB-thermal datasets to obtain reliable Structure-from-Motion (SfM) initializations and camera poses. For instance, models like ThermalGaussian actively rely on paired RGB images, often utilizing composite formats like MSX, to extract poses and provide rich texture guidance. Because they depend on visible-light data to bootstrap the underlying geometry, these existing works fail in purely thermal, unposed operational environments. None addresses the sparse-view setting in a generalizable, pose-free manner. To break this bottleneck, we ask: can a generalizable, feed-forward sparse-view reconstruction framework be made to work reliably in the thermal domain without known poses, RGB guidance, or per-scene training? We answer affirmatively with ThermalSplat, the first generalizable, feed-forward Gaussian splatting framework for sparse-view thermal 3D reconstruction. Built on NAS3R~ huang2026none , a large pose-free multi-view geometry backbone, ThermalSplat is adapted to the thermal modality through three complementary contributions. First, we construct an aggregated multi-source thermal training corpus from five publicly available datasets spanning indoor, outdoor, and aerial scenes. Second, to address the blurring of structural boundaries, we introduce a boundary loss that explicitly preserves the temperature discontinuities that constitute the primary geometric cues in thermal imagery. Third, to resolve the intensity shifts caused by view-dependent emissivity and sensor auto-ranging, we introduce a census loss that preserves local intensity relationships despite radiometric variations. Extensive evaluations on held-out thermal scenes demonstrate that ThermalSplat synthesizes sharp, multi-view consistent reconstructions of entirely unseen scenes in a single feed-forward pass. By combining thermal-specific adaptation with tailored structural supervision, our approach significantly surpasses existing generalizable frameworks fine-tuned on thermal data. More importantly, ThermalSplat establishes a strict advantage over scene-specific thermal Gaussian splatting methods in the sparse regime, and achieves superior perceptual fidelity even when these baselines are provided with their ideal dense capture settings, delivering exceptionally faithful thermal representations. We introduce ThermalSplat, the first generalizable feed-forward framework for sparse-view thermal 3D reconstruction. It successfully eliminates the need for camera poses, RGB assisted SfM initialization and per-scene optimization, setting a new state-of-the-art standard for the thermal domain. We strategically adapt a boundary loss and a census loss to address the geometric and structural challenges unique to thermal imagery. By integrating these structural losses, our framework seamlessly handles view-dependent emissivity and sensor auto-ranging while preserving critical temperature discontinuities without requiring external depth supervision. We conduct comprehensive experiments demonstrating that ThermalSplat . Our method significantly surpasses existing generalizable frameworks fine-tuned on thermal data, and it outperforms scene-specific thermal baselines in the sparse regime. Related Work sec:related Generalizable Gaussian Splatting. Classical novel view synthesis pipelines combine Structure from Motion (SfM)~ schonberger2016structure and Multi-View Stereo to recover camera poses and geometry before optimizing scene-specific representations. Recent advances in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)~ mildenhall2021nerf and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233d substantially improve rendering quality, but both rely on dense multi-view observations and per-scene optimization, making them brittle under sparse capture constraints. Generalizable feed-forward approaches address this by learning scene priors from large-scale datasets. PixelSplat~ charatan2024pixelsplat and MVSplat~ chen2024mvsplat introduced feed-forward Gaussian splatting from image pairs using depth estimation techniques. Recent methods have progressively eliminated the dependence on calibrated camera poses. SPFSplat~ huang2025no and NAS3R~ huang2026none achieve fully unposed reconstruction through joint pose prediction and global cross-view reasoning. Despite their success, all existing generalizable methods are trained exclusively on visible-light RGB datasets. Their learned priors and assumed appearance statistics fundamentally fail to transfer to the thermal domain. Thermal 3D Reconstruction. Thermal scene reconstruction has primarily focused on adapting NeRF and 3DGS through scene-specific optimization. ThermalGaussian~ lu2024thermalgaussian introduced thermal 3DGS by jointly optimizing RGB and thermal representations, while methods like Thermal3D-GS~ chen2026thermal3d and PhysIR-Splat~ gao2026physir explicitly model infrared-specific imaging physics to achieve physically consistent rendering. Similarly, ThermoNeRF~ hassan2025thermonerf , Thermal-NeRF~ lin2024thermalnerf , and ThermalMix~ ozer2024exploring explore joint multimodal scene representations, and Wild-Thermal~ aydin2026thermal addresses radiometric fluctuations through photometric stabilization. However, a critical limitation unifies the current literature: these methods universally rely on dense multi-view capture and computationally expensive per-scene optimization. In contrast, ThermalSplat is the first generalizable, feed-forward Gaussian splatting framework designed explicitly for unposed, sparse-view thermal reconstruction without requiring per-scene training. Dataset sec:data Aggregated Thermal Corpus No single existing thermal dataset provides sufficient volume and diversity for training a generalizable reconstruction model from scratch. We therefore aggregate scenes from five publicly available multi-view thermal datasets: MVTV~ xu2024leveraging , ThermalGaussian~ lu2024thermalgaussian , Thermal3DGS~ chen2026thermal3d , ThermalMix~ ozer2024exploring , and ThermoNeRF~ hassan2025thermonerf . Together these span indoor objects, outdoor structures, building facades, low-light scenes, and UAV aerial captures, providing a diverse range of scene types. Preprocessing Raw thermal images are single-channel grayscale with scene-dependent radiometric ranges, posing two compatibility issues for the RGB-pretrained backbone. First, to bridge the channel mismatch without modifying the network architecture, each single-channel thermal frame is replicated across three channels to satisfy the input requirements of the backbone. Second, since different thermal cameras operate with different radiometric ranges, calibration settings, and sensor characteristics, a scene-level global normalisation is applied to map all image intensities to a consistent range. To suppress the influence of outlier intensities arising from sensor artifacts or isolated hot spots, normalisation is performed using robust percentile bounds computed across all frames in the sequence. Specifically, each pixel intensity is normalised as: where and denote the lower and upper percentile values computed globally across the scene, with corresponding to the 1st and 99th percentiles~ Gonzalez2008 . Values of are subsequently clipped to to handle the small fraction of pixels that fall outside the percentile bounds. Frame-to-frame radiometric drift, a known characteristic of thermal sensors, is additionally suppressed by removing slow global intensity trends across the sequence prior to scene-level scaling. title: Visibility-Aware Task and Motion Planning with Task-Centric Perception
summary: Long-horizon manipulation under uncertainty remains a challenging problem in robotics. We present \ourmethod{}, an algorithm for Visibility-Aware Task and Motion Planning. \ourmethod{} extends existing deterministic task and motion planning solvers to partially observable object rearrangement tasks, while still being able to take advantage of the efficiency and compositional generalization over long horizons of the base solver. This extension interleaves sensing actions into a plan skeleton that assumed full observability, and uses a novel persistent object-based memory to fuse observations into object mesh hypotheses and an observed occupancy map. We evaluate \ourmethod{} on real-world tabletop rearrangement tasks which feature heavy occlusion and partial visibility and demonstrate that it outperforms baselines that do not perform active perception or have persistent memory.
full_text: Long-horizon manipulation under uncertainty remains a challenging problem in robotics. We present , an algorithm for Visibility-Aware Task and Motion Planning. extends existing deterministic task and motion planning solvers to partially observable object rearrangement tasks, while still being able to take advantage of the efficiency and compositional generalization over long horizons of the base solver. This extension interleaves sensing actions into a plan skeleton that assumed full observability, and uses a novel persistent object-based memory to fuse observations into object mesh hypotheses and an observed occupancy map. We evaluate on real-world tabletop rearrangement tasks which feature heavy occlusion and partial visibility and demonstrate that it outperforms baselines that do not perform active perception or have persistent memory. INTRODUCTION sec:intro A longstanding challenge in robotic manipulation is completing long-horizon tasks in heavily occluded environments with unfamiliar objects. When object models and poses are known a priori, Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) solvers~ garrett2020pddlstream, shen2024differentiable can efficiently compose manipulation skills to achieve a goal. Otherwise, object models can be estimated from an observation and passed to a TAMP solver~ curtis2022long,shen2026tiptop . These approaches assume that the initial observation models the scene accurately enough to find a goal-achieving plan. Consider a tabletop rearrangement task, such as the one illustrated in Figure~ fig:teaser , where the robot has to place the cleaning supplies on the red tray. In the initial observation, the full extent of the tray (which already has other cleaning supplies on it) is not visible to the robot, and the cleaning supplies that the robot has to manipulate are partially occluded by the cardboard boxes. This setting is partially observable; the robot does not know the full shape of any of the objects in the scene, and thus it must make a plan from raw observations which are noisy and incomplete. The naive approach to this problem, re-estimating and replanning with every new observation, suffers from two main shortcomings. First, any single observation is not sufficient to accurately model the scene. Second, TAMP solvers output strictly goal-oriented plans, meaning that they cannot direct the perception toward the task-relevant parts of the scene or remove occluding objects. In Figure~ fig:teaser , no single view shows the far edge of the tray, and a plan that only reaches for the eraser never looks behind the boxes that occlude it. On the other end of the spectrum, belief space planners explicitly model uncertainty in the environment state and search for plans by reasoning over full observation distributions obtained by each action~ curtis2022task, bry2011rapidly, platt2016efficient, hauser2010randomized . However, modeling geometric uncertainty requires reasoning over extremely high-dimensional distributions which quickly becomes intractable. Our approach exploits the compositional generalization and efficiency of TAMP solvers while tracking object model accuracy and unobserved regions of space. augments off-the-shelf TAMP solvers with action constraints requiring the robot to verify its object models before interacting with the objects. These constraints induce information gathering actions that provide observations for refining the models. In order to build and refine our scene representation as we observe more of the scene and objects move, we define an Object-Based Memory module (OBM). The OBM collects a history of observations and maintains two complementary representations of the scene. The first representation is an occupancy grid, which accumulates depth data and tracks the regions of space that have not yet been observed. The second representation is a set of objects that are believed to exist in the scene after being detected in individual observations. The OBM associates these detections on a per-object basis and leverages a generative image-to-3D reconstruction model~ chen2026sam,zadaianchuk2026recgen to hypothesize a complete 3D mesh geometry from partial RGBD observations. The OBM is resource-rational and task-centric: it focuses its computation time on objects that the planner has decided are relevant to the task. In the example, the eraser and tray are refined into complete meshes (Figure~ fig:teaser-d ) while the cardboard boxes are left as the coarse hulls from the first frame (Figure~ fig:teaser-b ). Given a set of object meshes, we can leverage existing classical TAMP solvers to generate a plan skeleton: an optimistic plan that assumes the current object meshes are accurate and is entirely goal-oriented. To guard against this optimism, we require that every plan be justified. This means that any time the plan requires the robot to move through space, it must have observed that the space is collision free. Any time the plan requires the robot to grasp an object at a given pose, it must have observed that the object surface exists in between the fingers at that pose. To justify a plan, the planner has to find motions that move the camera to viewpoints where the desired regions are visible. The initial hull of the green eraser (Figure~ fig:teaser-b ) does not justify a grasp; the planner inserts the wrist view in Figure~ fig:teaser-c , which reveals the eraser's full extent and lets the grasp proceed. extends fully observed TAMP to partially observed domains by coupling object-based memory with scene-model verification. The memory supplies object meshes and an occupancy grid, and the planner constructs a goal-reaching plan that also validates the meshes. As observations arrive, the remaining plan guides refinement of task-relevant objects. Figure~ fig:method-overview illustrates this coupling. Our contributions are as follows. augments classical TAMP solvers with a persistent memory system and task-driven information gathering behavior. We show that this method outperforms systems which don't perform active perception or do not associate object detections across observations. Accurately modeling a scene is a computationally expensive task, with state-of-the-art completion models taking 4-5 seconds per object in a single frame. Rather than completing every object in every frame, the OBM prioritizes reconstruction on objects that are task-relevant and do not yet have a good model. We use the result of an existing TAMP solver to define which regions of space the robot interacts with, either as motion in assumed free space or contact with assumed object surfaces. We make the observation of these regions of space a precondition to acting, forcing the robot to collect more observations and update its models as needed. RELATED WORK Visibility-Aware Planning Goretkin et al.~ goretkin2018look formulate visibility-aware motion planning by requiring a robot to observe a region as empty before moving through it. Muguira-Iturralde et al.~ muguira2023visibility extend this formulation to allow the robot to move occluders on the trajectory. Ashur and Sintov~ ashur2026sampling instead treat visibility as an objective and seek configurations with a clear line of sight to a target. Next-best-view planners~ Lauri_RAL2020, delmerico2018comparison select views to collect information efficiently, but are generally task-agnostic. Our method uses visibility constraints to verify both free space along planned motions and object surfaces at planned grasp contacts. The resulting observations also guide refinement of the object geometry. Task and Motion Planning Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) is a well-studied problem formulation, and here we focus on TAMP approaches that operate without access to the ground-truth state. Curtis et al.~ curtis2022long and Shen et al.~ shen2026tiptop estimate the scene from an initial observation and treat this estimate as ground truth for a deterministic TAMP solver. builds on the same class of solvers, but verifies and updates the estimate as the plan executes. Another class of TAMP approaches plan in belief space using determinized observation models~ Menell2015Modular, garrett2020online or by weighting observation outcomes by their likelihood~ kaelbling2013integrated . These approaches replan when new observations invalidate the current plan. Curtis et al.~ curtis2024partially avoid determinization by learning a belief-space MDP from simulated operator rollouts and solving that MDP. Our OBM instead keeps a single mesh hypothesis per object at a time and evaluates how well it explains the accumulated observations, without explicitly maintaining a distribution over possible geometries. Recent work has also used Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to handle uncertainty in TAMP problems. Zhao et al.~ zhao2025seeing use a VLM to classify predicates as known or unknown and plan observation actions to resolve the unknown ones. Tanaka et al.~ tanaka2026evidence and Oloo et al.~ oloo2026robot use VLMs to propose observation actions and decide whether the robot has enough information to act. These methods use VLMs to reason about symbolic uncertainty and select observations. instead addresses continuous geometric uncertainty by deriving observation targets from planned motions and contacts. Scene Representation Mitash et al.~ mitash2020task choose each object's representation according to its role in the plan. Objects to be grasped are represented by minimal alpha shapes, which restrict grasps to observed surfaces. Objects to be avoided are represented by conservative hulls that include their unobserved shadows. Our OBM instead updates object meshes throughout the episode, using the observations to evaluate each mesh and the plan to prioritize refinement. To fuse observations over time, Gu et al.~ gu2024conceptgraphs build a persistent 3D scene graph by associating objects using geometric overlap and visual feature similarity. Du et al.~ du2022learning learn an object-based memory that updates each slot's shape estimate as new observations arrive, including in scenes where objects move. Task-agnostic reconstruction methods use generative image-to-3D models to estimate complete object meshes and poses from sparse views~ agarwal2025scenecomplete, huang2026simulation, yu2026picasso . Zadaianchuk et al.~ zadaianchuk2026recgen jointly estimate object pose, scale, and geometry. Our OBM instead updates a persistent scene representation as observations arrive and objects move, while allocating reconstruction effort according to the current manipulation plan. The robot manipulator has a set of fully observed joint angles and is embedded in an environment with an unknown number of objects. Each object in the object set is a posed mesh , where is a tuple of surface vertices and faces, and is the pose of the mesh centroid relative to a known world frame. Neither the object geometries nor their poses are provided a priori, and both must be inferred from observations. The state space of a POOR problem is the space of possible sets of geometries and robot configurations. title: BWM-Forge: Agentic World Programming for Embodied Intelligence
summary: Generating diverse robot videos requires control over scene geometry, robot motion, and viewpoints. End-to-end video generation offers limited direct access to these variables, making targeted edits and reuse across tasks difficult. We present BWM-Forge, a code-driven framework for controllable video generation in robotics. Given robot assets and a task description, the framework accepts an initial image, an image with motion data, or a human demonstration video. A coding agent constructs editable Blender scene programs that specify objects, robot motion, and cameras. The resulting proxy videos provide structural and motion references for a video generation model, which adds visual detail. A multi-agent harness coordinates input processing, scene construction, review, and rendering. Automated evaluation and user feedback support iterative refinement, while an experience repository stores and retrieves reusable modeling and rendering rules. This design supports multiple robot embodiments, synchronized viewpoints, and appearance variation from a shared scene program. We evaluate the framework on 15 tasks covering five robot types. Compared with LingBot-World Base Cam on these tasks, BWM-Forge achieves higher aesthetic quality, imaging quality, subject and background consistency, motion smoothness, and RoboJudge-9B physical adherence and instruction alignment scores. The baseline scores higher in dynamic degree. Qualitative cases illustrate viewpoint control, scene variation, feedback-driven edits, and experience reuse across scenes. These results demonstrate a practical approach to generating controllable robot videos through editable, executable scene representations.
full_text: 0pt generates controllable robot videos using editable scene programs and proxy videos. Introduction Video provides a natural representation of physical-world dynamics, motivating video world models that predict future visual observations. When world state is represented implicitly in generated frames, however, users have limited direct access to scene objects, robot configurations, and camera trajectories for editing and reuse. For embodied data generation, these limitations concern changing a task object while preserving the surrounding scene, observing the same interaction from another camera, and adapting an existing scene to a different robot. Recent code world models offer a complementary approach. WorldCoder and subsequent work represent world dynamics as executable programs for prediction and decision making tang2024worldcoder,lehrach2026codeworldmodels . Code World Model and Code2Worlds extend this direction toward code-mediated visual generation and the construction of 3D scenes and motion chen2026codeworldmodel,zhang2026code2worlds . These approaches motivate an explicit, executable representation through which scene structure and motion can be inspected, modified, and rendered. Inspired by this direction, we introduce , a framework for agentic world programming that generates controllable videos for embodied intelligence (Figure fig:motivation ). In , world programming means expressing scene objects, spatial relationships, robot motion, and camera states as executable scene programs; agents construct, execute, inspect, and revise these programs using tools and feedback. The goal is to generate diverse visual data across tasks, robot embodiments, and viewpoints, motivated by the need for broad robot interaction coverage reflected in datasets such as DROID and BridgeData V2 khazatsky2024droid,walke2023bridgedata . A unified pipeline accepts robot assets and task descriptions together with an initial image, an image with motion data, or a human demonstration video, and produces high-fidelity videos of interactions between robots and their environments. The same workflow covers robotic arms, humanoid robots, quadrupeds, and dexterous hands by loading their corresponding assets and using the available motion evidence. These videos provide potential training material for embodied video generation and world modeling. Prior work uses language models to generate robotic simulation tasks and scenes wang2024gensim,wang2024robogen , while robot-conditioned video generation uses explicit robot structure or rendered conditions to guide visual synthesis kim2026robotfactored,huang2026roborender . combines executable scene construction with appearance generation through proxy videos as an intermediate representation. A coding agent controls Blender to construct task scenes, import robot description packages for different embodiments, and coordinate robot motion and camera trajectories. Scene geometry, motion, and viewpoints remain directly editable in the program. Loading a different robot description package adapts the model to the target embodiment's structure, while the scene program retains editable objects and camera parameters. A 3D engine executes the program and renders proxy videos, which provide structural and motion guidance for a video generation model to add visual detail. This representation supports interactive refinement and flexible viewpoint control. The coding agent can modify scene code and parameters in response to user feedback, including object placement, robot motion, and camera settings. Multiple fixed cameras produce synchronized views of the same task, while camera trajectories enable continuously varying viewpoints. Because proxy videos share a scene program and motion timeline, their geometric relationships and motion remain temporally aligned. These shared references guide subsequent high-fidelity generation. This provides complementary observations of the same interaction for learning robot motion and its relationship to the environment. Reusing the scene program with different robot assets or camera configurations provides a practical basis for expanding visual observations across embodiments and viewpoints. The agentic workflow is implemented by a Harness that coordinates four specialized agents. The Preprocessing Agent parses requests, validates robot assets and motion data, and extracts visual evidence. The Building Agent constructs and animates scenes through code. The Review Agent inspects visual and numerical evidence, identifies defects, and applies local corrections. The Rendering Agent uses the resulting proxy videos, reference images, and prompts to generate and evaluate high-fidelity outputs. Automated checks and optional user feedback guide revisions to both proxy and rendered videos. Stage summaries and execution traces supply candidate experience entries, which the Harness consolidates and retrieves for later tasks. This cycle of programming, execution, review, and experience reuse connects the framework's editable world representation to its embodied data generation goal. Our main contributions are as follows: Agentic world programming for embodied data generation. We introduce , a framework that converts multimodal task inputs into executable scene programs and uses their rendered outputs to guide high-fidelity robot video generation. Explicit control over scenes, embodiments, and viewpoints. Editable scene programs expose object geometry, robot motion, and camera states for targeted revision, synchronized multi-view rendering, and adaptation to different robot assets. A collaborative generation and refinement workflow. A four-agent Harness combines input validation, scene construction, evidence-based review, rendering, user feedback, and reusable experience to support iterative video generation across tasks. Related Work Code World Model Current Code World Model approaches use Coding Agents to build executable worlds, compute state changes through code, and generate visual results with rendering models to better reflect physical laws. Early uses of coding focused on games and task planning, including state transitions, game rules, action validity checks, and simulations of future outcomes for search and decision making. For example, WorldCoder tang2024worldcoder builds world models with Python programs for state prediction and decision making in grid worlds and planning tasks; Code World Models for General Game Playing lehrach2026codeworldmodels converts game rules into executable code and uses Monte Carlo tree search for decision making. Code World Model: Coding Agent as World Brain chen2026codeworldmodel further maintains world states through code, converts them into proxy videos, and uses a video generation model for realistic rendering. Later work extends coding to the construction and maintenance of 3D scenes, objects, cameras, and motion, as in Code2Worlds zhang2026code2worlds , which generates Blender scenes and animation scripts with a Coding Agent and refines them through visual feedback. Coding also supports physical inference by proposing mechanisms from video, building executable models, and revising them based on differences between simulation and observation; Code as Worlds wang2026codeasworlds follows this process to build world representations for quantitative physical reasoning. These studies show a shift from rule writing and state prediction toward 3D scene construction and physical inference, with video generation also used to combine executable models with visual realism. uses a Coding Agent to generate executable and editable Blender scenes and motion programs, renders videos with proxy models to define spatial relationships and motion paths, and then uses Seedance to add visual detail. Evaluation feedback guides further revisions. Compared with direct video generation, this approach keeps scenes and motion in code, reduces the need for the video model to infer them freely, and improves visual realism while retaining control over world states and motion. Robotics Simulation Coding Agents are also widely used in robot task planning and physical simulation. Code as Policies converts natural language instructions into executable robot control code, while VoxPoser generates 3D value maps through code and combines them with motion planning to control robot arms. GenSim wang2024gensim and RoboGen wang2024robogen use LLMs to generate robot simulation tasks, scenes, and training data; Eureka writes and optimizes reward functions to help robots learn complex motions. More recently, Code2Worlds-2 zhang2026code2worlds2 converts generated 3D scenes into executable MuJoCo environments for navigation, grasping, and object interaction, with validation based on collisions, contact, stability, and task success rates. Work also connects robot motion with visual generation: APOLLO Blender messina2025apollo imports URDF robot models into Blender and generates joint animations. Robot-Factored World Models kim2026robotfactored uses robot kinematics and explicit rendering to separate robot motion constraints from visual prediction of the environment, while RoboRender huang2026roborender generates realistic robot manipulation videos from conditions such as simulated depth videos and robot masks. Our Robotics Simulation work uses URDF models, motion data, and demonstration videos to provide structural and motion constraints. A Coding Agent constructs robot motions and object interactions, and video generation improves visual realism. The robot's defined joint structure, kinematic constraints, and task goals provide an editable basis for motion and support evaluation through joint errors, collisions, contact relationships, and task completion. This feedback then guides further improvements. Robot Training Data Embodied intelligence models need robot training data with diverse interactions to adapt to different objects, scenes, and viewpoints. However, collecting real-world demonstrations requires robot hardware and human operation, which makes continuous data expansion costly. DROID khazatsky2024droid points out that the training data for many robot manipulation policies are still collected in a limited number of environments, with insufficient scene diversity. BridgeData V2 walke2023bridgedata provides a large-scale manipulation dataset collected across 24 environments. However, all data are collected using the WidowX 250 robot arm, so the dataset does not cover different robot embodiments. RT-1 brohan2023rt1 uses about 130,000 real-robot demonstrations and covers more than 700 tasks. However, its public dataset provides images from only one camera view and does not include synchronized multi-view observations of the same interaction. Synthetic data generation provides another way to expand robot training data, but there is still room for improvement in real-world transfer and visual quality. RoboGen wang2024robogen uses generative models to automatically create tasks, scenes, and training supervision, allowing robot skill demonstrations to be generated continuously. However, its transfer to real environments is still limited by the simulation-to-real gap. ReBot fang2025rebot combines simulated robot and object motions with inpainted real-world backgrounds. Its reported VBench visual quality score is 66.4 , which is close to but still lower than the 70.1 score of real robot videos. To address the need for more diverse robot visual data, this work develops a video generation pipeline that supports different environments, robot embodiments, and observation viewpoints. The pipeline focuses on texture details, material and lighting quality, scene integration, and motion consistency in the generated videos. Current visual examples demonstrate the performance of the pipeline in these aspects. The pipeline can also incorporate external demonstrations, providing a practical way to increase both the scale and visual diversity of robot vid

title: What Can a VLA Learn from the Agent That Calls It? Task-Level Experience Distillation for Embodied Navigation
summary: Navigation agents use a large language model (LLM) planner to call a vision-language-action (VLA) model. Each episode needs the LLM, adding cost and delay. We distill successful agent experience into the VLA instead of distilling the planner. The VLA then navigates alone at test time. Agent sessions are not VLA demonstrations. They include motions driven by planner tools and sub-instructions, along with detours. We present H2E, a task-level experience distillation method that converts these sessions into VLA training data. Every motion becomes a VLA action under the original task instruction, with the resulting poses as targets. H2E masks the loss on steps that move away from the goal. It labels every visited state within 1 m of the goal as a stop. We then update the VLA with low-rank adaptation. The VLA learns to stop at the goal and find goals the base model never reaches. On all 3,189 REVERIE-CE val-unseen episodes, H2E raises the success rate of an 8B VLA from 35.0% to 44.9%.

Introduction sec:intro Goal-directed navigation asks a robot to find a remote object that an instruction describes, such as go to the second-floor hallway and pick up the picture above the table~ qi2020reverie . The robot sees only its own camera views~ krantz2020vlnce,wang2025dynam3d . Strong recent systems split this task in two~ navgpt3,navmcp . A frontier LLM planner looks at the scene and keeps a map of visited places. It hands short goals to a vision-language-action (VLA) model and corrects the VLA when it goes wrong. The planner calls the LLM throughout every episode. On our test episodes this costs a median of 70k tokens per episode, and an episode takes more than twice as long as with the VLA alone. The sessions of such an agent show the VLA succeeding with help. We ask whether the VLA can learn from these sessions and then work alone. Current agents keep the VLA frozen~ navgpt3 , and distillation from such agents has so far shrunk the planner~ tinyastral,omnibrain0,guava . We instead train the VLA itself and remove the LLM at test time. A session is hard to use as training data for the VLA. The planner often moves the robot with its own tools, and it often gives the VLA new sub-instructions. Together these produce 45 of the motion in our sessions. The sessions also contain detours that the planner later fixes, so nearly a quarter of the steps move away from the goal. We present , a task-level experience distillation method. Figure~ fig:pipeline gives an overview. uses three simple rules. First, it labels every motion in a session as a VLA action under the original task instruction, whoever made the motion. Second, it masks the loss on steps that move away from the goal. Third, it labels every visited state near the goal as a stop. title: Memory-Efficient Parallel Policy Learning for Collapse-Reactive Retreat via Hybrid Terrain Modeling
summary: At disaster sites and on unstable slopes, robot contact can collapse uninspected terrain, requiring retreat upon support loss. Massively parallel reinforcement learning of collapse-reactive retreat requires independent state--action experiences. However, on shared rigid-body collapsible terrain, one robot's collapse alters others' contacts without direct interaction. We call this indirect interference. Duplicating terrain objects prevents this but is memory-intensive, limiting parallel sampling. Our key insight is that policy learning does not necessarily require rigid-body collapse modeling, which is feasible but computationally expensive; collapse-induced contact responses can suffice. We therefore propose a memory-efficient parallel policy-learning framework for collapse-reactive retreat via hybrid terrain modeling. Hybrid terrain modeling combines rigid-body simulation of non-collapsible terrain with virtual contact forces for collapsible regions. A State-Multiplexed Contact Model shares terrain geometry and a contact-response law while maintaining environment-specific collapse states, enabling independent experiences without terrain objects for collapsible regions. The framework trains a proprioceptive policy for both normal locomotion and collapse-reactive retreat. It supports over 100 times as many parallel environments as fine-resolution rigid-block terrain within the same GPU memory limit. This scalability and improved sample efficiency enable over 50 times faster policy convergence with comparable retreat performance. Sim-to-sim and real-robot experiments demonstrate retreat under multiple collapse conditions. A supplementary video is available at: https://youtu.be/_RrhwjzEPE0

Massively parallel reinforcement learning of collapse-reactive retreat requires independent state--action experiences. However, on shared rigid-body collapsible terrain, one robot's collapse alters others' contacts without direct interaction. We call this indirect interference. Duplicating terrain objects prevents this but is memory-intensive, limiting parallel sampling. Our key insight is that policy learning does not necessarily require rigid-body collapse modeling, which is feasible but computationally expensive; collapse-induced contact responses can suffice. We therefore propose a memory-efficient parallel policy-learning framework for collapse-reactive retreat via hybrid terrain modeling. Hybrid terrain modeling combines rigid-body simulation of non-collapsible terrain with virtual contact forces for collapsible regions. A State-Multiplexed Contact Model shares terrain geometry and a contact-response law while maintaining environment-specific collapse states, enabling independent experiences without terrain objects for collapsible regions. The framework trains a proprioceptive policy for both normal locomotion and collapse-reactive retreat. It supports over 100 times as many parallel environments as fine-resolution rigid-block terrain within the same GPU memory limit. This scalability and improved sample efficiency enable over 50 times faster policy convergence with comparable retreat performance. Sim-to-sim and real-robot experiments demonstrate retreat under multiple collapse conditions. A supplementary video is available at: Robots deployed at disaster sites and on unstable slopes may cross ground that gives way only after it is touched, so that cameras or prior inspection cannot reveal the hazard. This paper presents a way to train, in simulation, a single control policy for a wheeled quadruped that drives normally and, when a wheel loses support, keeps its balance and backs out to firm ground using only its onboard joint and inertial measurements. Training such a policy requires thousands of simulated robots that each experience their own ground collapse. Giving every robot its own copy of a collapsible terrain model quickly exhausts GPU memory, whereas letting the robots share one model allows a collapse caused by one robot to affect the others. Our framework instead represents the collapsible ground by computed contact forces that depend on a small collapse state kept for each robot, while the rest of the terrain is simulated as usual. On a single GPU, this supported over 100 times as many simulated robots as fine rigid-block terrain and reached a converged policy more than 50 times faster, and the trained policy worked without additional training on a real robot in four constructed collapse scenarios. New types of collapse can be added by defining their state and update rules, without building new terrain geometry. Because the policy relies only on proprioception, it may mistake a traversable downward step for a collapse; where such steps are common, combining it with terrain sensing is advisable. Terrain modeling, Parallel simulation, Reinforcement learning, Wheeled-legged robots Introduction sec:intro Disaster sites and unstable slopes may contain terrain that subsides or collapses under robot contact, altering support conditions for subsequent contacts~ godon2022mud,godon2025walking . For legged robots, including wheeled-legged systems, localized loss of support can disturb posture and cause falls~ raibert1990trotting,hutter2016anymal,bjelonic2020rolling,he2025residual . Collapse risks may not be apparent from visual cues before traversal and may emerge only after contact~ haddeler2022traversability,haddeler2022digitaldouble . This paper therefore aims to learn a policy for a wheeled quadruped without prior terrain inspection or exteroceptive detection of hazardous regions. Using only proprioceptive observations, the policy performs normal locomotion, responds to collapse-induced posture disturbances and support loss, and retreats to non-collapsible terrain ( , top). Reinforcement learning (RL) is a promising approach to acquiring such a policy by optimizing it with samples from diverse robot--terrain interactions~ hwangbo2019learning,lee2020learning,tan2018sim2real,peng2020learning . To collect samples efficiently, massively parallel RL is widely used for locomotion-policy learning, simulating many robots simultaneously~ legged_gym,makoviychuk2021isaac,mittal2023orbit . For fixed terrain, multiple robots can share a single terrain model within the same simulation space while maintaining independent experiences by disabling direct robot--robot interactions~ legged_gym . Because contact does not alter fixed terrain, one robot cannot change the terrain conditions experienced by others. This sharing avoids per-robot terrain duplication, reducing memory consumption and the computational load on the physics engine. However, this terrain-sharing approach cannot be directly applied when robot contact changes the terrain state (i.e., its shape and support conditions). Although rigid bodies can simulate ground collapse~ kim2021nonrigid , sharing changing terrain causes a region collapsed by one robot to affect the contact conditions and motion of others, even when direct robot--robot interactions are disabled. We refer to this terrain-mediated effect as indirect interference ( , bottom). Assigning independent changing terrain to each robot prevents this interference but requires duplicating terrain objects, i.e., the simulated bodies and colliders that represent the terrain, across parallel environments~ kim2021nonrigid,millard2023granulargym,kadokawa2025prpd . Finer terrain discretization further increases the number of terrain objects and memory requirements, limiting the number of environments that can run simultaneously~ kadokawa2025prpd . Thus, the challenge is to achieve computationally efficient parallel policy learning while ensuring that the state--action experiences needed to learn collapse-reactive retreat are generated without indirect interference. Our key insight is that, although ground collapse can be simulated using rigid bodies, explicitly modeling the collapsing terrain as rigid bodies is not necessarily required for policy learning. The goal is not to reproduce collapse processes in detail, but to efficiently generate the state--action experiences needed to learn collapse-reactive retreat. We therefore represent collapse through changes in contact responses, particularly support loss and contact forces. Based on this insight, we propose a memory-efficient parallel policy-learning framework for collapse-reactive retreat via hybrid terrain modeling. The framework adopts hybrid terrain modeling, which combines rigid-body simulation of the robot and non-collapsible terrain with virtual contact forces for collapsible regions, eliminating the need for terrain objects in these regions. To enable independent robot--terrain interactions within this hybrid approach, we introduce a State-Multiplexed Contact Model (SMCM) that 1) shares reference terrain geometry and a contact-response law across parallel environments, 2) maintains independent collapse states, and 3) computes virtual contact forces according to these states. This allows each robot to experience support loss, subsidence, and lateral slip without indirect interference. Using this environment, we train a proprioceptive policy for both normal locomotion and collapse-reactive retreat through massively parallel RL. Simulation experiments show that the framework supports over 100 times as many parallel environments as fine-resolution rigid-block terrain within the same GPU memory limit. This scalability speeds up sample collection and, together with improved sample efficiency, enables over 50 times faster policy convergence with comparable retreat performance. Sim-to-sim and real-robot experiments further demonstrate successful retreat under multiple tested collapse conditions. Related Works This section reviews two lines of work to which our approach contributes: task strategies for locomotion on collapsible terrain ( , ) and simulation methods for state-changing terrain in parallel reinforcement learning ( , ). Locomotion Strategies for Collapsible and Uncertain Terrain subsec:rw-strategy Previous works on safe locomotion and navigation over uncertain or hazardous terrain have often formulated the problem as traversability or foothold assessment before contact kalakrishnan2011learning,fan2021step,yan2026learning . Vision-based methods predict terrain properties ahead of the robot wellhausen2019where , and perceptive locomotion policies combine exteroceptive terrain representations with proprioception miki2022robust,fang2026motl,luo2026perceptive . Terrain-probing methods instead assess the ground by physical contact, either with a dedicated probing device at locations selected by vision haddeler2022traversability or with the robot's legs kolvenbach2019haptic,SPS . In particular, probe-before-step strategies such as the stepping-probing strategy (SPS) test each foothold before transferring body weight onto it and thereby avoid stepping onto ground that may collapse under load SPS . These approaches are appropriate when hazardous regions can be identified before traversal, but visual cues may be insufficient for hidden voids or weak support, and repeated probing can substantially limit locomotion speed in time-critical disaster-response tasks haddeler2022traversability,SPS . Other works handle uncertain terrain during traversal rather than before it. Reinforcement learning has produced robust proprioceptive locomotion that transfers from simulation to real robots hwangbo2019learning,lee2020learning,kumar2021rma , learned locomotion has been extended to vertically movable tiles kim2021nonrigid and granular media choi2023deformable , and model-based control has been developed for walking in mud godon2025walking . These controllers aim to continue the commanded locomotion on such terrain rather than to stop or retreat after support fails. In other works, hazard handling is added outside the locomotion controller. A real-time digital double (RTDD) detects collapse-related anomalies during walking from discrepancies between the robot and a synchronized physics-based simulation of it haddeler2022digitaldouble ; predictive proprioception (PrePARE) detects slip events and switches the robot to a more conservative gait dey2022prepare ; and safety frameworks for legged robots, such as Agile But Safe (ABS), switch from a task policy to a dedicated recovery policy or controller when an unsafe state is predicted or detected he2024agile,yang2022safe,zhang2025hierarchical . In these designs, the hazard response relies on a separate detector or switching rule and on whether the activated controller can maintain posture under the hazard. summarizes these locomotion strategies. Among the closest approaches, Deformable RL~ choi2023deformable learns a proprioceptive policy for deformable terrain but does not explicitly address retreat after support loss. RTDD~ haddeler2022digitaldouble detects terrain collapsibility through proprioceptive responses but does not provide a corresponding recovery strategy, while PrePARE~ dey2022prepare responds to predicted slip events through gait switching rather than learning collapse-reactive retreat. These studies highlight a remaining challenge: learning a unified locomotion policy that not only traverses uncertain terrain but also reacts to unexpected support loss by retreating from the affected region. To address this challenge, we train a single proprioceptive policy for both normal locomotion and collapse-reactive retreat, without prior terrain inspection, explicit hazard detection, or switching to a separate recovery controller. title: ManiLadder: Benchmarking Robot Manipulation Through a Categorized and Multi-Difficulty Level Task Ladder
summary: Recent advances in robotic manipulation have enabled increasingly complex and dexterous behaviors, yet existing benchmarks still focus on simple pick-and-place tasks and lack a systematic framework for measuring progress in robot learning along the axis of task difficulty. We present ManiLadder, a large-scale and organized simulation benchmark for robotic manipulation. ManiLadder contains 112 carefully designed tasks stratified into 4 difficulty levels, with 8 categories in each level, spanning rigid-body and deformable-object manipulation, single-arm and dual-arm settings, and gripper and dexterous-hand end-effectors. To calibrate difficulty, we fix the data amount the same for every task and use a unified flow- matching imitation learning policy under the same training and evaluation protocols, then use its evaluation success rate as an operational empirical difficulty signal. All tasks are iteratively refined until they fall into target difficulty ranges, which are then verified across different random seeds, policies, and agentic learning systems. We further analyze the task properties, compare different policy performances and training settings, analyze task transfer and data scaling behaviors, and conduct real-world experiments showing that the designed tasks preserve their difficulty ordering beyond simulation. ManiLad- der provides a calibrated ladder for measuring, comparing, and advancing robotic manipulation capabilities. More results are available at https://maniladder-benchmark.github.io/.

The difficulty of each task is calibrated and iteratively refined by the success rate of a standardized imitation-learning policy and later verified under different seeds and policies, enabling evaluation of both whether a model can solve a task and the level of manipulation difficulty it can reliably reach. fig:intro Recent advances in robotic manipulation have enabled increasingly complex and dexterous behaviors, yet existing benchmarks still focus on simple pick-and-place tasks and lack a systematic framework for measuring progress in robot learning along the axis of task difficulty. More results are on https://maniladder-benchmark.github.io/ . Introduction Recent years have witnessed remarkable progress in robotic manipulation, driven by increasingly accessible hardware~ act,leaphand , large-scale datasets~ oxe,chen2026objectworld , powerful foundation models~ pi05 , effective learning algorithms~ dp , and agentic learning systems~ rax . Robots can now perform highly complex real-world tasks such as scrambling eggs~ skild_ai , tying plastic bags~ gao2023iterative , and cardboard box folding~ dreamcan . However, current benchmarks in robotic manipulation lag considerably behind this huge progress: most existing robotic simulation benchmarks~ libero,robocasa,behavior1k primarily expand task diversity horizontally, by recombining relatively simple manipulation skills across different scenes and objects, such as pick-and-place, pushing, and door opening. While they are useful for evaluating generalization or semantic reasoning, they offer limited resolution for measuring the vertical growth of manipulation capability, i.e., they cannot reveal whether a model has truly expanded the frontier of solvable manipulation tasks. We therefore ask a capability-oriented question: what level of manipulation difficulty can a model reliably solve? Answering this requires a benchmark organized by calibrated difficulty levels, so that the capability boundaries of current methods can be measured directly. Building such a benchmark raises two challenges: (1) how to determine task difficulty, and (2) how to construct diverse tasks with well-calibrated difficulty. Prior works characterize difficulty through theoretical measures~ informationinvariant , subskill composition~ dmil , manually defined predicates~ tamp , or contact patterns~ classifying , but these abstractions are difficult to scale to diverse modern manipulation tasks. Instead, we adopt an empirical definition: under a standardized training protocol, what success rate can a robot learning algorithm achieve on the task? This becomes increasingly practical as modern imitation learning methods~ flowmatching,act perform effectively across a broad range of tasks. Meanwhile, although modern simulators and procedural generation tools~ genesis,isaaclab simplify task creation, they do not guarantee task difficulty. Initialization ranges, perception complexity, and object geometry can make tasks unintentionally too easy or too hard. Constructing a meaningful difficulty ladder therefore requires iterative, metric-driven task calibration. In this work, we present , a large-scale simulation benchmark that evaluates robotic manipulation along two complementary axes: calibrated task difficulty and manipulation diversity, as shown in Figure~ fig:intro . \ contains 112 carefully designed tasks across 4 difficulty levels, organized by object properties, robot embodiments, and manipulation skills. The tasks cover both rigid-body and deformable-object manipulation, spanning four embodiment types: single-arm grippers, single-arm dexterous hands, dual-arm grippers, and dual-arm dexterous hands. Within each task suite, we further cover disparate manipulation skills or object types, resulting in 3 to 4 concrete tasks per suite. For example, in each deformable-object manipulation suite, we design tasks targeting 1D (e.g., rope), 2D (e.g., cloth), and 3D (e.g., clay) deformable object types, respectively. To stratify task difficulty, we provide a fixed number of demonstrations for every task and train a unified flow-matching~ flowmatching imitation learning policy under a standardized protocol, using its evaluation success rate as an empirical difficulty signal. We then iteratively calibrate each task to the desired difficulty range by adjusting interpretable factors such as object geometry, initial randomization, perceptual difficulty, temporal coordination, and error tolerance. The calibrated task difficulties are then verified across demonstration recollection, retraining, different policies, and agentic learning systems. Building on these calibrated difficulty levels, we establish standardized benchmarking protocols and an Attained Level metric to quantify the highest task difficulty level a given algorithm can reliably solve. This makes not only broad in task coverage but also explicitly calibrated as a ladder of manipulation difficulty. To highlight the flexibility and potential of \ for studying manipulation capability across different dimensions, we conduct a set of studies, including: 1) analyzing the task properties across different levels; 2) comparing small and large VLA models~ pi05 on ; 3) studying the multi-task training results compared to single-task training results; 4) studying task transfer ability and data scaling behaviors across different task families; 5) examining whether the difficulty ordering calibrated in simulation is preserved between simulation and real-world settings. Together, \ provides a platform for studying many future questions in robot learning, and also provides a calibrated and organized difficulty ladder that measures how far robotic manipulation has climbed toward general-purpose manipulation intelligence, and how far it still has to go. Related Works Robot Manipulation Benchmarks Robot manipulation benchmarks span simulation and real-world settings. Simulation benchmarks can offer diverse tasks~ rlbench,robosuite and study of long-horizon execution~ calvin,robocasa , multi-task, transfer, and continual learning~ libero,metaworld,cril , robustness~ colosseum , and dexterous~ dexart or bimanual manipulation~ chen2025robotwin . Real-world evaluation efforts promote comparability through standardized objects~ ycb , assembly protocols~ furniturebench , distributed policy comparisons~ roboarena , and in-person challenges~ amazonchallenge . RoboDojo~ chen2026robodojo further connects simulation and real-world evaluation. Simulation enables controlled, scalable, and reproducible evaluation, while real-world benchmarks directly assess performance under physical deployment conditions. We develop primarily in simulation and focus on calibrating difficulty across diverse tasks through controlled configurations and repeated evaluation. We further evaluate selected real-world counterparts across task categories, providing a preliminary assessment of whether the relative difficulty trends persist in physical execution. Robot Manipulation Task Taxonomies Developing a systematic taxonomy for robot manipulation is inherently challenging because task complexity arises jointly from object properties, interaction modes, embodiment, and temporal structure~ classifying . Existing taxonomies have been developed based on grasp and contact modes~ cutkosky1989grasp , predefined skills or primitives~ huang2021robotic , and specialized domains such as deformable~ tdom,flip,chen2025metafold or bimanual manipulation~ bimanual . While useful for describing manipulation structure, these taxonomies are often tied to specific interaction patterns or skill decompositions, making them difficult to apply consistently to heterogeneous, multi-stage tasks, and unsuitable for studying task difficulties. We instead organize manipulation tasks along two complementary axes: horizontally by task diversity, primarily characterized by manipulated objects and robot embodiments, and vertically by empirical difficulty, measured by success rates under a unified policy, training, and evaluation protocol. This provides a common behavioral scale for comparing heterogeneous manipulation tasks without relying on hand-crafted notions of complexity. Task Construction and Difficulty Calibration sec:construction In this section, we describe how \ is constructed as a difficulty-calibrated simulation benchmark for robotic manipulation across diverse task categories. We first introduce the design principles and detailed task construction process, then we introduce how to iteratively refine tasks to calibrate their difficulty levels. This leads to the final standardized benchmark, which will be introduced in the next Section. Design Principles and Task Organization sec:construction:organization \ is designed to have four difficulty levels and to measure the level of manipulation difficulty that a robot learning policy can reliably solve. To make such a comparison convincing, tasks in each level must be diverse enough as well as organized in a structured way, so that the performance differences mostly reflect changes associated with task difficulty. We design \ along three axes: all levels contain unified task suites organized by object property, robot embodiment, and manipulation skill, as shown in Figure fig:intro . The first design axis is object physical property. We divide tasks in each level into rigid-body manipulation and deformable-object manipulation. Rigid-body tasks include both objects with fixed geometry, such as blocks and mugs, and articulated objects with movable parts, such as doors and drawers. Deformable-object tasks are grouped by geometric dimensionality: 1D deformables such as ropes and cables, 2D deformables such as cloths and towels, and 3D deformables such as clay, plasticine, and liquid. This distinction allows ManiLadder to cover qualitatively different interaction regimes. We curate object assets from multiple open-source repositories~ ycb and custom designs to support broad task coverage. These assets are rescaled, cleaned, and processed with convex decomposition to improve simulation stability. For deformable-object manipulation, we create assets in Blender and convert them into simulation-ready formats with Trimesh, and use different physical representations for different object categories: 1D ropes are represented as articulated chains of capsule-shaped rigid bodies, 2D cloths are simulated with a PBD solver, and 3D deformable materials are modeled with solvers such as MPM for clay-like objects and SPH for liquids. title: Remember What Changes the Odds: Critic-Gated Event Memory for Long-Horizon Manipulation
summary: In long-horizon manipulation, a robot may need to take different actions under identical observations, depending on task progress and the outcomes of earlier attempts. We refer to this ambiguity as decision aliasing. Resolving it requires the policy to maintain memory of its execution history. To reduce the cost of processing full observation histories, recent methods build compact event memories using perceptual, semantic, or kinematic cues. However, these criteria may miss events that matter for task success. We instead propose an outcome-grounded principle: remember events that substantially change the predicted probability of eventual success. Following this principle, we introduce CGEM, a critic-gated event memory that uses a critic to select events with large estimated changes in success probability. Positive and negative changes are encoded as progress and failure records, respectively. Failure records are discarded once the corresponding subtask is completed. In a ten-subtask diagnostic environment with exactly computed success probabilities, CGEM achieves 88.0% success, compared with 0.0% for both a 36-step observation window and a kinematic event memory. Removing failure records reduces success to 1.7%.

The current observation may look the same before a press, after a recoverable failure, and after a successful press. Yet these situations call for different action strategies: attempt the press, retry, or advance to the next subtask. We call this ambiguity . Reactive policies based on robot foundation models~ black2024pi0,pi2025pi05 generate actions from current observations and language instructions. When these inputs are identical, the policy cannot distinguish whether an interaction remains untried, has failed, or has succeeded. Resolving decision aliasing therefore requires the policy to maintain a memory of its execution history. To reduce the cost of processing full observation histories, recent methods build compact memories around key events selected using perceptual, semantic, or kinematic cues~ zeng2026kemo,mark2026bpp,yang2026eventvla,yang2026memorywam . However, these cues may miss events that matter for task success. A large arm motion may be easy to detect without changing what the robot should do next. A failed contact may leave no lasting visual trace but require a different retry strategy. Selecting events for memory therefore requires more than detecting changes in appearance or motion. To decide what to remember, we seek a signal that reflects what each event reveals about the likelihood of completing the task. Learned value estimates provide information about task progress or expected return~ chen2026sarm,fang2026habc,pi2025pistar06 . We use a critic's prediction of eventual success to obtain such a signal for memory selection. A substantial change in this prediction indicates that an event has provided new information about the estimated chance of task success. This leads to our outcome-grounded principle: remember events that substantially change the predicted probability of eventual success. Following this principle, we introduce (Critic-Gated Event Memory), which uses a critic to select events with large estimated changes in success probability ( b). Positive and negative changes are stored as progress and failure records, respectively. These records track which subtasks have been completed and which strategies have failed. Retaining failure records allows the policy to distinguish an untried subtask from a failed attempt and adjust its retry strategy. After subtask completion, obsolete failure records are discarded. Theoretically, under a fixed reference policy and threshold, we establish a horizon-independent bound on the expected number of large changes in conditional success probability, motivating sparse event selection. We also characterize when event records preserve the information needed for subsequent decisions. We evaluate this mechanism in an exact-value diagnostic that isolates the effects of event selection, failure records, and consolidation.
