title: I See What You Want: Decoding Hierarchical Operator Intent from Visual Teleoperation History
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have become a powerful foundation for robotic scene understanding, task planning, and language-conditioned control. A natural question follows: can these models also decode what a human operator intends while teleoperating a robot, without any explicit instruction? We formulate this as hierarchical intent prediction, jointly inferring the ongoing atomic action and the broader mission it serves from a short visual teleoperation history. To study this, we introduce VI AMO (Vision Intention Action and Mission Ongoing), a dataset of 6,600 episodes from eleven robot sources with 13,653 temporally aligned action annotations and 9,702 mission annotations. Large proprietary models struggle with this problem: on held-out episodes, GPT-4o reaches Sentence-BERT similarities of only 0.563 and 0.470 for action and mission, and GPT-5.6 Luna achieves only 0.581 and 0.554. Fine-tuning a VLM on VI AMO yields our Vision-Intention Model (VIM), which raises these scores to 0.825 and 0.821 and still reaches 0.726 and 0.717 on the 35.4% of test actions with both labels absent from training. Finally, as a downstream application, VIM's predicted mission enables a vision-language-action (VLA) policy to take over from the operator mid-task in a real-world environment unseen during VIM fine-tuning, reducing human teleoperation time by 34.6% relative to GPT-4o and 39.8% relative to GPT-5.6 Luna, while cutting intent-prediction latency by roughly 70% on average.
full_text: Vision-language models (VLMs) have become a powerful foundation for robotic scene understanding, task planning, and language-conditioned control. A natural question follows: can these models also decode what a human operator intends while teleoperating a robot, without any explicit instruction? We formulate this as hierarchical intent prediction, jointly inferring the ongoing atomic action and the broader mission it serves from a short visual teleoperation history. To study this, we introduce VI AMO (Vision Intention Action and Mission Ongoing), a dataset of 6,600 episodes from eleven robot sources with 13,653 temporally aligned action annotations and 9,702 mission annotations. Large proprietary models struggle with this problem: on held-out episodes, GPT-4o reaches Sentence-BERT similarities of only 0.563 and 0.470 for action and mission, and GPT-5.6 Luna achieves only 0.581 and 0.554. Fine-tuning a VLM on VI AMO yields our Vision-Intention Model (VIM), which raises these scores to 0.825 and 0.821 and still reaches 0.726 and 0.717 on the 35.4 of test actions with both labels absent from training. Finally, as a downstream application, VIM's predicted mission enables a vision-language-action (VLA) policy to take over from the operator mid-task in a real-world environment unseen during VIM fine-tuning, reducing human teleoperation time by 34.6 relative to GPT-4o and 39.8 relative to GPT-5.6 Luna, while cutting intent-prediction latency by roughly 70 on average. INTRODUCTION sec:intro Vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as a key backbone for robotic perception and reasoning. SayCan~ ahn2022saycan grounds language plans in learned affordances, Code as Policies~ liang2023code generates executable robot programs from language, and Inner Monologue~ huang2022inner closes the loop with textual feedback. PragmaBot~ qu2026pragmatist uses visual feedback and lessons from real-world experience to refine robot task plans. On the execution side, vision-language-action (VLA) policies map a language instruction and visual observations directly to motor commands~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvlaopensourcevisionlanguageactionmodel,black2026pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel,intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld . All of these translate human language into robot behavior. We ask the inverse question: given only the partial visual history of a teleoperated robot, can a VLM decode what the human operator intends, without an instruction ever being provided? Recent work has begun to explore this direction. VOSA~ belsare2025zeroshotuserintentrecognition identifies candidate target objects through detection and segmentation, and CASPER~ liu2025casper uses VLM reasoning over teleoperation history to select a skill--object pair from a predefined library and then executes that skill. Both represent intent at the level of the current step, as a target object or position, or as a skill drawn from a predefined library. However, these methods do not explicitly infer the broader mission behind the current action, yet it is what a robot needs in order to continue: grasping an apple does not by itself reveal whether the apple should go on a plate, to a person, or into a basket. Progress is further limited by data: existing demonstration corpora~ walke2023bridgedata,khazatsky2024droid,openx2023 mainly provide episode-level instructions, while existing intermediate supervision is either synthetically generated from task instructions~ zawalski2024ecot , or annotated at the primitive-skill level~ chen2024rh20tp , rather than providing temporally aligned action--mission supervision for instruction-free intent inference. We therefore model operator intent as a hierarchy. The ongoing action~(OA) is the atomic manipulation step currently being performed, such as ``pick up the apple,'' and the ongoing mission~(OM) is the immediate goal it serves, such as ``put the apple on the plate.'' Both are expressed as open-vocabulary natural language, so the predicted mission can serve as the instruction of a language-conditioned policy without a fixed skill library. The difficulty is that a useful prediction must arrive early: at handoff time only part of the action has been observed, so the model must commit from a few frames and a short record of what has already been completed. To study this problem, we introduce VI~AMO (Vision Intention Action and Mission Ongoing), a dataset of 6,600 episodes from eleven robot source families with 13,653 temporally aligned action annotations and 9,702 mission annotations. Without task-specific training, even strong proprietary models fall short in predicting the ongoing mission: GPT-4o and GPT-5.6 Luna reach mission Sentence-BERT (SBERT) similarities of only 0.470 and 0.554. Fine-tuning an open-source VLM on VI~AMO yields the Vision-Intention Model~(VIM), which outperforms the two proprietary VLMs, two robotics-specialized foundation models, and its untuned backbone across different evaluation metrics, achieving a mission SBERT similarity of 0.821 compared with at most 0.564 for the baselines. On the 35.4 of test actions whose action and mission labels are both unseen during training, VIM achieves 27.2 higher action SBERT and 27.1 higher mission SBERT than the strongest baseline for both action and mission prediction. Finally, we test the utility of the inferred mission in shared autonomy, where a robot continues a task that the operator began~ 9501975,losey2022learning . VIM's predicted mission conditions a VLA policy that takes over mid-task and completes the remaining manipulation in real-world scenarios unseen during VIM fine-tuning. With five trials per task for each VLM condition, VIM reduces human teleoperation time by 34.6 relative to GPT-4o and 39.8 relative to GPT-5.6 Luna. Each intent prediction takes approximately 0.7 s on a consumer GPU, compared with 1.9--3.5 s for the API-based baselines. Our main contributions are as follows: We formulate hierarchical intent prediction from visual teleoperation history, jointly predicting the ongoing action and the mission it serves as open-vocabulary language, and introduce VI~AMO, a dataset of 6,600 episodes with aligned action--mission annotations to train and evaluate it. We present VIM, a VLM fine-tuned on VI~AMO that outperforms GPT-4o, GPT-5.6 Luna, two embodied foundation models, and its untuned backbone on different metrics, reaching 0.825 and 0.821 Sentence-BERT similarity for action and mission on the VI~AMO test set versus at most 0.581 and 0.564 for the best baseline. We evaluate VIM as the intent module of a shared-autonomy system across five real-world tasks in scenarios unseen during VIM fine-tuning. Its predicted missions serve as language instructions for a VLA policy, reducing human teleoperation time by 34.6 relative to GPT-4o and 39.8 relative to GPT-5.6 Luna. VI~AMO, the annotation pipeline, and the VIM weights will be released at https://see-want.github.io/ . RELATED WORK sec:related Operator Intent Inference Early shared-autonomy methods~ Dragan-2012-7532,dragan2013policy,javdani2015hindsight,jain2019probabilistic,admoni2016predicting estimate user goals from control inputs or gaze to guide assistance. Recent approaches use different observations and intent representations. VOSA~ belsare2025zeroshotuserintentrecognition constructs object-goal candidates from visual perception, while AHEAD~ kim2026ahead predicts grasp objects and placement targets from tracked hand and head motion with scene context. CASPER~ liu2025casper infers a skill--object pair from visual teleoperation history for user-confirmed skill execution. Adaptor~ liu2026adaptoradvancingassistiveteleoperation learns latent intention representations from teleoperation trajectories to condition action generation. These representations support target selection, skill execution, or action generation, but these functions do not by themselves require separate descriptions of the current manipulation and its mission. That distinction matters for continuation because the same action can serve different goals. We therefore study joint prediction of the ongoing atomic action and the immediate mission it serves, making action recognition and goal inference separately evaluable. Hierarchical Intent Supervision and Benchmarks Supervision for hierarchical intent prediction links observed actions to the goals they serve. In human activity understanding, Ego4D Goal-Step~ song2023ego4dgoalstep annotates goals, steps, and substeps, while AntGPT~ zhao2024antgpt infers goals from recognized action histories to anticipate future actions. For robots, BridgeData V2~ walke2023bridgedata , DROID~ khazatsky2024droid , and Open X-Embodiment~ openx2023 provide diverse manipulation demonstrations. RH20T-P~ chen2024rh20tp adds manually segmented primitive skills, and RoboVQA~ sermanet2024robovqa supports multi-horizon video reasoning. Embodied chain-of-thought reasoning (ECoT)~ zawalski2024ecot uses intermediate reasoning supervision for instruction-conditioned control, while IntentVLA~ lian2026intentvla uses visual history for instruction-conditioned action generation and introduces AliasBench to evaluate ambiguous continuations. Building on these resources, we ask whether an ongoing robot action and its mission can be jointly inferred before action completion, without the task instruction. Answering this question requires paired semantic targets aligned with the observations available at each prediction time. VI~AMO therefore associates temporally bounded atomic actions with their immediate missions and evaluates both predictions on episode-disjoint data at multiple stages of action progress. PROBLEM FORMULATION sec:problem Hierarchical Intent Prediction sec:io An atomic action is an individual manipulation step, such as ``pick up the apple'' or ``place the apple in the basket''. A mission is a sequence of consecutive atomic actions serving a single goal, such as ``put the apple in the basket''; the two form a hierarchy of goals and steps. Whether consecutive actions belong to the same mission is a commonsense judgment based on the scene: picking up an apple next to an empty basket naturally continues into placing it there, whereas an action without an evident continuation forms a mission on its own. At decision time , the ongoing action and ongoing mission denote the action and mission the operator is currently executing. Given these definitions, let denote time-ordered visual observations collected up to time , and an execution context summarizing behavior completed before . An intention model predicts where both outputs are free-form natural-language descriptions generated without a predefined set of candidates. Both levels are needed because the same action can serve different missions: grasping an apple may precede placing it in a basket or handing it to a person. Application: Shared Autonomy sec:handoff In shared autonomy, a robot autonomously continues a task initiated through teleoperation. We realize this with a language-conditioned VLA policy with action chunk , observations , robot state , and language instruction . Since the operator provides no instruction, the intention model supplies it: at the switch time , the robot executes for all , i.e., the predicted mission from~ serves as the instruction in~ . We assume a single switch and use only the teleoperation history up to ; the repeated switches in our real-world experiments apply the same procedure at each switch. METHOD sec:method Our method centers on learning hierarchical intent from partial visual observations. We first introduce VI AMO, which pairs temporally localized atomic actions with the missions they serve. These annotations support both supervised learning and a benchmark for predicting ongoing action (OA) and ongoing mission (OM). We then train the Vision-Intention Model (VIM) to generate both descriptions from visual history and the completed-action context (Fig.~ fig:overview ).

title: HALO: Human-Aligned Data Collection for WhoLe-body MObile Manipulation
summary: Learning whole-body mobile manipulation requires demonstrations that coordinate bimanual actions with locomotion across extended workspaces. However, existing interfaces trade off direct robot control, perception and action alignment, and natural operator mobility, making such demonstrations difficult to collect. We introduce HALO, a human-aligned data collection system for whole-body mobile manipulation. The system aligns the operator's perception and action space with the robot while preserving direct physical feedback and natural locomotion. Operators guide the robot end-effectors through kinesthetic teaching and move a low-resistance platform without the deployed mobile base while performing bimanual manipulation. This interface enables more natural whole-body demonstrations, but the close human-robot coupling introduces discrepancies between the demonstration and deployment settings. We address these discrepancies with deployment-aligned demonstration processing, which calibrates and temporally aligns platform motion with the deployed base response and masks and inpaints demonstrator hands in recorded observations. Compared with Mobile ALOHA and VR teleoperation, HALO enables up to 2.9x faster demonstration collection while maintaining comparable or higher success rates. Policies trained with HALO perform precise manipulation tasks, including zip-tie fastening, and achieve a 73.3% success rate on a six-stage long-horizon mobile manipulation task involving repeated coordinated base and arm motion. Project page: https://robbyant-research.github.io/Lingbot-ALOHA/
full_text: HALO: Human-Aligned Data Collection for WhoLe-body MObile Manipulation Shuai Yang , Fangyi Xu , Yishu Shen , Kecheng Zheng and Yinghao Xu The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Robbyant Equal Contribution. Corresponding author (e-mail:justimyhxu@ust.hk) .3in Learning whole-body mobile manipulation requires demonstrations that coordinate bimanual actions with locomotion across extended workspaces. However, existing interfaces trade off direct robot control, perception and action alignment, and natural operator mobility, making such demonstrations difficult to collect. We introduce , a human-aligned data collection system for whole-body mobile manipulation. The system aligns the operator's perception and action space with the robot while preserving direct physical feedback and natural locomotion. Operators guide the robot end-effectors through kinesthetic teaching and move a low-resistance platform without the deployed mobile base while performing bimanual manipulation. This interface enables more natural whole-body demonstrations, but the close human--robot coupling introduces discrepancies between the demonstration and deployment settings. We address these discrepancies with deployment-aligned demonstration processing, which calibrates and temporally aligns platform motion with the deployed base response and masks and inpaints demonstrator hands in recorded observations. Compared with Mobile ALOHA and VR teleoperation, enables up to faster demonstration collection while maintaining comparable or higher success rates. Policies trained with perform precise manipulation tasks, including zip-tie fastening, and achieve a 73.3 success rate on a six-stage long-horizon mobile manipulation task involving repeated coordinated base and arm motion. Project page Introduction End-to-end robot policies and imitation learning~ aloha,dp,kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0,va,vla have achieved strong performance across a wide range of real-world manipulation tasks. However, most prior work focuses on tabletop settings, where robots are confined to a fixed workspace. Real-world applications instead require robots to extend their workspace through mobility while continuing to manipulate objects, motivating coordinated whole-body bimanual manipulation~ mobile_aloha . Learning such behaviors requires efficient collection of demonstrations that jointly capture locomotion and manipulation. Existing approaches to whole-body data collection make different trade-offs in preserving natural human coordination. Indirect teleoperation methods (e.g., VR-based interfaces~ zhu2022bottom,rakita2018autonomous,honerkamp2025whole ) provide less direct manipulation control and lack force feedback. Leader--follower systems (e.g., Mobile ALOHA~ mobile_aloha ) provide more direct manipulation through leader arms and kinesthetic teaching, but the spatial separation between the operator's hands, viewpoint, and robot end-effectors introduces a perception gap and constrains natural operator mobility. R fig:motivation Retargeting-based approaches (e.g., UMI~ umi and HoMMI~ xu2026hommi ) instead preserve unconstrained human motion by mapping human demonstrations to robot behavior through retargeting or whole-body control. Taken together, existing approaches balance direct robot control, perception--action alignment, and natural operator mobility in different ways, often emphasizing one property over another. These trade-offs across perception, manipulation, and mobility are summarized in~ . Effective whole-body demonstration requires preserving the robot's native action constraints and direct physical feedback while aligning the operator's perception--action space with the robot and preserving the operator's natural mobility, as illustrated in~ . We adopt two design principles: First, the manipulation interface should preserve direct robot control and feedback. We therefore retain the robot arms and use kinesthetic teaching~ akgun2012trajectories , keeping the operator close to the end-effectors to reduce the perception gap while preserving direct visual and force feedback. Second, the mobility interface should preserve the operator's natural locomotion without requiring control of the mobile base. We therefore remove the mobile base during demonstration, reducing the mobility gap and allowing natural body motion for repositioning. While these interfaces enable more natural whole-body demonstrations, the resulting human--robot coupling introduces visual and control distribution shifts between demonstration data and autonomous deployment~ xu2026hommi . We identify these discrepancies and introduce a deployment aligned post-processing pipeline that removes demonstrator-induced artifacts from both visual observations and control signals, aligning the collected demonstrations with policy execution. Together, these design choices improve demonstration efficiency and whole-body coordination. Compared with Mobile ALOHA and VR teleoperation, enables up to faster demonstration collection while maintaining higher success rates. The resulting policies achieve sub-millimeter manipulation precision and a 73.3 success rate on a six-stage long-horizon mobile manipulation task involving repeated coordinated base and arm motion. These results demonstrate that human-aligned data collection supports efficient, dexterous, and coordinated whole-body policy learning. Our contributions are threefold: Human-aligned data collection system. We introduce a whole-body bimanual teaching system that aligns the operator's perception--action space with the robot while preserving natural mobility, enabling efficient collection of coordinated and dexterous mobile manipulation. Deployment-aligned data post-process. We identify and mitigate demonstrator-induced artifacts in visual observations and control, enabling demonstrations collected under tight human--robot coupling to be used for autonomous policy learning. Systematic real-world evaluation. We evaluate the proposed system in terms of data-collection efficiency and demonstration success, and we further study the effects of different inference strategies as well as the achievable precision and efficiency of the learned policies. Related Work Robot Demonstration Collection Traditional teleoperation minimizes the embodiment gap by directly controlling the target robot, but interfaces such as SpaceMouse devices, joysticks, and VR controllers remain indirect~ zhu2022bottom,rakita2018autonomous,honerkamp2025whole,wong2022error . Kinematic replicas, such as ALOHA~ aloha,mobile_aloha , GELLO~ gello,jiang2025behavior , and exoskeleton-based approaches~ citron2026modpack,chen2026supersuit , provide more intuitive control but typically lack force feedback, although some recent systems incorporate it~ liang2026universal ; they also become cumbersome in mobile settings. UMI~ umi enables scalable in-the-wild data collection, while recent extensions~ shen2026fomi,xu2026hommi,yu2025egomi incorporate force feedback, egocentric sensing and whole-body controllers for mobile manipulation; however, base motion remains difficult to control precisely, and visual and control gaps persist. Our system instead aligns the operator with the robot, providing direct visual and force feedback. Human-to-Robot Demonstration Transfer Transferring human demonstrations to robot policy learning requires bridging the visual and action gaps between human embodiment and robot execution. DexUMI~ xu2025dexumi removes the human hand through inpainting and uses action replay to obtain the corresponding foreground dexterous robot hand. EgoBridge~ punamiya2025egobridge aligns human and robot demonstrations using dynamic time warping. Ego2Robot~ wang2026ego2robot first estimates the human hand pose and then replaces the hand with the robot arm through inpainting. Human2Sim2Robot~ lum2025crossing uses a single human demonstration together with reinforcement learning to derive robot-executable actions. In contrast, since our kinesthetic teaching interface directly provides ground-truth robot actions, we only need to mitigate demonstrator-induced artifacts in visual observations and control, without additional action annotation or replay. Learning-Based Mobile Manipulation Hierarchical models separate task-level manipulation prediction from whole-body execution, using planners or whole-body controllers to coordinate the base and arm~ zhu2026emma,umi_on_legs,yuan2026hermes,xu2026hommi,zhao2025combined . However, many real-world tasks require tight and continuous coordination between mobility and manipulation, making such modular designs less suitable for unified whole-body control and introducing additional system complexity. Unified policies~ wu2024tidybot_1,pi05,mobile_aloha , in contrast, directly model coupled base and manipulation actions, which is particularly effective when mobility and manipulation must evolve simultaneously. We find that simply concatenating base actions with arm actions already yields strong whole-body control without additional architectural design. Method HALO combines kinesthetic teaching with a low-resistance mobility interface to collect coordinated whole-body demonstrations. We first describe the manipulation interface in~ and the mobility interface in~ . We then introduce deployment-aligned demonstration processing in~ , including visual processing and base-motion alignment, to address the discrepancies caused by close human--robot coupling and base-free data collection. Finally, we describe policy learning and asynchronous execution in~ . [33] R fig:demo fig:mobile Manipulation Interface sec:manipulation-interface A data collection interface should adapt to the operator rather than require the operator to adapt to the robot. ALOHA's leader--follower design enables intuitive bimanual control, but the operator's hands remain spatially separated from the follower end-effectors, and the operator's egocentric view differs from the robot viewpoint. These gaps weaken perception--action alignment and direct robot control. We therefore use kinesthetic teaching to more closely align the operator's perception and action space with the robot. As shown in~ , the original ALOHA end-effector is not designed for this type of physical interaction. Its handle limits the working space, while the scissor mechanism is less suitable for forceful manipulation. These features make stable grasping and force application less convenient in compact or contact-rich tasks. So we redesign the end-effector for kinesthetic teaching by removing the handle-and-scissor mechanism and adopting a compact, high-contact design. As shown in~ , the redesign reduces the end-effector size by more than half and increases the available pitch angle by about , enabling closer and more flexible manipulation while preserving direct visual and force feedback. This close human--robot coupling makes bimanual demonstrations more natural, but it also causes the operator's hands to appear in the robot observations. We address this visual discrepancy in the deployment-aligned demonstration processing stage described in~ . Mobility Interface sec:mobility-interface The mobility interface preserves natural operator locomotion while maintaining the motion constraints of the deployed base. Mobile ALOHA's powered base occupies the operator's movement space~ mobile_aloha . We remove the base during data collection and let natural body motion directly drive a low-resistance demonstration platform, as shown on the left of~ and~ . This allows the operator to control mobility implicitly while focusing on bimanual manipulation. The deployment system uses an AgileX Tracer AGV 2 differential-drive base, whereas the collection platform uses passive wheels and two fixed-direction wheels placed along the drive-wheel axis. This configuration mechanically constrains the collection platform to the same nonholonomic motion space as the deployed base, preserving kinematic compatibility

title: STVLA: Spatial-aware and Temporal-memory forVision-Language-Action Models
summary: Robotic manipulation often requires both spatial scene understanding and task history. However, many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely primarily on current observations, without explicitly integrating spatial structure and task history. Appearance-based memories can be sensitive to occlusion and viewpoint changes, while spatial representations of the current scene alone do not preserve how the scene has changed during task execution. We introduce STVLA, a framework that incorporates features from a pretrained visual geometry foundation model into temporal memory alongside visual representations. This allows the policy to recall past scene structure as context for current action decisions. To select informative history, STVLA uses a mathematically grounded scoring rule that balances relevance to the current observation with complementary evidence from memory. Across evaluations on LIBERO, LIBERO-Mem, MIKASA-Robo, and SimplerEnv Bridge, STVLA achieves the highest average success rate among the compared methods on each benchmark. On real-world block stacking, object organization, and phone packaging, it improves success over $π_{0.5}$ by $58.33$, $30.00$, and $35.00$ percentage points, respectively. These results support integrating scene geometry into temporal memory to improve manipulation requiring both spatial precision and task history. Project website: \href{https://stvla.github.io/}{https://stvla.github.io/}
full_text: We present , a spatial-aware and temporal-memory vision-language-action model for robotic manipulation. combines compact spatial representations distilled from a frozen visual geometry model with a bounded visual--spatial memory, enabling the policy to retrieve and fuse task-relevant historical evidence during action generation. Across real-world block stacking, object organization, and phone packaging, the tasks collectively stress geometry-sensitive manipulation and progress tracking through multi-step execution. Across four simulated benchmarks and three real-world manipulation tasks, consistently outperforms strong VLA, memory-augmented, and spatially aware baselines. fig:teaser v Robotic manipulation often requires both spatial scene understanding and task history. INTRODUCTION sec Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have achieved strong performance in robotic manipulation openvla,pi0,pi05 , yet many condition each action primarily on the current observation, leaving both task history and spatial scene structure only implicitly represented. Everyday manipulation tasks are often non-Markovian from the policy's perspective: visually similar observations can correspond to different task states, causing a current-frame policy to repeat completed steps or stall. When the action further depends on the geometric structure of the scene --- the height of a surface, whether a location is still free --- 2D features extracted from a single frame and a single view do not express that structure. In everyday manipulation, the two demands often arise together. Memory-augmented policies retain information from previous observations to support decisions over longer horizons hiveformer,vima,eventvla,kemo,memoryvla , while spatially aware policies enrich visual representations with depth, 3D structure, or features learned by geometry models threedvla,spatialvla,spatialforcing . These capabilities, however, are commonly introduced as separate components. A memory built on appearance features inherits the weaknesses of appearance itself: once the gripper occludes the workspace or the viewpoint changes, the current frame no longer resembles the stored frame that shares its physical configuration, and retrieval fails in exactly the situations where memory should matter most. A spatial representation computed on the current observation alone has the mirror-image problem: it describes what the scene is, but not which parts of it the policy has already changed. This motivates a simple principle: the spatial representation of the scene should be part of what the policy remembers. We introduce , a VLA architecture that integrates spatial representations directly into bounded temporal memory(Fig.~ fig:teaser ). A frozen pretrained visual geometry model wang2026vggtomega extracts scene geometry features from a multi-frame window of RGB observations, and a trainable compressor maps its intermediate features into compact spatial tokens. These spatial tokens are paired with the backbone's visual tokens and stored in a single bounded memory bank. At each step, the current visual and spatial representations jointly retrieve relevant information from the stored history through cross-attention. Retrieved spatial information conditions the action expert through a dedicated prefix segment. This design allows spatial information and temporal context to interact during memory retrieval while preserving the backbone's pretrained image-language representation. Our contributions are summarized as follows: 1pt We introduce a memory paradigm for VLA policies that incorporates features from a pretrained visual geometry foundation model into temporal memory. This makes past scene structure available for action generation, enabling the policy to use both appearance and geometry as historical context. We develop a joint visual-spatial retrieval mechanism for conditioning action generation on useful history. A relevance--non-redundancy score, computed from current--memory feature similarity and normalized feature difference, serves as an entry-level attention prior without introducing an auxiliary learned scorer. We evaluate on four simulation benchmarks and three real-world tasks. improves average success over our baseline on each simulation benchmark and improves success by -- percentage points on real-world tasks that jointly stress geometry-sensitive manipulation and progress tracking. RELATED WORK sec:related Vision-Language-Action Policies Recent VLA models extend pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) to robot action generation. OpenVLA~ openvla discretize robot actions and predict them autoregressively as tokens. In contrast, and ~ pi0,pi05 condition dedicated continuous-action modules on VLM representations and generate action chunks through flow matching. Memory for Robot Policies Memory-augmented robot policies retain past information through different history-selection and memory-management mechanisms. Early dense-history methods append encoded observations and actions to the Transformer context: Hiveformer~ hiveformer retains the full multi-view history, while VIMA~ vima models interleaved observation--action tokens; their sequence length and attention cost grow with retained history. Sparse keyframe-memory methods reduce the retained context: EventVLA~ eventvla predicts future keyframe probabilities from VLA hidden states, whereas KEMO~ kemo identifies candidate events from kinematic cues and filters them by visual change using a frozen encoder. Rather than selecting only keyframes, MemoryVLA~ memoryvla maintains a bounded Perceptual--Cognitive Memory Bank, retrieves task-relevant entries, and, when full, merges the most similar temporally adjacent pair in each perceptual and cognitive stream. Spatial Reasoning for Manipulation Recent works introduce spatial information into robot policies through different representations and architectures. 3D-VLA~ threedvla links 3D perception, reasoning, and action through a 3D generative world model. SpatialVLA~ spatialvla injects Ego3D position encodings into VLA observations, while DepthVLA~ depthvla incorporates a pretrained depth transformer alongside the VLM and action expert. Spatial Forcing~ spatialforcing aligns intermediate VLA features with representations from a pretrained 3D foundation model without requiring explicit 3D inputs at inference. These methods strengthen spatial or spatiotemporal reasoning; differs by storing paired appearance and explicit 3D scene tokens as retrievable per-episode memory and exposing the recalled geometry directly to the VLA action pathway. METHOD sec:method Architecture overview sec:method:overview As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:arch , augments the PaliGemma-based vision--language model~ paligemma and flow-matching action expert of ~ pi05 with spatial tokenization and bounded visual--spatial memory. Current observations are encoded into visual tokens by SigLIP~ siglip and compact spatial tokens through a frozen geometry model and a trainable compressor. These tokens jointly retrieve historical visual--spatial features through score-biased cross-attention. Gated fusion combines the retrieved features with the current representations, which then condition action generation through separate policy-prefix segments alongside the task instruction and robot state. Spatial tokenization sec:method:spatial We leverage frozen ~ wang2026vggtomega to support spatial scene understanding in the policy, complementing the backbone's 2D visual representations. Given a window of RGB observations, the model uses preceding frames as context to extract spatial features of the current scene. Only the features corresponding to the current frame are passed to the compressor. To incorporate these features within the policy-prefix token budget, a trainable compressor uses learned-query cross-attention to aggregate patch features into compact latent representations. A variational bottleneck regularizes these representations before projection to the language-model width, producing spatial tokens . The compressor is jointly trained with the policy under the objectives defined in Sec.~ sec:method:loss . Spatial tokens occupy a dedicated prefix segment under the block-causal attention mask in Fig.~ fig:mask . Visual and instruction--state tokens attend bidirectionally within a shared block, while spatial tokens attend only within their own segment and are masked from the original prefix tokens. Action tokens attend to all prefix tokens and all tokens within the action chunk. This preserves the original prefix attention pattern while making spatial information directly accessible to action generation. Bounded temporal memory sec:method:stm We maintain a bounded memory of paired visual and spatial representations, allowing the policy to retrieve appearance and geometry cues from past observations jointly. At step , let concatenate the current visual tokens and spatial tokens before memory fusion. The bank contains entries from earlier steps in the same episode: where indexes retained steps with , and is the memory capacity. The current tokens query the bank through stacked cross-attention layers: Each query can attend to both visual and spatial tokens across historical entries, enabling cross-modal retrieval rather than restricting each modality to its own history. A learned element-wise gate~ memoryvla combines the retrieved features with the current tokens. The fused outputs retain separate visual and spatial token groups for policy conditioning. After retrieval, is appended to the bank, and the oldest entry is discarded when capacity is exceeded. With no history available, the current tokens pass through unchanged. title: Reins: Frontier Multimodal Models Driving Real Robot Arms on Long-Horizon Tasks, Zero-Shot
summary: Frontier models such as GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 can now plan and call tools, yet they still struggle to drive real robots through long-horizon, contact-rich manipulation, blind while the arm moves and while they think. We present Reins, a harness in which an off-the-shelf model operates a dual-arm robot with 3D perception tools and atomic actions that report contact and grip. The model chains actions in one call, each with a condition that must hold, stopping at the first that fails; a second instance, the narrator, watches the cameras continuously and reports what changed with every result. From images, Reins also builds a simulation-ready twin of the scene for continual policy learning. With natural-language prompts and no task-specific code, GPT-6.1 Sol succeeds in 88% of real episodes on five tasks; without the harness, it fails every shell game, taking 8 times as long. Three frontier models perform alike but differ in tracking a scene that changes while the actor thinks. Code will be released upon publication.
full_text: Frontier models such as GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 can now plan and call tools, yet they still struggle to drive real robots through long-horizon, contact-rich manipulation, blind while the arm moves and while they think. We present Reins, a harness in which an off-the-shelf model operates a dual-arm robot with 3D perception tools and atomic actions that report contact and grip. The model chains actions in one call, each with a condition that must hold, stopping at the first that fails; a second instance, the narrator, watches the cameras continuously and reports what changed with every result. From images, Reins also builds a simulation-ready twin of the scene for continual policy learning. With natural-language prompts and no task-specific code, Sol succeeds in 88 of real episodes on five tasks; without the harness, it fails every shell game, taking 8 times as long. Three frontier models perform alike but differ in tracking a scene that changes while the actor thinks. Code will be released upon publication. Introduction and Related Work Frontier models that plan and call tools~ react2023,toolformer2023 now run as robot policies without robot training, mostly in simulation, where benchmarks find a gap between understanding and executing a task~ . On real hardware, Show-Harness~ showharness2026 moves a Franka and a bimanual AgileX in 2--4\,cm steps, mostly pick-and-place. Trained policies struggle too: on RoboDojo's real Sweep Blocks, ten vision-language-action models trained on 100 demonstrations each never succeed~ robodojo2026 . Earlier language-model systems compose skills, write programs or spatial targets, or feed scene descriptions back to the model~ saycan2022,text2motion2023,codeaspolicies2023,progprompt2023,chatgptrobotics2024,voxposer2023,rekep2024,moka2024,innermonologue2022,socratic2023,reflect2023 ; others learn control from robot data~ aloha2023,diffusionpolicy2023,rt22023,openvla2024,pi02025,pi052025,geminirobotics2025 or sequence learned skills~ geminier2026,roboclaw2026,autort2024 . In Reins, the model drives the arms through atomic actions, with no skill library or task code; two choices set it apart. First, the model attaches stopping conditions to each chain of actions, checked at every step, as in guarded moves~ will1975,lozanoperez1984 and the action conditions of task and motion planning~ garrett2021tamp , but written at run time; Show-Harness runs its action chunks open-loop~ showharness2026 . Second, another instance of the model, the narrator, watches every camera frame while the actor thinks and keeps a running account; VoLo's agent monitors its own execution at 0.2\,Hz~ volo2026 . We contribute (i)~Reins with its guarded chains, (ii)~the narrator and its latency analysis, and (iii)~a real-robot evaluation of three frontier models on five long-horizon tasks, with time and cost. Method Actor loop. At decision , the actor, an off-the-shelf model given a task prompt , outputs a tool call or chain of calls ; its result (measurements, new images, both arms' state and the narrator's entries since ) joins the history (App.~ app:context ). An episode of decisions lasts , model latency plus execution. A chain of thought takes time: latency is 41--78 of in our runs, so each decision should cover several checked steps (1.6--3.4 on average), and the scene may change while the actor thinks. Perception and atomic actions. Of the eighteen tools (App.~ app:tools ), find (SAM~3~ sam3 on RGB-D) and measure turn an object name or image point into a 3D point in the base frame, to about 1.6\,mm with the arm's own wrist camera. Atomic actions move an arm, tilt its tool or work its gripper; move until contact stops when joint current indicates contact, and close gripper reports whether the fingers hold anything. The next window closes when the call returns, , so each window lasts as long as the previous call, and the newest frame reported is 1--2 latencies old. Experiments and Findings Setup and tasks. Two 6-DoF AirBot Play arms with stock parallel grippers share a table, with RGB-D cameras on the head and each wrist; episodes start at the zero pose and the operator judges success. We run five episodes per condition with GPT-6.1 Sol (Ultrafast tier), GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5, at high reasoning effort. In the shell game, the first of three mugs lifted after a 20--30\,s shuffle must cover a hidden red object; the drawer is opened by its 3--4\,mm lip, filled with a block and closed; a towel is folded twice, a shirt sleeves-in and then twice; in sweep, one arm holds a dustpan and the other brushes objects in. The drawer and sweep prompts add grip and pose hints. The narrator and the harness. All three models open the drawer every time; the shell game, whose scene changes while the actor waits, separates them. Without the narrator, Sol wins only 2 of 5. By Eq.~ , a faster narrator sees more: Sol's (Ultrafast tier) answers in 1--6\,s and sees a shuffle in 8--11 windows; Astra's and Opus's (standard tier) take 3--40\,s and see it in 2--4 (Fig.~ fig:results b). Astra's narrator still tracks the red object in 4 of 5 episodes, Opus's in none; Opus's two wins were guesses. Without the harness (raw images, straight-down moves, wait, look), Sol never lifts the correct mug: in four episodes it closes the gripper 6--9 times in 60 calls but lifts no mug, and once it lifts the wrong one. Limitations and Future Work Limitations. Task knowledge enters only through natural-language prompts; contact is sensed only from joint current and gripper width; we test one platform, five episodes per condition; and a slow narrator reports fast changes late (Eq.~ ). Future work. Every episode is fully logged (100\,Hz state, images, text); we will turn successful episodes into reusable chains and checks, rehearsed in simulation twins (App.~ sec:twin ), so that the same model finishes tasks faster, from shorter prompts. Context, Caching and Memory app:context What the actor keeps. The text of an episode stays in the history until the end: every reasoning step, tool result and measurement. Images do not. A result's images remain available for the following decisions, but once the prompt has grown by 30k tokens since the last compaction, all images except those of the newest image-bearing turn are replaced at once by one-line stubs. What the model derived from an old image remains: the object ids that find registered, the pixels it measured and the results. A chain returns only the images of its last run. Why rarely and in bulk. On the provider route we use, the prompt cache only reuses a prompt that extends one it has already served in full, so any edit of earlier history costs one full re-read. Two alternatives performed worse. Compacting whenever the text exceeded a fixed budget edited the history on every call: after the first compaction of a 65-call episode, every call re-read 45--54k tokens at full price, 90 of that episode's uncached tokens. A sliding window that kept the two newest image turns and edited the history before every call reduced the cached prefix to the 6.3k-token system prompt and raised the actor's cost per call from \ 0.85 on the Ultrafast tier, without making calls faster. Compaction triggered by growth costs one re-read per compaction, after which the cache holds again. For Claude, whose provider caches only a prefix that the request marks, the harness adds the marker. The narrator's context. The narrator reports by exception: it replies only with what a window adds (an entry, a correction, or NO CHANGE), and the harness stamps the reply with the window's time span and appends it; consecutive quiet windows are merged into one line. An earlier version that rewrote the whole account on every call spent 11\,s and 666 output tokens on a window in which nothing had changed. The calls form one continuing conversation, so each window is a new turn on a cached prefix; re-sending the account in a fresh prompt for each window was cached in none of 41 calls. The conversation restarts every 60 frames (about a minute), seeded with the episode's first frame and the account so far, so old frames are dropped in bulk with one uncached read per restart. We count frames rather than tokens because models encode a frame differently: Claude Opus 5.5 spends about 600--700 tokens on a frame that GPT-6 encodes in about 240, so a 15k-token budget restarted Opus's narrator every 1.9 calls (43 restarts in one drawer episode, with 32 of its input cached). A 60k-token ceiling still bounds every model's conversation. Memory within an episode. Besides the text history and the narrator's account, four records persist across calls. (i)~Objects: find registers each object as an id with a 3D position, drawn on every later image and listed in every result. (ii)~Measured shapes: measure can turn a visible contour, such as a cloth edge or a drawer lip, into base-frame points that remain valid after the arm occludes it, and follow path can travel through them. (iii)~A task ledger: plan records the steps and mark step the evidence for each; done is refused while a planned step is pending. (iv)~What each arm holds, with the finger gap measured at the grasp. The narrator names identical objects by where it first saw them (``the original middle mug''), which lets an identity survive a shuffle. Measured. Table~ tab:context summarizes the 45 counted episodes. Tools app:tools Table~ tab:tools lists the eighteen tools the actor can call. Every result returns the state of both arms (tool position and angles, gripper gap, what each arm holds), fresh camera images and the narrator's entries since the previous result. On the dual-arm robot, the motion and gripper tools take the name of the arm to move. Simulation-Ready Twins of the Scene sec:twin Reins can also rebuild the scene in front of the robot as a MuJoCo simulation from one calibrated head-camera RGB frame. This tool, model scene, was not used in the episodes of Section~3. The model names the objects in the image and gives each a category, a box and any hint it can read off the image, such as an upside-down mug or a hidden handle. The tool returns a scene in the robot's world frame with, for every object, a closed mesh, collision geometry, mass, inertia, joints and surface appearance, together with the calibrated head camera, the bases of both arms and a verdict on whether each object is ready for simulation. Geometry. Each object is built as a parametric model of its category, by code that drives Blender, rather than fused from depth: a mug is a hollow lathe profile with a swept handle, a drawer cabinet has its drawers on prismatic joints, and a towel or shirt is a deformable sheet; bricks, caps, sponges, brushes and dustpans have builders of their own, and a new category is one more builder. SAM (ViT-H)~ kirillov2023sam segments each object from its box, and the mask's footprint on the table gives a first guess of position, axis and size. The logs keep only the head camera's RGB frames, so depth comes from a monocular network, scaled by the table's calibrated height. The models are then fitted to the masks through the calibrated camera by silhouette IoU, with Nelder--Mead over position, yaw and size, and discrete structure, such as a brick's stud count or the side a mug's handle is on, is found by enumeration. Collision geometry is built for contact: a mug's wall is a ring of 16 thin boxes, so an upturned mug can cover a cap and push it along

title: EgoX: Egocentric Cross-Embodiment Manipulation with Embodiment Dreaming
summary: Generalist manipulation policies can benefit from the complementary experience of humans, real robots, and simulated agents. However, differences in morphology, sensing, and control interfaces make it difficult to learn effectively from their combined demonstrations. We introduce EgoX, an egocentric cross-embodiment learning framework that organizes heterogeneous demonstrations through semantically corresponding observation and action modalities. EgoX pretrains a Modularized Cross-Embodiment Transformer with Embodiment Dreaming (MXT+) on this mixture and fine-tunes it on target-embodiment demonstrations. Within each embodiment, MXT+ assigns a dedicated tokenizer to each observation modality and a dedicated expert to each action modality, with a Transformer trunk shared across embodiments. A training-only embodiment-dreaming objective predicts latent representations of future visual and proprioceptive states, encouraging the shared trunk to model each embodiment's dynamics. Across 13 task-embodiment pairs spanning five tasks and six robot embodiments, including five physical robots and one simulated humanoid, cross-embodiment pretraining raises MXT+'s average normalized task progress from 0.63 to 0.80 over training from scratch. The gains are particularly pronounced under out-of-distribution conditions, where average task progress increases from 0.53 to 0.77. Ablations demonstrate the benefits of broader pretraining mixtures, modular interfaces, and embodiment dreaming, with dreaming producing more similar latent geometry across embodiments. Project page: egox-dream.github.io.
full_text: 0pt Generalist manipulation policies can benefit from the complementary experience of humans, real robots, and simulated agents. However, differences in morphology, sensing, and control interfaces make it difficult to learn effectively from their combined demonstrations. We introduce EgoX, an egocentric cross-embodiment learning framework that organizes heterogeneous demonstrations through semantically corresponding observation and action modalities. EgoX pretrains a Modularized Cross-Embodiment Transformer with Embodiment Dreaming (MXT+) on this mixture and fine-tunes it on target-embodiment demonstrations. Within each embodiment, MXT+ assigns a dedicated tokenizer to each observation modality and a dedicated expert to each action modality, with a Transformer trunk shared across embodiments. A training-only embodiment-dreaming objective predicts latent representations of future visual and proprioceptive states, encouraging the shared trunk to model each embodiment's dynamics. Across 13 task--embodiment pairs spanning five tasks and six robot embodiments, including five physical robots and one simulated humanoid, cross-embodiment pretraining raises MXT+'s average normalized task progress from 0.63 to 0.80 over training from scratch. The gains are particularly pronounced under out-of-distribution conditions, where average task progress increases from 0.53 to 0.77. Ablations demonstrate the benefits of broader pretraining mixtures, modular interfaces, and embodiment dreaming, with dreaming producing more similar latent geometry across embodiments. Introduction sec:introduction Large-scale pretraining has driven rapid progress in natural language processing~ devlin2019bert,brown2020language and computer vision~ radford2021learning,dosovitskiy2021image , demonstrating the potential of learning reusable knowledge from diverse data. A corresponding ambition in robotics is to develop generalist models that accumulate manipulation knowledge across tasks and environments and can be adapted to different robot embodiments. We envision a future populated by robots with complementary physical capabilities: tabletop arms, wheeled mobile manipulators, humanoids, and quadrupeds offer different combinations of mobility, reach, and workspace access, while grippers, dexterous hands, and specialized tools support different forms of object interaction~ pfeifer2007self,baines2024robots,kirschner2025categorizing . Their different ways of perceiving and interacting with the world also provide complementary experience for learning. However, collecting data and training models separately for every embodiment, task, and scene is costly and limits the reuse of this experience. How can we draw on experience across these embodiments to develop shared manipulation knowledge while allowing each robot to adapt it to its own body and environment? Several complementary data sources offer a path toward this goal. Cross-embodiment robot learning draws on demonstrations collected across different bodies, sensors, and action spaces~ o2024open,team2024octo,kim2024openvla,doshi2024scaling,wang2024scaling,team2025gemini15 . Egocentric human data captures diverse physical interactions in real-world settings beyond existing robot deployment environments~ kareer2025egomimic,niu2025human2locoman,qiu2025humanoid,zheng2026egoscale . Simulation enables scalable data collection and has supported policy pretraining, sim-to-real transfer, and co-training with real-world demonstrations~ deshpande2026molmobot,bjorck2025gr00t,maddukuri2025sim,lin2026humanoidmimicgen . Together, these sources can broaden the objects, scenes, and interaction strategies available for learning beyond the demonstrations collected for any individual robot. Realizing this potential, however, requires training recipes that can make effective use of heterogeneous experience. Demonstrations from different embodiments encode interactions through distinct morphologies, viewpoints, proprioception, action semantics, and motion dynamics, making it challenging to turn their combined experience into useful manipulation capabilities across robots. Recent work has examined scaling laws and data composition for robot manipulation~ lin2025data,lin2026systematic,trilbm2025careful . Alongside these questions, we focus on how experience from heterogeneous embodiments should be collected, represented, and used for shared learning. Our central concern is the design of representations and learning interfaces that allow diverse demonstrations to contribute to a common manipulation model while preserving the differences that matter for each embodiment's sensing and control. We treat humans, real robots, and simulated agents as embodiments on equal footing, each contributing its own observations and actions. Through joint pretraining and adaptation to target embodiments, we investigate how this shared experience can improve downstream manipulation across different robot bodies and end-effectors. Fig.~ fig:kitchen_bread_cross_embodiment illustrates this perspective through corresponding stages of Kitchen-Bread performed by human, real-robot, and simulated embodiments. We introduce EgoX (Fig.~ fig:framework ), an egocentric cross-embodiment learning framework built around a single methodological premise: transfer should occur through semantically corresponding modalities, while sensing and control interfaces remain embodiment-specific. The framework has three components. First, organizes human, real-robot, and simulated demonstrations in a unified observation-action representation, grouping heterogeneous signals into anatomically or functionally relevant modalities and expressing poses in a unified egocentric frame system. Second, MXT+, a Modularized Cross-Embodiment Transformer, adopts a fine-grained modular design: within each embodiment, each observation modality has its own tokenizer and each action modality its own expert, while a shared Transformer trunk integrates information across modalities and embodiments. Third, MXT+ uses embodiment dreaming, an auxiliary objective that predicts future embodiment latents from the current shared representation. This training-only branch encourages the trunk to encode how each embodiment's visual and proprioceptive state evolves, without requiring pixel reconstruction or deployment-time computation. We evaluate EgoX on five manipulation tasks, from long-horizon loco-manipulation to precise insertion and tool use (Kitchen-Bread, Kitchen-Cleanup, Sort, Insert, and Scoop), across six robot embodiments: G1-Dex5, xArm7-Dex4, G1-Sim-Dex3, LocoMan-Dex2, R1Lite-Gripper, Z1-Tool. Human demonstrations provide an additional pretraining source. Our experiments compare MXT+ variants with baseline policies across all tasks and ablate the pretraining mixture, embodiment dreaming objective, and MXT+'s modular design. Cross-embodiment pretraining raises MXT+'s average task progress from 0.63 to 0.80, yielding the highest average score among the evaluated methods and the best performance on 12 of 13 task--embodiment pairs. The gains from pretraining are particularly pronounced under out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions, where average task progress increases from 0.53 to 0.77. Broader pretraining mixtures transfer better, and embodiment dreaming raises task progress from 0.63 to 0.78 across seven settings while making the trunk's latent geometry more similar across embodiments. In summary, our contributions are: A unified, modality-structured representation for egocentric cross-embodiment manipulation. organizes human, real-robot, and simulated demonstrations into a common observation--action structure based on anatomically or functionally corresponding modalities, while retaining embodiment-specific sensing and control interfaces. MXT+, a modular cross-embodiment Transformer with embodiment dreaming. Within each embodiment, MXT+ assigns dedicated tokenizers and action experts to individual observation and action modalities, connected through a shared Transformer trunk. Embodiment dreaming encourages the trunk to model each embodiment's transition dynamics through future-latent prediction used only during training. A systematic study of cross-embodiment transfer. Experiments across five tasks and six diverse robot embodiments demonstrate the benefits of cross-embodiment pretraining, particularly under OOD conditions. Ablations show benefits from broader pretraining mixtures, modular interfaces, and embodiment dreaming, with dreaming also producing more similar latent geometry across embodiments. Related Work sec:related_work Cross-embodiment robot learning aims to train policies that benefit from data collected on different bodies, sensors, and control interfaces. Large robot datasets and generalist policies demonstrate the value of scaling policy learning across tasks and robot embodiments o2024open,kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi_,team2025gemini , and recent work extends such pretraining to include human data luo2026beingh05,bjorck2025gr00t . Prior methods handle embodiment heterogeneity with shared-trunk policies that use embodiment-specific tokenizers or action heads doshi2024scaling,niu2025human2locoman,wang2024scaling , with a single embodiment-conditioned action head li2026xdiffvla , or with image editing that aligns robot appearance across embodiments chen2024mirage,lepert2024shadow . Existing methods either cover a relatively narrow range of embodiments and end-effectors or preserve heterogeneity by giving each embodiment a separate interface, leaving the extent of modality-level sharing unclear. In contrast, EgoX covers highly heterogeneous embodiments and end-effectors: it is evaluated on humanoid, wheeled bimanual, tabletop-arm, quadrupedal, and simulated platforms, with three- to five-fingered dexterous hands, two-finger and parallel-jaw grippers, and a tool. MXT+ combines embodiment-specific interfaces with modality-level sharing through modular tokenizers and action experts, and adds embodiment dreaming as a training signal through the prediction of future embodiment latents. Egocentric human data offers a scalable source of manipulation experience spanning diverse tasks, objects, and environments. Recent advances in wearable devices, such as XR headsets and smart glasses, have improved the quality and scale of such data chen_arcap_nodate,hoque2025egodex,punamiya2026egoverse . Human videos have been used to learn transferable priors through visual, affordance, and latent-action objectives nair2022r3m,srirama2024hrp,ye2024latent,bu_univla_2025,zhang_clap_2026 . Other methods use human demonstrations directly for policy learning, through domain adaptation punamiya2025egobridge , pretraining or co-training kareer2025egomimic,yuan_motiontrans_2025,yang_egovla_2025,zheng2026egoscale,shi2026egohumanoid,zhu_emma_2025,bi2026hrdt,wei2026psi0 , and transfer without additional target-robot demonstrations xu2026hommi . Much of this literature emphasizes transferring human experience to target robot embodiments, while EgoX focuses on collecting and jointly learning from egocentric demonstrations across human and heterogeneous robot embodiments, and investigates how this shared training benefits manipulation across diverse platforms. World models learn to predict how the world evolves under actions assran2025vjepa2,goswami_world_2025,gao2026dreamdojo . World action models couple such prediction with policy learning by jointly predicting actions and future observations, with targets including pixels, pretrained visual features, and 3D motion flow li_egowam_2026 , embeddings from frozen or separately pretrained encoders zheng2025flare,luo2026beingh07 , and future tactile signals or tactile latents niu2026learning,lou2026dreamtac . These works show that predicting future observations provides a useful training signal for policy learning. Other methods model the embodiment itself, either by predicting its dynamics or kinematics fu_met

title: SALA: Semantically Aligned Latent Actions Enable Dual-Axis Scaling of Embodied Foundation Models
summary: Embodied foundation models hinge on diverse robot interaction data, which are costly to collect. Egocentric human videos offer a complementary source of experience, and latent action models (LAMs) provide a popular means of leveraging these videos for policy supervision. Compared with world-action models (WAMs), LAMs can offer greater training efficiency and potentially lower inference costs by avoiding explicit pixel prediction during policy learning and execution. However, most existing LAMs learn latent actions solely through video reconstruction, which can cause their representations to cluster by visual appearance rather than by the underlying actions. As a result, they struggle to align human actions with their robot counterparts. To bridge the gap, we introduce SALA, which emphasizes establishing the semantic correspondence for latent actions. Without requiring paired data, we use the language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarities and supervise cross-embodiment correspondence. Specifically, we translate these similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents, while robot action reconstruction grounds the latent space in control. The resulting shared latent action space provides a unified supervision signal for training an embodied foundation model on both human and robot videos. Notably, latent action supervision enables scaling along two axes: (1) pre-training on increasing amounts of general human video consistently reduces robot action prediction error on downstream tasks, and (2) post-training on increasing amounts of task-specific human video substantially improves real-world robot task success rates.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro Embodied foundation models, such as vision-language-action (VLA) models, connect visual observations and language instructions to robot actions, offering a path toward general-purpose robot control~ black2024pi_0,brohan2023rt,kim2024openvla . Their generalization depends on diverse interaction experience across tasks, objects, and environments, yet collecting such data through robot teleoperation remains costly. Egocentric human videos provide a complementary source of experience, capturing everyday manipulation without requiring robot hardware or teleoperation~ Grauman_2022_CVPR,hoque2026egodex,punamiya2026egoverse . Using this experience for policy learning, however, requires bridging the human-to-robot embodiment gap: the same operation can involve different motions and control mechanisms across humans and robots, and is often performed in scenes that differ from the robot's workspace. Latent action models (LAMs) are a popular way to incorporate human videos into robot policy training without explicit action labels~ ye2024latent,chen2024moto,bu2025univla . By encoding visual transitions in a shared latent space, they provide a common prediction target for human and robot experience. Compared with world-action models (WAMs), which predict future video frames together with actions~ wu2023gr1,yuan2026fastwam,li2026lingbotva , LAMs avoid explicit pixel prediction during policy learning, which can make training more efficient. However, most existing LAMs learn latent actions solely through video reconstruction, which constrains each latent to explain the transition within its own clip but does not relate human and robot executions of the same behavior. Their latents therefore tend to cluster by visual appearance, such as the scene, rather than by the underlying action, so semantically similar human and robot actions need not lie close together. Aligning human actions with their robot counterparts thus requires supervision that connects their meanings across embodiments. Our insight is that language can provide this supervision. Even when human and robot clips are unpaired, natural-language descriptions of their atomic actions, such as ``grasp the cup'', relate a human clip to multiple robot clips with different degrees of semantic similarity, as illustrated on the left of . We propose , which trains a latent action tokenizer by translating these similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents. Robot latents, grounded in control by action reconstruction, serve as anchors, and the alignment moves only human latents toward them. As the middle of shows, the resulting latent actions are organized by action semantics rather than by scene, giving human videos a prediction target that is meaningful for robot control. Once trained, the tokenizer labels videos from their frames alone, so its latent actions provide a unified supervision signal for training the policy on both human and robot videos, without action labels or atomic-action descriptions. This makes human video a scalable source of supervision along two axes. In pre-training, the policy can absorb large-scale general human videos spanning diverse everyday tasks. In post-training, because human and robot latent actions are aligned, task-specific human videos, , human demonstrations of the target task, supervise the same action expert that controls the robot. Since such demonstrations require no robot, they offer a practical way to improve a policy on a new task, one that robot-only policies cannot exploit. We evaluate in simulation and on a real robot. On RoboTwin 2.0~ chen2025robotwin , where videos of another robot arm stand in for human videos, achieves a higher average success rate than existing LAMs and WAMs trained on the same videos, with the largest gain in domain-randomized scenes. Analyses of the tokenizer show that language alignment organizes latent actions by atomic action semantics rather than by scene. On a real robot controlled in a 63-DoF action space, including two 22-DoF dexterous hands, human video helps along both axes. Pre-training on more general human video, up to 2 , 678 hours, consistently reduces the robot's action prediction error on downstream tasks without additional robot data. With teleoperated demonstrations fixed, post-training on more task-specific human video raises the average real-robot success rate from 53.75 to 72.5 . The right of shows both trends. Our contributions are as follows: We use language as relational supervision: atomic-action descriptions align human and robot latent actions from unpaired videos, with the alignment anchored on robot latents grounded in control. We turn human videos into latent-action supervision for the same action expert that controls the robot, which enables scaling along two axes: general human video in pre-training and task-specific human video in post-training. Experiments in simulation and on a 63-DoF real robot with dexterous hands show that outperforms prior LAMs and WAMs trained on the same cross-embodiment videos in average success rate, and that human video scales along both axes: more general human video in pre-training keeps reducing the robot's action prediction error, and more task-specific human video in post-training raises real-world success rates. Method sec:method Our goal is to use action-free egocentric human videos, which can be collected at scale, to facilitate the training of robot policies. We connect these videos to robot control through latent actions. This connection requires latent actions to establish semantic correspondence across embodiments, which a shared latent space trained only by reconstructing each clip does not guarantee. As outlined in , therefore learns a latent action tokenizer aligned across embodiments by language supervision from atomic-action descriptions, and uses it to leverage human videos in robot policy training. Preliminaries: Latent Action Models sec:prelim LAMs learn compact representations of visual transitions without action labels by coupling inverse and forward dynamics~ NEURIPS2025_d7b3cef7 . Given observations and separated by a horizon , an inverse-dynamics encoder infers a latent action that encodes the transition between the two observations. An information bottleneck produces , limiting how much information from the future observation reaches the decoder. The forward-dynamics decoder then reconstructs from the current observation and the compressed code . Training minimizes the reconstruction error in image or feature space over observed pairs. The inferred codes can serve as prediction targets for policy learning from action-free videos~ ye2024latent,bu2025univla . Their usefulness, however, depends on what they encode: accurate reconstruction does not guarantee that the latent captures controllable actions, since it may also retain scene information or changes unrelated to control~ NEURIPS2025_d7b3cef7 . For human-to-robot transfer, the representation must additionally connect semantically related behaviors across embodiments, a relation that reconstruction within individual clips does not explicitly constrain. We therefore augment this predictive formulation with robot action supervision and language-guided cross-embodiment alignment. Grounding Latent Actions in Robot Control sec:latent_representation We train the latent action tokenizer on a human dataset and an independently collected robot dataset : Each clip is represented by its endpoint observations, and and are the initial robot state and the subsequent action chunk, available only for robot data. The natural-language description specifies the atomic actions performed by the embodiment in the clip. As shown in (a), human and robot clips share the visual encoder , the quantizer , and the visual decoder , trained with visual reconstruction losses as in . Visual reconstruction alone does not ensure that the latent captures controllable actions. Teleoperation data, however, already provide ground-truth robot actions, which we exploit during tokenizer training. A robot-only action decoder reconstructs the action chunk from and the initial state , with loss , which grounds robot latents directly in control~ chen2026iclr-villax . Human clips share this space without action labels; the control-grounded robot latents later serve as anchors for cross-embodiment alignment. Robot-Anchored Semantic Transfer sec:semantic_transfer We align human latent actions toward the robot representations grounded by action reconstruction in . These robot representations serve as control anchors, while atomic-action descriptions determine how each human clip should relate to them. Atomic-action descriptions characterize what a clip does independently of the embodiment performing it. We therefore encode with a frozen text encoder and use the similarity between language descriptions to measure how semantically related a human clip is to each robot clip. Because human and robot clips are collected independently, a human clip rarely has an exact robot counterpart. It can nonetheless relate to several robot clips to different degrees; for example, grasping a cup is closer to grasping a bottle than to placing a cup. We therefore describe each human clip by a soft neighborhood over the robot clips in a batch, given by a softmax over its language similarities, and use it to supervise the clip's neighborhood in latent space. (a) illustrates this with and , the language and latent similarities between the human and robot clips in a batch: the dashed rows give the two neighborhoods of one human clip. Formally, the alignment loss is where and are the entries of and for human clip and robot clip , with ; the softmax temperatures are omitted for clarity. Here denotes cosine similarity averaged over tokens, and the stop-gradient makes alignment move human latents toward the control-grounded robot anchors rather than pulling the anchors toward human latents, which lack action supervision. Language thus supervises what visual and action reconstruction leave unconstrained: the semantic correspondence between human and robot latent actions. The choice of quantizer matters for this alignment. The relations in are graded, so alignment needs to move the pre-quantization latents continuously, while the policy's targets are the tokens that produces from them. A standard hard VQ~ vandenoord2017neurips-neural fits these graded relations poorly: its commitment loss pulls each toward the selected codeword, and its token, a one-hot assignment to a single codeword, changes only when switches to another code. We therefore instantiate with SoftVQ~ Chen_2025_CVPR , which represents each token as a categorical distribution over the codebook rather than a one-hot assignment, and forms from the codewords weighted by these distributions; we denote the tokens of a clip by . SoftVQ requires no commitment loss, and its distributions vary smoothly with , so the tokens can express graded differences between latents. As shown in , the alignment loss decreases with SoftVQ but stays near its initial value with hard VQ. The tokenizer is trained with the three signals described above: visual reconstruction of human and robot clips ( and ) captures visual transitions, action reconstruction ( ) grounds robot latents in control, and semantic alignment ( ) supervises the correspondence between human and robot latents.
