For a clip , the teacher outputs its latent action tokens , each a categorical distribution over the codebook. We keep these distributions rather than discretizing them into code indices, retaining the graded similarity structure of the latent space. The future observation

title: UAV-Flow++: A Unified Suite for Benchmarking and Learning Language-Guided UAV Flight
summary: Language-guided UAV navigation has largely focused on long-horizon route planning, leaving short-range, object-relative flight maneuvers underexplored. To address this gap, we formulate Flying-on-a-Word (Flow), a task requiring a UAV to convert concise natural-language instruction, egocentric visual observation, and current state dynamics into continuous flight actions. Flow encompasses both primitive motion commands and complex object-interactive behaviors, assessing motion intent comprehension and spatial context grounding. To enable policy learning and closed-loop evaluation, we introduce UAV-Flow, a comprehensive dataset comprising 30,692 expert-piloted real-world trajectories across eight distinct motion categories, alongside 10,109 simulation trajectories in the UAV-Flow-Sim environment equipped with task-specific completion criteria. Furthermore, we develop FlowVLA, which undergoes imitation pretraining on mixed real-sim demonstrations and online post-training via Tail-Aware GRPO (TGRPO). By leveraging group reward distributions, TGRPO effectively reinforces high-reward action sequences. Evaluated on 273 held-out UAV-Flow-Sim episodes, pretrained FlowVLA achieves a mean success rate of 75.58%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 6.72 percentage points, which TGRPO post-training further elevates to 93.16% with superior sample efficiency. Physical UAV experiments demonstrate robust execution of object-relative commands in both indoor and outdoor real-world scenes. Together, Flow establishes a novel benchmark and learning framework for language-conditioned flight maneuvers.
full_text: Language-guided UAV navigation has largely focused on long-horizon route planning, leaving short-range, object-relative flight maneuvers underexplored. To address this gap, we formulate Flying-on-a-Word (Flow), a task requiring a UAV to convert concise natural-language instruction, egocentric visual observation, and current state dynamics into continuous flight actions. Flow encompasses both primitive motion commands and complex object-interactive behaviors, assessing motion intent comprehension and spatial context grounding. To enable policy learning and closed-loop evaluation, we introduce UAV-Flow, a comprehensive dataset comprising 30,692 expert-piloted real-world trajectories across eight distinct motion categories, alongside 10,109 simulation trajectories in the UAV-Flow-Sim environment equipped with task-specific completion criteria. Furthermore, we develop FlowVLA, which undergoes imitation pretraining on mixed real-sim demonstrations and online post-training via Tail-Aware GRPO (TGRPO). By leveraging group reward distributions, TGRPO effectively reinforces high-reward action sequences. Evaluated on 273 held-out UAV-Flow-Sim episodes, pretrained FlowVLA achieves a mean success rate of 75.58 , outperforming the strongest baseline by 6.72 percentage points, which TGRPO post-training further elevates to 93.16 with superior sample efficiency. Physical UAV experiments demonstrate robust execution of object-relative commands in both indoor and outdoor real-world scenes. Together, Flow establishes a novel benchmark and learning framework for language-conditioned flight maneuvers. Introduction Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are widely deployed across diverse applications, serving as aerial perception platforms for object detection, tracking, counting, and human behavior understanding~ visdrone,uav123,animaldrone,droneswarm,uavhuman , as well as enabling precision agriculture, infrastructure inspection, emergency response, and entertainment applications~ blei2025cloudtrack, au2025contingency, wang2026Skyfind, yao2024aeroverse . In parallel, advances in motion planning and control have enabled increasingly autonomous flight and multi-UAV coordination in cluttered three-dimensional environments~ uavmotion,ego_planner,ego_swarm,usenko2017realtime . These capabilities provide a technical foundation for UAVs to operate as embodied agents that interpret human intent and execute tasks in the physical world. While modern UAVs are increasingly capable of autonomous flight, enabling them to follow high-level natural language instructions remains a fundamental challenge in achieving more intelligent human--UAV interaction. For example, executing a command such as ``Fly 3 meters in front of me and take a photo" requires UAVs to transform abstract human intentions into executable physical actions. This process demands that the system seamlessly interpret user intent, reason about the environment, and synthesize dynamically feasible, collision-free flight trajectories. In pursuit of language-guided aerial autonomy, recent efforts have extended vision-language navigation (VLN) paradigms from ground robots to UAV platforms anderson2018r2r,Chen_2022_duet,cma,Liu_2023_Aerialvln,lee2024citynav,gao2025openfly,wang2024openuav . Leveraging large-scale simulated environments airsim,unrealcv,gazebo,zhong2024unrealzoo,yao2024aeroverse , these approaches enable UAVs to follow language instructions for long-horizon target search and goal-directed navigation tasks. However, prevailing research mainly prioritizes high-level semantic reasoning and macro-level route synthesis anderson2018r2r,Chen_2022_duet,ku2020rxr,zhou2024navgpt,zhou2024navgpt2,lin2025navcot , operating on the premise that short-range execution can be offloaded to standard low-level planners and control modules uavmotion,ego_planner,ego_swarm . While this assumption has proven successful in many robotic systems, extending it to UAV platforms introduces additional challenges. UAVs must plan and execute dynamically feasible motions while avoiding obstacles in unconstrained 3D environments under real-world kinematic constraints uavmotion,ego_planner,usenko2017realtime . As a result, enabling language-guided low-level flight maneuver remains a critical yet largely underexplored problem in the development of intelligent UAV systems. We introduce the Flying-on-a-Word (Flow) task to formalize language-conditioned short-range maneuver execution. Given a concise instruction, egocentric observations, and UAV state estimates, the agent must interpret the intended motion and execute the corresponding flight behavior through closed-loop interaction. Flow covers primitive motion commands and object-interactive commands, assessing motion intent understanding and spatial context grounding. To support systematic evaluation and policy learning on language-conditioned short-range UAV flight, we present UAV-Flow, the first large-scale benchmark that integrates real-world expert demonstrations with an interactive simulation suite. Specifically, UAV-Flow comprises 30,692 expert-piloted real-world trajectories spanning eight major motion categories and diverse visual contexts. Complementing these demonstrations, UAV-Flow-Sim provides 10,109 simulated trajectories in an interactive environment, enabling controlled policy training and closed-loop evaluation. We further develop an automated evaluation method for UAV-Flow-Sim to assess task success by jointly considering maneuver execution quality and final state instruction compliance. Next, we introduce a staged policy learning framework that jointly exploits expert demonstrations and simulation-based interaction to make effective use of task-specific data. In the first stage, imitation learning is used to ground the policy in the distribution of expert flight behaviors, enabling the model to acquire instruction-compliant maneuvers from offline demonstrations. However, during closed-loop execution, control deviations can lead the policy to states outside the demonstration distribution. We further improve the policy through environment interaction in UAV-Flow-Sim, using task-level completion feedback to guide policy optimization. Guided by this task-level feedback, we seek to learn more effectively from the action sequences of trajectories with higher completion scores. Therefore, we build upon GRPO~ shao2024deepseekmath and introduce a tail-aware advantage derived from the group reward distribution, producing tail-aware GRPO (TGRPO). This advantage construction assigns greater weight to reward intervals reached by fewer trajectories within each group, strengthening learning from high-reward execution while making fuller use of outcomes that are sparsely represented in group. For physical deployment, we use a ground-drone collaborative architecture in which the ground station performs VLA inference and the UAV executes the commands. The execution layer selects look-ahead waypoints according to the measured end-to-end delay, accounting for UAV motion during communication and inference to support continuous closed-loop flight. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We define the Flying-on-a-Word (Flow) task, which formulates language-conditioned UAV navigation as fine-grained, short-range trajectory execution from egocentric observations, assessing the policy's ability to understand motion intent and execute object-grounded spatial behaviors. (2) We build UAV-Flow, a real-world expert demonstration dataset, and UAV-Flow-Sim, an interactive simulation suite, together forming the large-scale real-world benchmark for language-conditioned UAV short-range navigation. We also provide an automated task-level closed-loop evaluation protocol in the simulation benchmark. (3) We propose a staged policy learning framework that combines imitation learning and reinforcement learning through imitation pretraining on mixed real-world and simulated demonstrations, followed by closed-loop post-training with Tail-Aware GRPO (TGRPO). (4) We have conducted extensive experiments. The pretrained FlowVLA policy achieves a success rate of 75.58 , which TGRPO post-training further raises to 93.16 , achieving the highest overall success rate among evaluated methods. Comprehensive ablation studies validate the effectiveness of the policy learning framework. This paper is built upon UAVFlow~ wang2026uav , our conference version, and extends it in several important aspects. First, we further develop an upgraded closed-loop simulation evaluation suite, UAV-Flow-Sim, equipped with newly introduced automated task-level evaluation metrics for more fine-grained and reproducible assessment. Second, we develop FlowVLA with mixed-demonstration pretraining followed by online RL post-training, incorporating a tail-aware advantage into GRPO to strengthen learning from the action sequences of high-reward trajectories and improve success rates on challenging Flow tasks. Third, we provide a much more comprehensive experimental study, including comparisons with prior methods, ablation studies, and qualitative analyses. Compared with the conference version, the extended method achieves clear performance improvements and provides a more complete benchmark, training, and evaluation framework for language-conditioned UAV maneuvers. Related Work Datasets and Benchmarks Language-guided UAV research is evolving from vision-and-language navigation (VLN) toward vision-language-action (VLA) learning, while gradually extending from simulation-based studies toward real-world data. Early benchmarks primarily focus on long-horizon route or goal navigation in simulated environments. AVDN~ fan2023aerial investigates dialog-guided flight, while CityNav~ lee2024citynav extends goal-oriented navigation to reconstructed urban environments. AerialVLN~ Liu_2023_Aerialvln further studies long-horizon language-guided flight in city-scale simulations using a discrete 4-DoF action space. Subsequent works explore more diverse task and action settings: OpenUAV~ wang2024openuav introduces continuous trajectories, OpenFly~ gao2025openfly scales up simulator-based aerial VLN, IndoorUAV~ liu2025indooruav combines long-horizon VLN with short-horizon VLA data, and HUGE-Bench~ guo2026hugebench evaluates high-level multi-stage VLA tasks. As shown in Table~ tab:uav_benchmarks , these benchmarks cover increasingly diverse tasks and action spaces, but the dataset and environment interactions remain primarily simulation-based. Beyond navigation, AeroVerse~ yao2024aeroverse broadens the scope of aerial embodied intelligence to include scene awareness, spatial reasoning, navigational exploration, task planning, and motion decision-making. Meanwhile, existing real-world UAV datasets mainly focus on visual perception~ visdrone,uav123,animaldrone,uavhuman , with relatively few providing demonstrations that align language instructions, visual observations, UAV states, and executable actions for policy learning. UAV-Flow~ wang2026uav addresses this gap by providing real-world language-vision-action demonstrations for fine-grained flight control learning, together with UAV-Flow-Sim for reproducible closed-loop evaluation. This combination advances language-guided UAV research beyond simulation-based navigation toward learning and evaluating action policies grounded in real-world flight demonstrations. End-to-End Vision-Language-Action Models End-to-end VLA models map visual observations and language instructions to executable actions. OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla autoregressively predicts discretized action tokens, whereas ~ black2024pi0 and ~ physicalintelligence2025pi05 employ flow-matching action experts conditioned on pretrained VLM features to generate continuous action chunks. Building on these architectures, OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025openvlaoft improves action generation and control efficiency through action chunking, parallel decoding, and continuous action regression. title: Topology-Aware 4D Gaussian Splatting for Egocentric Videos
summary: Reconstructing dynamic scenes and objects from monocular egocentric video is crucial for embodied AI, yet existing 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) approaches struggle with everyday interactions involving topological changes, such as cutting, assembly, opening, or closing. Since 4DGS methods rely on deforming a fixed representation, events that split, merge, or reveal surfaces cause severe visual artifacts. To address this challenge, we introduce TopoEgo, the first benchmark dedicated to topological changes in egocentric video (covering fission, fusion, open, and close), alongside Topo-4DGS, a topology-aware reconstruction method. Topo4DGS jointly models part-level motion and time-varying surface support by assigning independent rigid transformations to interacting parts and dynamically activating or deactivating Gaussians as surfaces appear, disappear, or separate. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Topo-4DGS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art 4DGS approaches across topological changes, especially on post-event frames. Code and data will be made publicly available.

Introduction Dynamic 3D reconstruction from egocentric videos is important for robotics and AR applications, as it directly captures the physics and geometry of human-object interactions~ zhang2024egogaussian,wang2025degauss . However, everyday manipulation rarely involves purely rigid motion; it inherently induces complex object transformations and topological changes, such as cutting, assembling components, and opening containers (see Fig.~ fig:teaser and fig:topoego_examples ). Because egocentric videos capture daily activities from the actors' viewpoint, such events are ubiquitous. Our analysis identifies them in over of Ego4D~ grauman2022ego4d and over of EPIC-KITCHENS~ damen2022epickitchens annotated videos. Dynamically reconstructing these interactions in 3D requires more than estimating object motion: a method must determine which parts move together and adapt its geometric representation as surfaces are created, exposed, or concealed. In particular, topological events violate the persistence assumptions of Gaussian-based monocular 4D reconstruction methods in two ways. First, motion structure may change: regions that initially move together can become independent, whereas canonical deformation methods continuously deform fixed geometry~ yang2024deformable3dgs,wu2024fourdgs , tracking-based methods preserve primitive identities~ luiten2024dynamic3dgs , and EgoGaussian~ zhang2024egogaussian assigns a single rigid motion to each object. Second, surface support, i.e., the set of 3D surface locations represented by an object's Gaussian primitives, may change as surfaces are created, exposed, or concealed, causing persistent canonical primitives to produce missing geometry or ghosting ~ yang2024deformable3dgs,wu2024fourdgs,luiten2024dynamic3dgs (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). However, topology-changing reconstruction remains largely underexplored: existing benchmarks rely on controlled capture with synchronized views or depth~ park2021hypernerf , and none systematically evaluate topological changes in real-world egocentric video. To enable systematic evaluation of reconstruction across topological events, we introduce TopoEgo, a benchmark curated from EPIC-KITCHENS~ damen2022epickitchens and Ego4D~ grauman2022ego4d , two of the largest egocentric video datasets. TopoEgo captures diverse, in-the-wild instances of fission, fusion, open, and close, spanning changes in both object connectivity and surface visibility (see Fig.~ fig:topoego_examples ). It contains 24 sequences, with 34 topological events and 36 dynamic objects. Each sequence includes event annotations and topology configurations, together with camera poses and hand-object masks. To address this challenging benchmark, we introduce Topo-4DGS, a topology-aware reconstruction method that explicitly models the two consequences of topological events: changes in part-level motion and variations in surface support. This leads to Topo-4DGS's two main components. First, Motion Bifurcation enables parts that initially move together to follow independent rigid motions after an event. Second, Topological Boundary Resolution updates the represented surface support by adding or removing Gaussians as surfaces are created, exposed, or concealed. Our main contributions are: TopoEgo, a real-world benchmark for egocentric topological reconstruction, comprising 24 in-the-wild sequences with 36 dynamic objects, 34 annotated events, topology configurations, camera poses, hand-object masks, and standardized evaluation protocols. Topo-4DGS, an event-conditioned representation for topology-aware 4D reconstruction, jointly modeling part-motion bifurcation and evolving surface support. State-of-the-art performance across topological events, with the largest gains after event boundaries, where fixed-topology assumptions fail most severely. Related Work sec:related_work Dynamic neural fields and canonical 4D representations. Dynamic novel-view synthesis models scenes whose geometry and appearance change over time. A common approach maps observations to a canonical representation: D-NeRF~ pumarola2021dnerf and Nerfies~ park2021nerfies continuously deform a canonical neural field, while Deformable 3D Gaussians~ yang2024deformable3dgs and 4DGS~ wu2024fourdgs apply this principle to Gaussian primitives. Dynamic 3D Gaussians~ luiten2024dynamic3dgs instead tracks persistent Gaussian identities, and MoRel~ kwak2025morel introduces locally canonical anchors for improved long-term consistency. Despite their different motion models, these methods preserve a fixed set of scene elements and do not explicitly change an object's part structure at topological events. Topo-4DGS instead branches object motion into event-conditioned rigid parts while updating the surface support created, exposed, or concealed by each event. Egocentric reconstruction and scene decomposition. Egocentric reconstruction requires separating manipulated objects from the background and hands while accounting for rapid object and camera motion. EgoGaussian~ zhang2024egogaussian pioneered dynamic object reconstruction in egocentric videos. It is our closest baseline, representing each object in a canonical space and tracking it with a single rigid transformation. DeGauss~ wang2025degauss decomposes static and dynamic scene content to reduce distractors, while DP-DeGauss~ chen2026dpdegaussdynamicprobabilisticgaussian routes Gaussians into semantic background, hand, and object branches. These methods separate scene-level components but do not decompose one manipulated object into independently moving parts or update its surface support across an event. Topo-4DGS fills this gap by extending EgoGaussian's rigid prior to event-conditioned part-level motions. Topology-changing and temporally adaptive surfaces. Reconstructing topological events requires a representation that can change both object connectivity and surface support over time. HyperNeRF~ park2021hypernerf addresses changing connectivity by embedding a canonical scene in a higher-dimensional space, but is designed for more controlled capture than monocular egocentric video. Other topology-aware approaches obtain stronger geometric constraints from RGB-D observations~ li2020topology,cai2022neural or synchronized and sparse multi-view capture~ hartley2024neural,chen2025atgs,zheng2025gaustar,wu2026fourdsurf . These observations are unavailable in egocentric video, where topology changes must be inferred despite camera motion, limited viewpoints, and hand occlusion. A complementary line of work changes surface support over time. TED-4DGS~ ho2025ted4dgs learns temporal activation windows that allow individual Gaussians to appear and disappear. We adopt this parameterization but explicitly condition it on structural events: our Topological Boundary Resolution activates Gaussians for created or exposed surfaces and deactivates them when surfaces become concealed. Moreover, we address topology-changing interactions using only a single moving RGB camera, without synchronized views or measured depth. Benchmarks for dynamic and egocentric reconstruction. Existing datasets cover either dynamic reconstruction or egocentric scene understanding, but not their intersection under topological change. D-NeRF~ pumarola2021dnerf , Neural 3D Video~ li2022neu3d , and HyperNeRF~ park2021hypernerf evaluate dynamic scenes under controlled capture conditions. EPIC-Diff~ tschernezki2021neuraldiff benchmarks dynamic-object segmentation and novel-view synthesis in egocentric videos, labeling objects by motion rather than topological change. EPIC-Fields~ tschernezki2023epicfields , VISOR~ darkhalil2022visor , and Ego4D~ grauman2022ego4d provide egocentric camera geometry, object segmentation, and interaction annotations, but lack event-level topology labels and reconstruction protocols. Consequently, no existing benchmark systematically evaluates fission, fusion, open, and close in monocular egocentric video. TopoEgo fills this gap with manually annotated events and standardized 4D reconstruction evaluation. TopoEgo Benchmark sec:dataset We define a topological event as a temporally localized manipulation that changes an object's part connectivity, motion structure, or surface support. Each event separates two intervals: pre-event and post-event, to depict the object before and after the transformation, respectively. Reconstructing both intervals requires accounting for parts that begin or cease to move independently and surfaces exposed, concealed, created, or removed. The TopoEgo benchmark captures these transitions in unscripted, close-range interactions with camera motion, hand occlusion, and limited views (Fig.~ fig:topoego_examples ). Benchmark construction. TopoEgo is curated from EPIC-KITCHENS~ damen2022epickitchens and Ego4D~ grauman2022ego4d . The two datasets provide different forms of temporal action annotation, which we use only to retrieve candidate clips. Ego4D provides annotations for interactions that change an object's state. Each annotation specifies a state-transition type and the estimated frame at which the transition becomes irreversible. We map deconstruct transitions to fission, construct to fusion, and relevant activate/deactivate to open and close. Instead, EPIC-KITCHENS provides temporally bounded action segments with verb and noun labels. We retrieve segments whose verbs are associated with our taxonomy: cut, chop, slice, peel, grate, crack, break, snap, and disassemble for fission; attach, screw, and tie for fusion; open and uncover for open; and close and cover for close. \\ We then manually review every candidate at its native frame rate. We retain a clip only when the mapped event is clearly visible, the manipulated object is identifiable, and sufficient pre- and post-event context frames are available. We reject candidates in which the event occurs off-screen, is fully occluded, is not realized within the annotated interaction, or does not change object connectivity or surface support. We select three clips for each event-family--source pair, yielding six clips per event family and 12 clips from each source dataset. TopoEgo expands the scale of dynamic, egocentric novel-view synthesis benchmarks. It contains 24 clips, 4,618 frames, 36 annotated dynamic object instances, and 34 topological events, providing -- more evaluation sequences than existing benchmarks~ zhang2024egogaussian,tschernezki2021neuraldiff,wang2025degauss,park2021hyperne

title: ProtoVis-Nav: Prototypical Visual Imagination for Visual-Spatial Aligned UAV Navigation
summary: Vision language navigation (VLN) is very challenging for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) since small errors in 3D motion prediction can lead to navigation errors and collisions. Unable to fathom execution outcomes in 3D environments, existing methods often struggle to predict accurate navigation waypoints from language instructions. To solve this, we introduce the Prototypical Visual Imagination framework, shortened as ProtoVis-Nav, which forces the model to imagine an outcome-associated local visual representation for the intended next UAV movement. Specifically, we predict feature prototypes and use their linear combination to estimate the visual feature of the target region. In this manner, the VLN model first imagines the local visual representation of the next intended location, and then uses predicted prototypes as context for generating the final action, promoting alignment between visual context and waypoint outputs. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the ProtoVis-Nav framework and show substantial improvements over existing baselines.
full_text: Vision language navigation (VLN) is very challenging for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) since small errors in 3D motion prediction can lead to navigation errors and collisions. Unable to fathom execution outcomes in 3D environments, existing methods often struggle to predict accurate navigation waypoints from language instructions. To solve this, we introduce the Prototypical Visual Imagination framework, shortened as ProtoVis-Nav, which forces the model to imagine an outcome-associated local visual representation for the intended next UAV movement. Specifically, we predict feature prototypes and use their linear combination to estimate the visual feature of the target region. In this manner, the VLN model first imagines the local visual representation of the next intended location, and then uses predicted prototypes as context for generating the final action, promoting alignment between visual context and waypoint outputs. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the ProtoVis-Nav framework and show substantial improvements over existing baselines. Data and code are available at link . Introduction Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) is a challenging problem in embodied AI, enabling agents to navigate complex environments while following natural language instructions gu2022vision,park2023visual . Although early VLN research predominantly centered on indoor navigation for ground-based robots krantz2020beyond,ku2020room,zhou2024navgpt,huang2023visual , a growing body of recent work focuses on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) cai2025flightgpt,liu2023aerialvln,wu2025aeroduo,zhang2025grounded,xiao2025uav , where navigation involves a more challenging 3D action space and requires precise motion control and reliable 3D trajectory planning wang2024towards . Despite the rapid progress of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) bai2025qwen3vl,wang2025internvl3,hong2025glm,team2026kimi , applying them to UAV navigation remains difficult as they struggle to navigate 3D environments accurately and safely wang2025uavflow,xiao2025uav . A major reason for these navigation errors is the inability to associate motion predictions with their potential outcomes nie2025wmnav . In fact, most methods directly predict continuous waypoints from visual observations and language instructions arafat2023vision . Since their training objective penalizes only the waypoint error, the model can hardly anticipate the execution outcomes of its own actions Koh_2021_ICCV , increasing the risk of generating trajectories that are potentially unsafe in the 3D environment. To address this problem, an emerging trend in visual language navigation is to equip the agent with future-aware visual predictive capabilities, often framed as navigation world models bar2025navigation . Specifically, they usually predict the future observation via a specific video generation model Koh_2021_ICCV, bar2025navigation or as outputs of the same VLN model yao2025navmorph, huang2026unemo, Wang2026monodream . UAV navigation requires accurate fine-grained motion control grounded in local visual evidence ding2026history . In fact, precise flight actions are often determined by small and localized visual regions (e.g., a narrow gap to fly through). This raises a key question: rather than generating the global future scene, can we enforce future-aware grounding by strictly focusing on these localized visual regions most critical to the upcoming movement? In this work, we propose the Prototypical Visual Imagination framework for UAV navigation, dubbed as ProtoVis-Nav. The method is motivated by a simple idea: rather than modeling an entire future scene or a long-horizon latent rollout, the agent should focus on the exact regions most relevant to its precise movement by imagining an outcome-associated local visual representation. To this end, we project the next intended UAV location onto the current image plane, crop the surrounding local region, and use its visual feature as the supervision target. Compared with using the entire future frame or the future-frame center, this projected region provides a supervision target that more directly grounds 3D motion prediction in the current image space, while avoiding the intractable imagination of future observations. Plus, we introduce a prototype-based feature prediction method. Instead of using multi-layer perceptrons to directly estimate the target feature, this approach predicts a set of Prototypical Visual Imagination (PVI) tokens, which are then combined through a softmax-normalized mixing matrix, so that their linear combination matches the target-region feature. The predicted PVI tokens are less susceptible to overfitting and are then used as context for waypoint prediction, encouraging tighter alignment between visual context and continuous action outputs. We experimentally verify the effectiveness of the proposed method on OpenUAV wang2024towards and HUGE-Bench guo2026hugebench . Results show that ProtoVis-Nav substantially improves navigation performance over strong baselines and leads to more reliable continuous UAV navigation. Related Works Vision language navigation for UAVs. Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) has traditionally focused on guiding ground agents through structured, near-planar indoor environments krantz2020beyond,ku2020room,zhou2024navgpt,huang2023visual,zhao2022target,10495141,zhang-etal-2025-mapnav . Recently, the field has naturally extended to Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs). UAV-based VLN requires agents to ground language instructions into complex, continuous flight dynamics, demanding a stronger understanding of 3D spatial reasoning. Several realistic and continuous UAV VLN benchmarks have recently emerged wu2025aeroduo,xiao2025uav,wang2024towards,wang2025uavflow , providing an essential foundation for open-world UAV VLN research. Building upon them, TravelUAV wang2024towards directly regresses the next waypoint based on current observations and UAV kinematics. NavFoM zhang2025embodied further explores a cross-embodiment and cross-task navigation foundation model trained on large-scale navigation data, showing strong generalization across different navigation tasks and robotic platforms, including UAV navigation. To better process historical context, LongFly jiang2025longfly introduces a history-aware spatiotemporal modeling strategy that transforms fragmented and redundant historical data into structured, compact, and expressive representations. To improve policy learning, OpenVLN lin2025openvln formulates a reinforcement learning framework to optimize VLMs for UAV navigation tasks. It efficiently fine-tunes the VLM using rule-based policies under limited training data, and incorporates a long-horizon trajectory planner that generates precise UAV actions via value-based rewards. Despite these advancements, most continuous UAV VLN methods still mainly rely on current observations, historical context, or geometric priors for waypoint prediction. Since their training objective focuses on waypoint error, the model receives limited guidance for identifying visual cues associated with the next intended location of the UAV, increasing the risk of generating trajectories that are potentially unsafe in the 3D environment. Navigation world models. An emerging trend in visual-language navigation is to equip agents with future-aware visual predictive capabilities, often framed as navigation world models. For example, Pathdreamer studies visual world modeling for indoor navigation, generating future 360 RGB, depth, and semantic observations along hypothetical trajectories with a two-stage structure-to-image generator Koh_2021_ICCV . Dreamwalker further adapts this idea to VLN-CE by constructing an explicit environment graph and using a scene synthesizer to imagine future panoramic observations, which are then evaluated through mental planning with Monte Carlo Tree Search Wang_2023_ICCV . HNR-VLN predicts multi-level CLIP-based semantic features for candidate future viewpoints via a hierarchical neural radiance representation, enabling more efficient path evaluation Wang_2024_CVPR . NWM scales this paradigm to video generation, where a diffusion transformer simulates future visual trajectories conditioned on actions and ranks or plans routes according to goal similarity bar2025navigation . More recent methods emphasize compact and adaptive latent prediction: UNeMo predicts the next visual state from visual features, language instructions, and candidate actions, feeding the predicted state back to refine navigation decisions huang2026unemo . MonoDream uses latent panoramic dreaming to predict current and future panoramic RGB-D features from a forward-facing RGB view, thereby compensating for limited field of view without explicit panoramic sensors Wang2026monodream . DriveVLA-W0 uses future-image prediction to supervise driving representations li2025drivevlaw0 , while ANWM predicts action-conditioned future observations for UAV trajectory evaluation zhang2025anwm . While effective for future-aware visual world models, they focus on generating global scene representations, such as full-frame videos or panoramic latents. However, UAVs require accurate fine-grained motion control, grounded in local visual evidence. Predicting the background and surroundings can provide general orientation, but precise flight actions are often determined by small and localized visual regions (e.g., a narrow gap to fly through). To bridge this gap, our proposed ProtoVis-Nav framework departs from the global imagination paradigm. Instead of predicting complete future frames or global features, we explicitly project the intended future 3D location onto the current 2D image plane and predict prototypical visual tokens strictly for that local region. This localized, prototype-based imagination encourages the UAV to ground its motion decisions in the most critical visual context for more accurate and reliable continuous aerial navigation in 3D space. Regarding local visual supervision, our method differs from ReconVLA~ song2025reconvla , which reconstructs gaze regions around the objects to be manipulated in the current image with a diffusion model to guide visual attention. ProtoVis-Nav constructs its local target by projecting the next intended 3D UAV location onto the current 2D image plane, linking local visual supervision to the intended execution outcome of the next action. -4pt ProtoVis-Nav Overall Pipeline As shown in Fig.~ fig:pipeline , ProtoVis-Nav uses Qwen3VL-2B-Instruct bai2025qwen3vl as the VLM backbone. The input consists of dual-view RGB observations (front-view and down-view images), the language instruction, and the current UAV state, including the previous displacement and current position. The Qwen3VL backbone is kept frozen, while the LoRA adapters inserted into the backbone and the newly added output heads are trained. title: Reconstruct What You Can: Distractor-free 4D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Dynamic reconstruction from casual video must preserve valid subject motion while suppressing transient occluders, shadows, and volumetric effects. Existing methods either suppress valid motion through static-scene assumptions or model all observations jointly, producing ghosting and unstable geometry. We introduce ReCan-GS, a 4D Gaussian Splatting framework that separates coherent scene content from inconsistent observations. It derives a Jacobian-based deformation-sensitivity score from the learned deformation field, using it as an empirical proxy for reconstruction ambiguity. The score guides separation into dynamic Core Gaussians and per-view Distractor Gaussians, or post-hoc pruning of sensitive Core Gaussians. The same criterion supports removal of spatial occluders, photometric artifacts, and evolving smoke or fog without masks, pretrained segmenters, or medium-specific supervision. Experiments on synthetic and real dynamic scenes and synthetic smoke/fog scenes demonstrate its usefulness across the evaluated distractor regimes.

The score guides separation into dynamic Core Gaussians and per-view Distractor Gaussians, or post-hoc pruning of sensitive Core Gaussians. The same criterion supports removal of spatial occluders, photometric artifacts, and evolving smoke or fog without masks, pretrained segmenters, or medium-specific supervision. Experiments on synthetic and real dynamic scenes and synthetic smoke/fog scenes demonstrate its usefulness across the evaluated distractor regimes. Introduction sec:intro Reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes from unconstrained monocular video remains challenging because real-world sequences often contain transient occluders, reflections, shadows, and flickers. These effects can introduce conflicting constraints on a shared scene representation. Standard dynamic reconstruction methods attempt to model them jointly with the subject, which can produce ghosting and unstable geometry. Static distractor-removal methods avoid this failure mode by treating dynamic content as noise, but therefore fail when the moving object is the reconstruction target. We instead define distractors by deformation-space instability rather than object identity, speed, or appearance. This lets reconstructable motion remain in the core scene while inconsistent content is routed away. The same criterion also handles slow-moving volumetric distractors such as fog and smoke: although they may appear photometrically stable, their evolving appearance can induce inconsistent deformation constraints and high scores, enabling removal by post-hoc pruning without fog-specific design. To this end, we present ReCan-GS, a 4D Gaussian Splatting framework for distractor removal in dynamic scenes. ReCan-GS derives a motion-stability uncertainty directly from the Jacobian of the learned deformation field. This signal is intended to highlight observations associated with sensitive or inconsistent deformation, allowing the model to route stable content into Core Gaussians and inconsistent content into a separate Per-View Distractor layer. ReCan-GS is primarily designed for dynamic scenes with transient distractors and for volumetric fog and smoke removal; its performance is more limited on standard static distractor benchmarks. Our main contributions are: A Jacobian-derived uncertainty metric that quantifies deformation-space instability in a continuous 4D Gaussian deformation field, providing a routing cue without explicit appearance models or speed thresholds. A unified distractor-removal framework for 4D Gaussian Splatting that separates geometrically consistent content from inconsistent observations, covering dynamic-scene occluders, photometric artifacts, and dynamic volumetric distractors such as fog and smoke. Empirical validation across synthetic and real dynamic scenes with distractors, plus fog/smoke scenes with clean ground truth. Related Works sec:related_work Handling Distractors Recent research (Table tab:method_comparison ) addresses the challenge of transient distractors within predominantly static scene assumptions. Approaches generally fall into three categories based on their distractor-handling strategies: Photometric and Uncertainty-Based Methods identify distractors through reconstruction error or predictive uncertainty. NeRF-W martinbrualla2020nerfw first separated static and transient components. BayesRays goli2023 extended this with probabilistic uncertainty, while FisherRF Jiang2023FisherRF used Fisher information. RobustNeRF Sabour_2023_CVPR uses robust statistics to mask high-error regions. Related work addresses reflections and inconsistent visibility through appearance and regularization strategies~ verbin2022refnerf, barron2021mipnerf, Niemeyer2021Regnerf, scaffoldgs . Concurrent work guo2026uncertainty estimates per-Gaussian reliability from recurring observations for motion propagation under occlusion; our score instead measures deformation-field sensitivity to separate transient content. Semantic Feature-Based Methods replace photometric cues with semantic information from pretrained vision models. In the NeRF domain, NeRF-HuGS chen2024nerf uses semantic segmentation, and NeRF On-the-go Ren2024NeRF leverages DINOv2-derived oquab2023dinov2 features. This trend extends to 3DGS, where SpotLessSplats sabourgoli2024spotlesssplats clusters text-to-image embeddings and Robust 3D Gaussian Splatting ungermann2024robust incorporates SAM-derived segmentations kirillov2023segany . Decompositional Methods explicitly separate static and transient content into distinct representational layers. Several methods model appearance variation using learned embeddings or fields (SWAG dahmani2024swagsplattingwildimages , GS-W zhang2024GS-W , Wild-GS xu2024wildgsrealtimenovelview ). Others use optimization strategies, such as WildGaussians kulhanek2024wildgaussians , which uses uncertainty masks for gradient scaling. A more explicit decomposition is used by DeSplat wang2024desplat , which models transients with per-view splats, and HybridGS lin2024hybridgs , which combines persistent 3D Gaussians with view-specific 2D Gaussians. Splatfacto-W xu2024splatfactownerfstudioimplementationgaussian also uses a hybrid approach with MLPs for background modeling and robust masks for transients. While these methods are effective in their respective contexts, they share a common limitation: all assume a static scene and ultimately aim to recover a single clean reconstruction, with uncertainty or transient handling largely heuristic or learned. In contrast, we address fully dynamic scenes corrupted by severe spatial and photometric inconsistencies and, importantly, show that uncertainty can be derived analytically, offering a principled and explainable view of the optimization process that prior work lacks. Fog and Volumetric Distractor Removal Volumetric distractors such as fog and smoke further challenge appearance-based removal, since they may appear photometrically stable while remaining geometrically inconsistent across views. Our method instead uses deformation sensitivity as a cue for removal without fog-specific supervision. The experiments evaluate this mechanism against general distractor-removal baselines; they do not establish competitiveness with dedicated smoke-removal methods. Dynamic Scene Reconstruction Reconstructing general dynamic scenes is a distinct but related challenge. Methods such as DeformableGS~ yang2023deformable3dgs , 4DGS~ Wu_2024_CVPR , GSLK~ xie2025gaussiansplattinglucaskanade , DynamicGS~ luiten2023dynamic , STGS~ Li_STG_2024_CVPR , Realtime4DGS~ yang2023gs4d , and dynamic NeRF variants~ pumarola2020d, park2021nerfies, park2021hypernerf, kplanes_2023 model time-varying scenes by learning motion jointly with appearance. However, they lack an explicit mechanism to separate transient distractors from core scene motion. As a result, they tend to average all visual phenomena, leading to severe artifacts such as ghosting when occluders are present. More recent approaches, such as Shape of Motion~ som2024 and MoSca~ lei2024mosca , leverage strong externally-derived priors from vision foundation models (e.g., point tracking or depth estimation) to regularize the motion field. While effective, these methods introduce additional complexity and depend heavily on the quality of the pretrained models. In contrast, our approach is orthogonal: we propose an analytical, prior-free method that explicitly separates geometrically consistent motion from temporal multi-view contradictions using an uncertainty signal derived directly from the deformation field, improving both robustness and interpretability. Preliminary sec:prelim 3DGS~ kerbl3Dgaussians represents a scene as a set of 3D Gaussians, each defined by a position , covariance , opacity , and view-dependent color via spherical harmonics. Gaussians are initialized from a sparse SfM point cloud~ Micheletti2015StructurePhotogrammetry and adaptively split or pruned during training. Pixel colors are computed by alpha-compositing depth-sorted 2D Gaussian projections: For dynamic scenes, a common approach is to learn a deformation field mapping a canonical representation to its configuration at a given time~ pumarola2020d, park2021nerfies, luiten2023dynamic, yu2023cogs . We adopt this strategy for Gaussian Splatting following~ yang2023deformable3dgs , using an MLP that maps each canonical position and time to position, rotation, and scale offsets. Method To robustly reconstruct dynamic scenes with transient distractors, ReCan-GS decomposes the scene into two geometric layers: dynamic Core Gaussians modeling stable, temporally consistent content, and per-view Distractor Gaussians capturing transient or view-specific phenomena. The separation is driven by a motion-derived uncertainty signal from the learned deformation field, reinforced by competition between the two layers during optimization, and requires no masks or annotations. Fig.~ fig:pipeline shows the pipeline. Definition of Distractors. We operationally identify candidate distractors as observations that induce inconsistent deformation constraints in the shared canonical space. Routing uses deformation sensitivity rather than an explicit threshold on speed or object identity. This criterion does not determine the intended subject: a well-observed distractor can admit stable deformation, while poorly observed target content can receive a high score. The separation therefore depends on observation coverage and the learned representation. Sec.~ sec:ablation evaluates coverage and speed (Fig.~ fig:ablation ), pruning sensitivity (Fig.~ fig:post_hoc ), and distractor localization; smoke results provide a further test of the same score (Fig.~ fig:smoke_results ). title: RICapBench: A Fine-Grained Visual Understanding Benchmark Dataset for Vision-Language Models in Remote Sensing
summary: Advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have improved remote sensing image analysis and supported geospatial decision-making. However, fine-grained understanding of remote sensing imagery remains challenging for VLMs. Large variations in object scale, complex geospatial relations among instances, and limited visual detail hinder precise instance localization, visible attribute identification, and spatial relation understanding, potentially leading to descriptions that lack visual grounding. Existing datasets and benchmarks insufficiently assess end-to-end instance localization and captioning without target-specific textual cues. To support this evaluation, we introduce RICapBench, a dataset and benchmark that unifies instance localization and fine-grained captioning in remote sensing. RICapBench contains 245,466 instance-level annotations and 498,005 spatial relation tuples spanning general remote sensing, UAV remote sensing, and dense small-object scenarios. Each annotation pairs an object's oriented bounding box with a natural language description of its visible attributes and spatial relations to surrounding instances and environmental elements. To evaluate the accuracy and completeness of spatial relation captioning, we propose a remote sensing spatial relation parser and the RelCap-F1 metric. We combine RelCap-F1 with instance localization and attribute captioning metrics into a composite metric, RICScore. Our evaluation of 15 advanced open-source and closed-source VLMs identifies instance localization as a major bottleneck for these models. LocateAnything achieves the highest RICScore of 31.68, but scores lower on spatial relation captioning than other task-fine-tuned open-source VLMs. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Xldln/RICapBench.

However, fine-grained understanding of remote sensing imagery remains challenging for VLMs. Large variations in object scale, complex geospatial relations among instances, and limited visual detail hinder precise instance localization, visible attribute identification, and spatial relation understanding, potentially leading to descriptions that lack visual grounding. Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language models (VLMs) have become an important research direction in deep learning and computer vision in recent years~ cho2025perceptionlm,xing2025conical . Vision and language underpin human perception of the external world and the expression of knowledge, respectively. Integrating them enables models to understand visual content and interact through natural language, supporting tasks such as visual question answering, image captioning, and object localization~ liu2023visual,liu2024improved . VLMs have also attracted considerable attention in remote sensing. They are increasingly applied to object detection and segmentation, change detection, and damage assessment, supporting urban planning and geospatial analysis~ kuckreja2024geochat,pang2025vhm,soni2025earthdial,li2025segearthov,shabbir2025geopixel,wang2024earthvqa . Although VLMs have the potential to reduce manual effort and improve analytical efficiency, they still face multiple challenges in fine-grained understanding of remote sensing imagery. Objects in remote sensing imagery vary greatly in scale, and some scenes contain densely distributed small objects with limited discernible visual detail. These characteristics make instance identification, counting, and precise localization more difficult~ zhang2025geovis . Beyond localizing and describing object instances, models must distinguish adjacent objects and use scene context to determine their positions relative to surrounding instances and environmental elements. Image-level captioning capabilities alone do not ensure an accurate understanding of these spatial relations. Furthermore, remote sensing VLMs may hallucinate, generating descriptions of objects, attributes, and spatial relations that contradict image content or lack visual grounding. Such descriptions can undermine the reliability of automated image interpretation~ an2025choice,pang2025vhm . These challenges place greater demands on models' fine-grained image understanding. As VLMs have developed in remote sensing, researchers have introduced vision-language datasets and benchmarks such as DIOR-RSVG~ zhan2023rsvg , VRSBench~ li2024vrsbench , EarthVQA~ wang2024earthvqa , and GEOBench-VLM~ danish2025geobenchvlm . These resources support the training and evaluation of both general-purpose and remote sensing VLMs. They cover image captioning, visual question answering, and referring expression grounding, with evaluations designed around typical remote sensing tasks and practical application needs. For example, GEOBench-VLM comprises 31 evaluation tasks across eight categories, assessing multiple aspects of vision-language understanding in remote sensing. Some of these tasks already address fine-grained visual understanding at the instance level. For example, referring expression grounding in DIOR-RSVG, VRSBench, and AerialVG~ liu2025aerialvg requires models to identify and localize target instances from natural language descriptions. EarthVQA evaluates models' understanding of spatial relations between geographic objects in remote sensing imagery through visual question answering that involves spatial relation reasoning. These tasks assess fine-grained understanding through aspects such as language--object correspondence and spatial relations between objects. However, tasks such as referring expression grounding typically condition predictions on a given target description. Target references, attributes, or relations in the text provide interpretive cues~ lai2024lisa and direct models' attention to specific objects. Performance under text-query guidance therefore does not fully reflect models' ability to autonomously achieve fine-grained understanding of remote sensing imagery without such cues. Previous work has also noted that clearly describing object appearance and location requires substantial manual effort~ wang2024omniq . In practical applications, constructing queries may likewise require users to specify objects of interest or inspect imagery beforehand. The resulting interaction overhead may delay processing in scenarios such as UAV-based disaster inspection and remote sensing emergency monitoring. Meanwhile, image-level captioning summarizes the scene content of an entire remote sensing image and generally does not require each description to be matched to a specific instance location. It therefore cannot fully assess models' fine-grained understanding of instance attributes and spatial relations. In general vision, previous studies have combined object localization with fine-grained language descriptions. For example, Dense Relational Captioning~ kim2019drc focuses on describing relations between objects, whereas LVISCap~ fiastre2026captionformer provides fine-grained object-level descriptions. RA-4M~ neau2026relateanything further provides annotations of inter-object relations expressed as free-text predicates. These studies inform the joint assessment of object localization, object captioning, and inter-object relation understanding. In remote sensing, FIT-RS~ luo2024skysensegpt explores models' understanding of fine-grained relations in remote sensing imagery through tasks such as region captioning and scene graph generation. Region captioning is conditioned on a given target region. Whole-image scene graph generation expresses inter-object relations through templated sentences and explicitly annotates object categories, locations, and relation predicates. FineGrip~ zhao2024finegrip combines foreground instance segmentation, background semantic segmentation, and fine-grained image captioning, but its captions describe entire images. Its evaluation neither directly measures the correspondence between instance locations and captions nor separately assesses the accuracy and completeness of spatial relation captioning. We further investigate whether VLMs can localize target instances in remote sensing imagery without additional cues from target-specific text queries. We also examine whether they can describe the instances' visible attributes and spatial relations to surrounding instances and environmental elements. To systematically evaluate fine-grained understanding under this setting, we introduce RICapBench, which unifies instance localization, attribute captioning, and spatial relation captioning within a single evaluation framework. This framework supports the analysis of capability differences and bottlenecks in general-purpose and remote sensing VLMs, as well as the exploration of potential improvements. Using RICapBench, we systematically evaluate 15 advanced general-purpose and remote sensing VLMs on fine-grained understanding of remote sensing imagery. The task examines whether models can localize target instances based on specific visual evidence and describe their attributes and spatial relations to surrounding geographic features or environmental elements. The results show that existing general-purpose and remote sensing VLMs continue to face challenges in fine-grained understanding of remote sensing instances and their spatial context. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We construct RICapBench, a dataset and benchmark for fine-grained spatial relation captioning of remote sensing instances. It contains 245,466 instance-level annotations and 498,005 spatial relation tuples spanning general remote sensing, UAV remote sensing, and dense small-object scenarios. Each annotation pairs an object's oriented bounding box with a natural language description of its visible attributes and spatial relations. These annotations support model fine-tuning and the evaluation of VLMs' instance localization and fine-grained understanding of spatial context without reliance on target-specific text queries. We develop a remote sensing spatial relation parser that converts spatial relations in natural language descriptions into structured spatial relation triples. We also propose RelCap-F1 to measure the accuracy and completeness of spatial relation captioning. We define RICScore as the composite metric for this task, calculated as the geometric mean of DetA, CapA, and RelCap-F1. It evaluates models' fine-grained understanding across three dimensions: instance localization, attribute captioning, and spatial relation captioning. We systematically evaluate 15 advanced VLMs on fine-grained understanding of remote sensing imagery, covering general-purpose open-source, closed-source, and remote sensing models. We analyze their capability differences and bottlenecks in instance localization, attribute captioning, and spatial relation captioning, providing empirical evidence and research insights to improve VLMs' fine-grained geospatial understanding. Related Work sec:overview Table~ tab:benchmark-comparison compares RICapBench with related datasets and benchmarks for fine-grained visual understanding in general vision and remote sensing. General VLM Benchmarks Several datasets and benchmarks focus on fine-grained visual understanding, providing a foundation for evaluating VLMs' understanding of objects and their context. Fiastre et al.~ fiastre2026captionformer extend LVIS and LV-VIS to create LVISCap and LV-VISCap, respectively, providing fine-grained object-level descriptions for images and videos. These datasets support combining object detection, segmentation, and video object tracking with object captioning. Their descriptions cover object appearance, actions, and interactions with the surrounding environment or other objects. BenSMOT~ li2024beyondmot addresses person-centered fine-grained video understanding in everyday scenes. It combines multi-object tracking with instance-level behavior captioning, recognition of interpersonal interactions, and video-level summarization. Benchmarks such as SEED-Bench~ li2023seedbench , SEED-Bench-2-Plus~ li2024seedbench2plus , and MMStar~ chen2024mmstar evaluate fine-grained perception through visual question answering. They cover complex perceptual tasks involving object attribute identification, object localization, relation reasoning, and interactions between instances. title: Pl@ntNet machine-to-machine identification service with Pl@ntNet API: enabling automated biodiversity monitoring through large-scale plant identification
summary: 1. Monitoring plant biodiversity requires identifying large numbers of plants across space and time. Although artificial intelligence (AI) can now identify plant species from images with high accuracy, most existing systems rely on users manually submitting images. As ecological monitoring increasingly generates large image collections from cameras, drones, robots and online platforms, there is a growing need for plant identification services that can be directly integrated into automated data-processing workflows. 2. Here, we present Pl@ntNet's machine-to-machine AI plant identification service. This service uses an application programming interface (API) to provide programmatic access to Pl@ntNet's plant recognition models and the associated taxonomic processing. This service enables the implementation of automated identification workflows without human intervention and can thus directly link large image collections and automated observation systems to an AI-based plant identification system. 3. We establish that this service, which covers 85,000 species from around the world, (1) has a species prediction accuracy of 0.89, (2) process images up to 666 times faster than workflows requiring human intervention, (3) and has processed over 84 million identification requests since its launch, including more than 40 million in 2025 alone. We demonstrate how it has already enabled the implementation of a new generation of ecological workflows: identifying plants from images of insects to reconstruct the plant-pollinator interactions, analysing geolocated images from social media to study plant distribution, detecting invasive plants using images taken at the roadside, and identifying weeds using agricultural robots. Finally, we illustrate its application using a reproducible example: identifying plants from insect photos on iNaturalist. In approximately 30 min on a standard laptop, 2,424 images were processed to generate a dataset of 708 plant-pollinator interactions, with a weighted precision of 0.98 for flower detection and an accuracy of 0.88 for genus plant identification. 4. In conclusion, this machine-to-machine species identification is already operating on a considerable scale and meets a genuine need. All of this paves the way for a new paradigm in biodiversity monitoring, in which automated sensors and image collections can be directly connected to AI-based identification services.

title: What Limits Thermal Infrared Drone Detection? A Cross-Dataset Benchmark Analysis
comment: Accepted at 2027 IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision Workshops (WACVW), Workshop "Real World Surveillance: Applications and Challenges, 7th"
summary: Thermal infrared (IR) imaging enables drone detection with reduced dependence on ambient illumination, supporting continuous surveillance beyond the limitations of visible-spectrum sensing. However, substantial and often undocumented variability in camera systems, processing pipelines, and annotation practices across public IR drone datasets complicates the assessment of detector performance and cross-domain generalization. To examine these sources of variability and their implications for drone detection, we systematically characterize existing IR datasets and establish an artifact taxonomy reflecting their origins across the acquisition and processing pipeline, encompassing optical and sensor effects, tone mapping and image enhancement, and recording-related artifacts. Focusing on long-wave IR data, we investigate the impact of training data composition and model characteristics on YOLO-based detection performance, generalization, and condition-dependent failure modes. Our results demonstrate that detection performance is governed more strongly by training data composition than by YOLO generation or model capacity, while cross-dataset generalization exhibits pronounced asymmetries. Even the best-performing configuration fails to detect over 40\% of drones, with elevated miss rates for very small targets, cluttered urban backgrounds, and thermal crossover, highlighting the shortcomings of existing datasets.
full_text: Thermal infrared (IR) imaging enables drone detection with reduced dependence on ambient illumination, supporting continuous surveillance beyond the limitations of visible-spectrum sensing. However, substantial and often undocumented variability in camera systems, processing pipelines, and annotation practices across public IR drone datasets complicates the assessment of detector performance and cross-domain generalization. To examine these sources of variability and their implications for drone detection, we systematically characterize existing IR datasets and establish an artifact taxonomy reflecting their origins across the acquisition and processing pipeline, encompassing optical and sensor effects, tone mapping and image enhancement, and recording-related artifacts. Focusing on long-wave IR data, we investigate the impact of training data composition and model characteristics on YOLO-based detection performance, generalization, and condition-dependent failure modes. Our results demonstrate that detection performance is governed more strongly by training data composition than by YOLO generation or model capacity, while cross-dataset generalization exhibits pronounced asymmetries. Even the best-performing configuration fails to detect over 40 of drones, with elevated miss rates for very small targets, cluttered urban backgrounds, and thermal crossover, highlighting the shortcomings of existing datasets. Introduction sec:intro The growing accessibility and operational capabilities of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), commonly known as drones, present increasingly complex challenges for low-altitude airspace surveillance and critical infrastructure protection~ Schneider:2021 . Unauthorized or malicious drone operations pose risks to public safety, critical infrastructure, and operational continuity~ Johnson:2026 , particularly in densely populated urban environments. Early and reliable drone detection is therefore essential for effective surveillance and threat mitigation~ Johnson:2026 . Camera-based systems -- particularly those operating in the visible (RGB) spectrum -- offer a promising and cost-effective approach, combining passive operation and compatibility with existing surveillance infrastructure. Coupled with deep learning (DL) architectures such as You Only Look Once (YOLO)~ Redmon:2016 , these systems support automated drone detection through real-time image analysis~ Wang:2024,Lenhard:2025 . However, RGB-based detection remains sensitive to adverse illumination and visibility conditions~ Johnson:2026 . By capturing emitted thermal radiation rather than reflected visible light, infrared (IR) imaging reduces reliance on ambient illumination~ Vollmer:2017 , providing a complementary modality for continuous, day-and-night drone surveillance. While IR-based drone tracking has received considerable research attention, standalone frame-wise detection remains comparatively underexplored~ Dong:2025 , despite its essential role in track initialization and target re-acquisition following tracking failures in operational surveillance systems~ Zhu:2023,Yu:2023 . Although YOLO-based detectors are increasingly employed for IR drone detection, variations in datasets, training protocols, and evaluation methodologies complicate meaningful comparisons across studies~ Dong:2025 . This challenge is compounded by substantial, often undocumented differences in camera systems, image processing, recording pipelines, and annotation practices across datasets (see Sec.~ sec:related_work ). Consequently, the relative contributions of detector design and dataset characteristics to reported performance remain difficult to disentangle. To address this gap, this work makes three contributions: (i)~We systematically characterize publicly available IR drone datasets and establish a taxonomy of artifacts based on their origin along the imaging pipeline. (ii)~Focusing on long-wave infrared (LWIR) imagery, the predominant spectral band in public datasets, we evaluate YOLOv8 and YOLO11 across training datasets, model architectures, and capacities. (iii)~We systematically examine detection failures in relation to target size, background characteristics, and and instance-level attributes to identify factors affecting detection reliability. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Sec.~ sec:related_work reviews related work on IR-based drone detection and tracking and characterizes publicly available IR drone datasets. Sec.~ sec:exp_setup details the experimental setup, followed by the results in Sec.~ sec:results . Key findings, conclusions, and future directions are discussed in Sec.~ sec:conclusion . Related Work sec:related_work This section provides a systematic overview of the state of the art in IR-based drone detection and tracking. It reviews existing methodological approaches, surveys publicly available datasets for model training and evaluation, and compares their key characteristics. Drone Detection Tracking sec:RW_drone_detection_and_tracking Within the IR domain, existing research has predominantly focused on tracking, largely driven by the Anti-UAV challenges~ Zhao:2021,Zhao:2023,Huang:2024 and dedicated IR tracking benchmarks~ Jiang:2023,Huang:2024 , while frame-wise IR drone detection as a standalone task remains comparatively underexplored~ Dong:2025 . Tracking approaches can broadly be categorized as (i)~detection-based, associating frame-wise detections over time, (ii)~Siamese-based, matching an initialized target template against subsequent frames, and (iii)~hybrid, combining both principles~ Dong:2025 . In practical tracking systems, frame-wise detection remains an essential component, supporting target initialization and re-detection after tracking failure~ Zhu:2023,Yu:2023 . Whether employed as standalone detectors or integrated into tracking pipelines, IR-based drone detection predominantly relies on YOLO architectures spanning multiple generations: YOLOv2~ Svanstroem:2021 , YOLOv3~ Huang:2026,Yu:2026 , YOLOv5~ Bhattacharya:2023,Huang:2026,Yu:2026,Hao:2025 , YOLOv6~ Bhattacharya:2023,Yu:2026 , YOLOv7~ Bhattacharya:2023,Bhattacharya:2025,Yu:2026 , YOLOv8~ Ustun:2025,Tavaris:2025,Yu:2026,Hao:2025 , YO\-LOv9~ Yu:2026,Hao:2025 , YOLO11~ Tavaris:2025,Peterson:2026,Yu:2026,Hao:2025 , and YOLO12~ Yu:2026 . The adoption of both earlier and recent YOLO generations -- whether as primary detector or as comparison baseline -- suggests that model selection is not strictly tied to recency, with YOLOv5, YOLOv8, and YOLO11 being the most frequently employed variants. Beyond standard YOLO implementations, several studies introduce targeted architectural refinements to enhance detection performance~ Bhattacharya:2025,Huang:2026 or computational efficiency~ Yu:2026 . Less prevalent alternatives include Faster R-CNN~ Chen:2017,Huang:2026 and RT-DETR~ Ustun:2025,Huang:2026,Yu:2026,Hao:2025 . Other approaches leverage signal-processing techniques ( , filtering)~ Kou:2023,Liu:2024 or integrate RGB and IR modalities to enhance detection robustness. However, this methodological breadth is accompanied by substantial heterogeneity in experimental design ( , dataset, training regimes, and evaluation protocols), thereby limiting direct cross-study comparability~ Dong:2025 . IR Drone Detection Tracking Datasets subsec:existing_datasets This section provides a systematic characterization of public IR drone detection and tracking datasets (Tab.~ tab:datsets_overview ). Beyond dataset size and spatial resolution, we analyze sensor technology and spectral band, in-camera processing, and the recording pipeline, with a particular focus on their influence on visual characteristics and artifact patterns. For consistency, camera system denotes the sensor, optics, and on-board processing, whereas recording pipeline comprises all subsequent acquisition and storage stages. Dataset Scale Dataset scale is commonly reported in terms of sequence and IR-frame counts (Tab.~ tab:datsets_overview ). Reported sequence counts vary substantially across datasets, although this variation partly reflects differences in recording and partitioning conventions. For instance, IRDST-real~ Sun:2023 comprises a total of 1 , 760 sequences and 40.65k frames, whereas USC~ Chen:2017 contains only 8 sequences but 36.6k frames. Individual sequence durations also differ considerably, ranging from 10\,s in Halmstad Data~ Svanstroem:2021_Data to several minutes in USC~ Chen:2017 . Comparability is further affected by the subdivision of longer recordings into shorter clips, as in Anti-UAV~ Jiang:2023 . Frame counts range from 29.6k in LRDDv3~ Peterson:2026 to 238k in CST Anti-UAV~ Xie:2025 . Depending on the dataset, individual frames can contain multiple drones, no drone, or other non-drone aerial objects ( , birds)~ Svanstroem:2021_Data,Peterson:2026 . For tracking-specific benchmarks such as Anti-UAV~ Jiang:2023 , Anti-UAV410~ Huang:2024 , and Anti-UAV600~ Zhu:2023 , dataset scale is even reported in annotated bounding boxes rather than frames. Resolution Spectral Band Spatial resolution is primarily determined by the camera system. While earlier datasets such as USC~ Chen:2017 and Halmstad Data~ Svanstroem:2021_Data employ 320-pixel formats, 640 512 pixels has become the predominant resolution since Anti-UAV~ Jiang:2023 . A notable exception is Hamburg2 (H2)~ Bhattacharya:2023 , with subsets at 640 480 and 1024 768 pixels, the latter being the highest resolution among the reviewed datasets. Thermal camera systems for drone observation operate primarily in the mid-wave (MWIR, approx.\ 3-5\, m) or long-wave infrared (LWIR, approx.\ 7-14\, m)~ Vollmer:2017 , as detailed in Tab.~ tab:datsets_overview . MWIR systems typically employ cooled photon detectors, whereas LWIR systems predominantly use uncooled microbolometers or, less commonly, pyroelectric barium strontium titanate (BST) sensors~ Vollmer:2017 . Beyond detector technology, MWIR and LWIR differ in their image-formation characteristics by sampling distinct regions of the electromagnetic spectrum. Under daylight conditions, MWIR imagery contains a substantial reflected-solar component, whereas LWIR imagery is governed predominantly by thermal emission~ Handbook:1997 . Consequently, the spectral band influences the appearance and contrast of drones, backgrounds, and atmospheric effects. Despite its relevance, explicit spectral-band information is available for only five of the nine datasets listed Tab.~ tab:datsets_overview . For the remaining four datasets, the spectral band is inferred from sensor-specific imaging cues. Overall, six datasets were acquired in the LWIR and three in the MWIR band. Artifacts Along the Imaging Pipeline Thermal imagery across the considered datasets exhibits artifacts introduced at distinct stages of the imaging pipeline, spanning image formation, in-camera processing, and recording. Their stage of origin provides a natural taxonomy, separating camera-inherent degradations from downstream processing and recording artifacts. Optics Sensor. Optical and sensor-level artifacts encompass both generic image degradations and detector-specific signatures. Common degradations include defocus~ Jiang:2023,Bhattacharya:2023,Zhu:2023,Sun:2023 , vignetting~ Jiang:2023,Bhattacharya:2023 , internal lens reflections~ Huang:2024 , sensor noise~ Svanstroem:2021_Data,Sun:2023 , and motion blur in both MWIR~ Jiang:2023,Huang:2024 and LWIR datasets~ Bhattacharya:2023,Peterson:2026 .
