title: Kosmo-GFM: A Production-Ready Geometry Foundation Model
summary: We present Kosmo-GFM, a scene reconstruction system that integrates a geometry foundation model (GFM), a pose optimization engine (PoseEngine), and reconstruction-derived supervision from KosmoWorld. GFM predicts camera parameters, depth, cross-view correspondences, and dynamic 3D points from images and videos. PoseEngine combines these predictions with geometric optimization to recover scene-level camera poses and geometry for downstream 3D and 4D Gaussian Splatting. KosmoWorld generates images and geometric supervision from reconstructed real-world scenes to improve GFM's geometric predictions. On the Sparse and Medium subsets of SpatialBench, GFM achieves the lowest absolute relative depth error and the highest relative-pose AUC at 5 degrees among the compared methods. It also achieves the lowest mean endpoint errors for dynamic points and scene flow across the five evaluated datasets. Across 34 scenes completed by all compared reconstruction systems, PoseEngine achieves the highest scene-averaged pose AUC at thresholds of 1, 3, and 5 degrees, with a cumulative runtime of 14.07 hours, approximately 20% of GLUEMAP's 69.67 hours. PoseEngine Flash provides a further accuracy-efficiency trade-off, with a measured mixed-precision runtime of 2.62 hours, approximately 4% of GLUEMAP's runtime. Separate scaling experiments show generally favorable trends with increased data, model computation, and training budgets. These results support the use of learned geometric priors within a scene-level reconstruction pipeline.
full_text: 0pt Introduction sec:introduction Recovering real-world geometry and motion from images and videos is a central problem in computer vision. Traditional reconstruction systems recover scenes through feature matching, camera pose estimation, and geometric optimization. While these methods benefit from explicit geometric constraints, they depend on reliable visual correspondences and sufficient overlap between views. Textureless regions, repetitive structures, wide baselines, and scene dynamics introduce uncertainty that can compromise both camera estimation and geometry recovery. As the number of input views increases, maintaining scene consistency can also incur substantial computational cost. Balancing reconstruction quality, efficiency, and robustness to complex scenes therefore remains an important challenge. Geometry foundation models offer a new approach to these challenges. Through large-scale pretraining, they learn transferable spatial priors and directly predict cameras, depth, cross-view correspondences, and dynamic geometry from visual observations. These predictions provide information where conventional geometric constraints are insufficient. However, model predictions do not inherently satisfy cross-view and temporal consistency across an entire scene, particularly for long sequences, large environments, and dynamic observations. Spatial priors and geometric optimization are therefore complementary: the former provide useful predictions and initialization, while the latter integrate them into coherent scene structure. The objective is not to eliminate optimization altogether, but to exploit model capabilities to reduce the optimization required for reliable reconstruction. Following this principle, we build Kosmo-GFM, a scene reconstruction system that combines a geometry foundation model, GFM, with a pose optimization engine, PoseEngine. GFM estimates camera parameters, depth, cross-view correspondences, and dynamic 3D points from images and videos, providing spatial priors for both static geometry recovery and dynamic scene understanding. PoseEngine leverages these outputs to efficiently recover scene-level camera poses and geometry, supporting the subsequent construction of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl2023gaussians representations for static scenes and 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS)~ wu2024fourdgs representations for dynamic scenes. The system thus connects geometric predictions from visual observations to scene-level reconstruction and renderable 3D and 4D representations. Beyond integrating the model and optimization engine, Kosmo-GFM emphasizes the continued improvement of spatial priors. We use high-quality real-world reconstruction data from KosmoWorld to train and improve GFM's understanding of scene geometry. As GFM improves, more reliable predictions can reduce uncertainty in subsequent geometry recovery and lessen the reliance on explicit optimization, providing a basis for simpler pose optimization and higher system efficiency. We therefore evaluate not only the accuracy of GFM's predictions, but also their practical role in the complete reconstruction system. We evaluate GFM on static and dynamic geometry, and evaluate PoseEngine by pose accuracy, runtime, and the quality of the resulting 3DGS reconstructions. We also conduct a separate scaling study using models developed specifically for those experiments. Our main contributions and findings are: 1pt 0pt GFM, a geometry foundation model with task-specific decoders. From images and videos, GFM predicts cameras, depth, cross-view matches, and dynamic 3D points, and can optionally take camera parameters as input. It achieves strong relative-pose accuracy on both SpatialBench subsets and reduces average endpoint error for dynamic points and scene flow. KosmoWorld, real-world reconstruction data for geometric priors. Adding KosmoWorld improves depth and relative-pose estimation on both SpatialBench subsets, demonstrating the value of real-world supervision. PoseEngine, a prior-driven reconstruction engine. Across scenes completed by all compared methods, PoseEngine improves mean pose accuracy over GLUEMAP with substantially lower runtime. PoseEngine Flash offers a further accuracy--efficiency trade-off. Scaling behavior of geometric reconstruction. Scaling experiments vary data volume, model scale, and training compute. Depth and camera accuracy generally improve with more training data, larger models, and increased training compute. Related Work sec:related Learned geometric prediction, cross-view matching, and scene-level optimization address complementary requirements of 3D and dynamic reconstruction. Learned models provide geometry and motion priors, matching connects observations across views, and scene-level optimization strengthens geometric consistency. This section reviews 3D reconstruction, 4D reconstruction, matching, and pose estimation systems from this perspective. Kosmo-GFM combines a shared geometry model with PoseEngine and reconstruction-derived training supervision from KosmoWorld, bringing learned prediction and geometric constraints together within a single reconstruction system. 3D Reconstruction sec:related-3d Static reconstruction recovers scene geometry and camera parameters from images or videos. Beyond prediction accuracy, its practical scope depends on how observations are processed and which camera models are supported. DUSt3R formulates reconstruction from uncalibrated image pairs as point-map regression~ wang2023dust3r , and MASt3R couples this geometry with local descriptors for matching~ leroy2024mast3r . Fast3R and MUSt3R extend pairwise prediction to multiple views in a common coordinate frame, reducing the need to align separate pairwise reconstructions rw_fast3r,rw_must3r . VGGT predicts multiple geometric attributes jointly~ wang2025vggt , whereas removes dependence on a designated reference view through a permutation-equivariant architecture~ rw_pi3 . SAIL-Recon scales scene regression by localizing additional images against an anchor-based neural scene representation~ rw_sailrecon , while FastVGGT reduces inference cost through training-free token merging~ rw_fastvggt . Another direction broadens the available inputs: Depth Anything 3 supports geometry recovery with or without known camera poses~ lin2025da3 , while MapAnything and WorldMirror incorporate optional geometric observations or priors into feed-forward reconstruction~ keetha2025mapanything,rw_worldmirror . OmniVGGT further studies the injection and fusion of auxiliary geometric modalities~ rw_omnivggt . AMB3R uses a compact volumetric backend for metric-scale geometric reasoning~ rw_amb3r , and VGGT- examines scaling model capacity and training data for static and dynamic reconstruction~ rw_vggtomega . These approaches extend direct prediction through richer conditioning, scene representations, and training scale, rather than treating image count as the only dimension of scalability. Streaming methods update a scene as observations arrive, balancing the retention of historical geometry against memory use and latency. Spann3R maintains external spatial memory~ rw_spann3r , while CUT3R carries a persistent recurrent state across observations~ wang2025cut3r . Point3R associates explicit spatial pointers with scene locations~ rw_point3r . StreamVGGT uses causal attention and cached features~ rw_streamvggt , and STream3R formulates sequential point-map prediction with a causal decoder-only transformer~ rw_stream3r . WinT3R combines windowed inference with a global camera-token pool~ rw_wint3r . Extending inference beyond the training sequence length also requires controlling drift and forgetting. TTT3R reinterprets memory updates as online learning~ rw_ttt3r , LoGeR combines parametric memory with sliding-window context~ rw_loger , and LingBot-Map combines an anchor context, a pose-reference window, and a trajectory memory~ chen2026lingbotmap . InfiniteVGGT uses a bounded rolling cache~ rw_infinitevggt . LongStream combines keyframe-relative pose prediction with scale modeling and cache management~ rw_longstream , whereas ABot-Recon instead emphasizes local temporal context and adjacent-frame relative predictions~ rw_abotrecon . Test-time training offers another memory mechanism: VGG-T distills scene information into a fixed-size network for scalable offline reconstruction~ rw_vggt3 , while Scal3R adapts a neural global-context representation at test time for long sequences~ rw_scal3r . VGG-T is related to streaming methods through its memory formulation, but does not require strictly causal inference. Video reconstruction must also account for scene dynamics. MonST3R adapts point-map prediction to recover geometry at individual timesteps~ rw_monst3r , while PAGE-4D separates the treatment of dynamic information for camera estimation and geometry reconstruction~ rw_page4d , and VGGT4D mines motion cues from a pretrained geometry transformer's attention to suppress dynamic interference in camera and geometry estimation without additional training~ rw_vggt4d . These methods predict cameras and geometry rather than scene motion. They address motion-induced inconsistency, complementing the memory and sequence-length concerns of streaming reconstruction. Panoramas offer wide spatial coverage, but spherical distortion and projection discontinuities limit direct transfer from perspective-image models. PanoSplatt3R adapts perspective pretraining to unposed, wide-baseline panoramas~ ren2025panosplatt3r . PanoVGGT instead incorporates modeling that accounts for spherical geometry to jointly predict cameras and dense geometry from panoramic inputs~ rw_panovggt . PaGeR adapts a perspective-pretrained geometry transformer using mixed perspective and panoramic training, jointly estimating depth, surface normals, and sky masks~ rw_pager . Data coverage is also important: Holo360D provides real-world continuous panoramic trajectories with aligned geometry and camera poses, supporting both training and evaluation rw_holo360d . Argus targets metric indoor reconstruction, using learned co-visibility to choose a reference view and geometric constraints to couple prediction branches~ rw_argus . CasaMaestro reconstructs house-scale geometry and camera poses from sparse multi-view panoramas~ rw_casamaestro . Together, these works extend panoramic reconstruction from adapting perspective priors to collecting suitable supervision and maintaining metric consistency across large indoor spaces. General camera models extend reconstruction beyond a fixed pinhole assumption. Wid3R conditions reconstruction on the camera model~ jung2026wid3r . CAM3R predicts ray directions and scene geometry for uncalibrated wide-angle images~ rw_cam3r , whereas X-Lens estimates metric depth from calibrated, heterogeneous fisheye and pinhole views~ rw_xlens . Fisheye3R adapts pretrained multi-view models to fisheye projection while retaining perspective-image capability~ rw_fisheye3r . RayTun3R instead adapts lightweight position- and camera-related components on a short segment of the test sequence, leaving the pretrained backbone fixed~ rw_raytun3r . Other approaches address camera heterogeneity through training data or ray-based representations. MEOW learns mixed-camera reconstruction from procedurally rendered training tuples without requiring camera-type labels or calibration at inference~ rw_meow . G-ray parameterizes rotary position encodings using camera-local ray angles~ rw_gray . Any3R uses a supplied dense ray field to condition angular positional encoding and solid-angle-weighted supervision, supporting heterogeneous central cameras in one reconstruction~ rw_any3r . At the single-image level, OmniPoint decouples ray direction from distance to predict metric point clouds across pinhole, fisheye, and panoramic projections, with optional geometric priors~ rw_omnipoint . title: Consensus Capture in Reference-Based UAV Video Stabilization: A Benchmark on Dynamic Urban Scenes
comment: 50 pages, 17 figures, 24 tables. Code at https://github.com/rfonod/stabilo-benchmark and data at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23623540 and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15050577
summary: Reference-frame stabilization registers every frame of a hovering-drone video onto one reference frame, keeping object positions comparable. The registration pipelines it relies on are selected on feature-matching benchmarks in which only the camera moves. Over a busy intersection, vehicles moving together supply mutually consistent correspondences that can draw the robust homography estimate toward their motion: consensus capture, which inlier statistics cannot flag. A two-part benchmark measures it and the object masking meant to prevent it. A static protocol scores ten pipelines under exactly known homographies on 4K aerial frames, tuned on a site-disjoint split at a matched resolution and feature budget. A dynamic protocol scores them at an offline and a real-time budget on hovers selected from the video alone to span the amount and coherence of moving foreground, plus a stationary control. It measures background alignment, object position error and the share of a moving group's displacement an estimate follows, against a pseudo-ground-truth reference audited with manually annotated ground control points, which also score every candidate. On static scenes, tuned AKAZE, RootSIFT, SIFT and BRISK lead, retuning the matcher thresholds raises the mean average accuracy (mAA) by at most 0.0062, and masking costs less than 0.005. Unmasked ORB is captured on 28 of 304 real-time dynamic pairs and on 6 offline; its real-time captured estimates have a median corner error of 18.8 px yet typical inlier counts and ratios. Masking removes capture for every pipeline and leaves the leading pipelines unchanged. Code, data and results are released.

UAV video stabilization image registration homography estimation feature matching oriented bounding box traffic monitoring Introduction sec:introduction Reference-frame stabilization is the registration model used when object positions must stay consistent over a long hover, during which wind keeps shifting and rotating the view: every frame is aligned directly onto one fixed reference frame, so that error does not accumulate and a position measured in frame is comparable with one measured minutes earlier. Trajectory extraction from high-altitude video is the application studied here, and traffic monitoring supplies the footage, but the requirement is shared by any analysis that compares moving objects across time in image or map coordinates, such as river surface velocimetry~ ljubicic2021comparison . The estimate is a homography, and the pipeline that produces it (feature detector, descriptor, matcher, robust estimator, and, where objects are annotated, a masking strategy that withholds them from feature detection) is assembled from components each of which has been benchmarked extensively~ jin2021image,efe2021effect,barath2023homography . Those benchmarks evaluate correspondence accuracy on scenes without independently moving content: planar surfaces, landmark facades, building walls. The only source of disagreement between their two views is the camera. A hovering drone over a busy intersection presents the opposite case. The camera barely moves, and dozens of objects in the frame move without it, many of them together: a platoon released by a green light translates as a unit, and every vehicle in it supplies correspondences that agree with one another under a single transform, the one describing their motion. If those correspondences win the consensus, the robust estimator does not fail. It solves the problem it was posed, returning a homography that is internally consistent and well supported but describes the vehicles rather than the road ( ). We call this failure consensus capture, and it has a consequence for evaluation before it has one for method design. Inlier count, inlier ratio, and reprojection error measure the self-consistency of a fit, and a coherently moving foreground is self-consistent by construction. Where it wins, these quantities are no longer merely weak proxies for accuracy, as they are already known to be on static scenes~ jin2021image,barath2023homography ; they become anti-informative, because the moving-object consensus can be the cleaner of the two available fits. An evaluation that reads them cannot detect capture. What is needed scores the alignment of the static world directly, makes a moving-object consensus observable, and relates it to how much of the frame moves and how coherently. To our knowledge no matching or registration benchmark provides this: none combines independently moving content with reference geometry ( ), so a risk flagged for airborne video~ kirchhof2006detection has gone unmeasured. Capture matters most where trajectories are used one at a time. Macroscopic quantities such as flow and density average a transient offset away, but microscopic analyses read individual trajectories and their derivatives: car following, lane changes~ kim2026lane , per-vehicle noise emission~ espadaler2023noise , and surrogate safety measures such as time-to-collision, post-encroachment time and the deceleration rate to avoid a crash~ abdelaty2023advances,espadaler2025swarm , which drone trajectory datasets now provide or are built to support~ zheng2024citysim, FONOD2025105205 . Under reference-frame registration each frame is registered on its own, so nothing ties a captured estimate to those of neighboring frames: its error follows the group's motion and is present only while the group holds the consensus. Speeds and accelerations are differences of positions over fractions of a second, so an error that varies from frame to frame in this way is amplified in them~ punzo2011assessment . The accuracy these datasets aim for is correspondingly tight: the inD dataset requires a positioning error below ~ bock2020ind , under two pixels at the of the footage studied here ( ), whereas the captured estimates of have a median corner error of px , about a meter on the ground, against the reference estimator. Since the estimates pulled toward the group keep typical inlier statistics, a pipeline captured on a few frames passes their error, unflagged, to every trajectory in those frames. Several of these datasets are also recorded lower than the 150 studied here: inD from up to at about per pixel~ bock2020ind and the intersections of CitySim from ~ zheng2024citysim ; a view that covers less ground can give a vehicle group of the same size a larger share of the frame and of its features. We provide such an evaluation in two parts. Part~I is a static protocol under exactly known homographies and photometric degradation, on 4K frames from a multi-drone experiment over Songdo, South Korea: one from each of the viewpoints from which its ten drones recorded intersections. It establishes what each pipeline can do when nothing moves and which of its settings matter, extending the campaign of FONOD2025105205 with paired trials, per-pipeline tuning on a site-disjoint split, and a matched resolution and feature budget. Part~II is a dynamic protocol on nine hovers over busy intersections, each registered onto a reference frame selected from the video alone to span the amount and coherence of moving foreground, plus a stationary control that separates the removal of moving objects from the removal of texture. It runs every pipeline at an offline and a real-time point of Part~I's budget grid. Real footage has no true homography, so Part~II measures background alignment outside the annotated objects, the position error a trajectory inherits, the direction of the error relative to the dominant motion, and the share of a moving group's displacement an estimate follows, which measures capture where it happens. Its pseudo-ground-truth reference estimator is audited against manually annotated (image positions of static ground points, not surveyed coordinates), which also score every candidate directly, so that the masking comparison does not depend on the reference estimator's own masking. Masking with and is a controlled axis throughout, since the shape of a mask could matter in either direction ( ). On hovers over Songdo intersections, the measurement finds capture. At the real-time budget, unmasked ORB is captured in all five cases that present a coherently moving group, the four with much moving foreground and the stationary control, on of the pairs that carry one, though of them in a single case. The within the first second are pulls toward the group; of the beyond it are breakdowns of the estimate, which unmasked ORB also shows with no group in view. At the offline budget capture is rarer (unmasked ORB, pairs in two cases). Estimates pulled toward a group cannot be told apart by their inlier statistics: their inlier counts and ratios match those of the same pipeline at the nearest offsets of the same case, at both budgets. Masking removes capture for every pipeline at both budgets while leaving the leading pipelines, SIFT, RootSIFT and AKAZE, where they were; for real-time ORB, whose feature budget it also returns to the ground, the captured pairs can account for at most a quarter of the gain. and do not differ at these densities and orientations, where the two geometries withhold nearly the same pixels. Averaged over all nine cases, four of which never present a moving group, the masking benefit is either not significant or smaller than the repeatability of the ( ). The conclusions are bounded by the moving share of these cases; the protocol is not, and it applies unchanged to footage from lower altitude or over denser traffic, where that share is larger. Contributions sec:contributions A benchmark for the complete registration pipeline of reference-based UAV stabilization in dynamic urban scenes: a static protocol under exactly known homographies ( ) and a dynamic protocol on real hovering-drone footage at an offline and a real-time compute budget ( ). It covers the pipelines a deployed stabilization library exposes, as a measurement of that system rather than a leaderboard of state-of-the-art matchers ( ). An evaluation methodology for dynamic scenes, where self-consistency statistics are unreliable: background-alignment measures that need no ground-truth homography, object-level errors that bound the position error a trajectory inherits, two measures that make consensus capture observable (the direction of the error and the share of a moving group's displacement an estimate follows), and a audit that measures the error of the pseudo-ground truth and supplies an independent comparison ( ), under a pre-specified analysis plan ( ). A case-selection procedure that measures from the video alone how much of the foreground moves, how coherently, and when, and chooses the cases and their reference frames to span these conditions, under which capture can arise; its measurements are validated against published vehicle trajectories ( ). A measurement of consensus capture and of object-aware masking on real footage: at the real-time budget unmasked ORB is captured in every case that presents a coherent group, its pull toward the group is invisible to inlier statistics, and capture disappears under masking at detection ( ). The public release of the benchmark implementation~ stabilo_benchmark and of its data~ stabilo_benchmark_data (annotated frames, cases, and every campaign's results), from which every benchmark number is regenerated by a command. Also released are hbb2obb~ hbb2obb , the SAM-assisted conversion of to that makes masks available at benchmark scale, and Songdo Vision OBB~ songdo_vision_obb , the version of Songdo Vision~ songdo_vision , together with the human-verified oriented reference against which the conversion is validated ( ). title: Spatial Foundry: A Multimodal Dataset for Spatial Intelligence
summary: Spatial intelligence requires connecting visual observations to the geometry, objects, and persistent state of an environment. Images alone leave these relationships implicit, while disconnected annotations make it difficult to study appearance, camera motion, and scene changes under a common reference. We introduce Spatial Foundry, a collection of 5,280 furnished residential 3D scene configurations with editable assets and aligned visual, geometric, and temporal data. Its modalities include floor plans, perspective and panoramic RGB, metric depth, point clouds, meshes, instance-level 3D bounding boxes, and camera trajectories paired with video. Shared scene coordinates link observations across views and time; editable source scenes enable additional camera paths and controlled object changes. We describe the data representation and construction workflow, and discuss applications in floor-plan-conditioned 3D generation, geometric reconstruction, instance-level perception, camera-conditioned video generation, shared world modeling, and scene editing. Controlled camera and scene variations support spatial perception and world-model research. The public project page provides videos and an interactive colored point-cloud preview.
full_text: Spatial intelligence requires connecting visual observations to the geometry, objects, and persistent state of an environment. Images alone leave these relationships implicit, while disconnected annotations make it difficult to study appearance, camera motion, and scene changes under a common reference. We introduce , a collection of 5,280 furnished residential 3D scene configurations with editable assets and aligned visual, geometric, and temporal data. Its modalities include floor plans, perspective and panoramic RGB, metric depth, point clouds, meshes, instance-level 3D bounding boxes, and camera trajectories paired with video. Shared scene coordinates link observations across views and time; editable source scenes enable additional camera paths and controlled object changes. We describe the data representation and construction workflow, and discuss applications in floor-plan-conditioned 3D generation, geometric reconstruction, instance-level perception, camera-conditioned video generation, shared world modeling, and scene editing. Controlled camera and scene variations support spatial perception and world-model research. The public project page provides videos and an interactive colored point-cloud preview. page: Introduction Understanding a three-dimensional environment requires more than recognizing objects in the current view. It requires knowing how objects are arranged in space and anticipating what would be observed from another viewpoint or after a change to the environment. Connecting visual observations to spatial structure and its changes is a central aspect of spatial intelligence. World models offer a way to learn these relationships by predicting subsequent observations conditioned on prior observations, camera motion, and actions that modify the scene. In three-dimensional environments, these predictions should be visually plausible, follow the specified camera trajectory, and preserve consistent geometry and object states across viewpoints and revisits. Learning and evaluating these capabilities requires images and videos explicitly associated with the underlying geometry, camera poses, and scene states, so that visual changes can be traced to their spatial causes. Existing datasets and simulation environments provide complementary foundations for spatial learning. RealEstate10K associates video observations with recovered camera trajectories~ realestate ; Hypersim pairs photorealistic indoor imagery with geometric and semantic annotations~ hypersim ; and ProcTHOR provides diverse procedural environments for embodied interaction~ procthor . As summarized in Figure~ fig:datacomparison , these resources differ in their coverage of paired layouts, visual observations, geometry, and editable scene states. Access to individual modalities does not by itself provide matched sequences in which camera motion and object changes can be varied independently. Studying such controlled spatial variation requires observations, camera trajectories, and persistent object identities coordinated within a common scene reference: the same route observed before and after an object edit, or the same scene state observed from multiple viewpoints. To support these controlled comparisons, we introduce , a collection of 5,280 furnished residential 3D scene configurations and a scene-based pipeline for producing aligned visual, geometric, and temporal data. Each configuration combines a residential layout with a furnishing arrangement. GPT-6 generates structured layouts from residential rules, human reviewers check their spatial usability, and Blender assembly with Infinigen assets produces the furnished source scenes. The collection spans US-style residential layouts with varied room compositions and furnishing arrangements. Editable source scenes retain metric geometry and object structure, supporting perspective and panoramic RGB observations, depth maps, meshes, point clouds, and instance-level 3D bounding boxes. Camera trajectories associate video observations with per-frame camera poses, while scene edits provide explicit records of changes to object placement and appearance. The source scenes allow additional observations to be rendered under specified cameras and object configurations. The central organizing principle is to separate changes in observation from changes in the environment. With a scene held fixed, different camera trajectories produce observations of the same geometry and object configuration. With a camera trajectory held fixed, controlled edits produce corresponding sequences before and after a scene change. Multiple observer cameras can additionally record a shared sequence of scene states. These controlled comparisons connect appearance to the spatial variables that determine it, supporting supervision and evaluation beyond isolated images. Potential applications include geometric reconstruction, 3D instance perception, camera-conditioned video generation, and prediction of the visual consequences of scene edits. This data organization supports floor-plan-conditioned 3D scene generation, geometric reconstruction, instance-level spatial perception, camera-conditioned video generation, multi-agent shared world modeling, and state-conditioned scene editing. Paired floor plans and furnished environments connect layout constraints to 3D structure and appearance, while aligned observations and state records connect camera motion and object changes to their visual consequences. Together, these applications span static scene understanding and the prediction of observations during exploration and interaction. This report makes three contributions: A collection of furnished residential environments with metric geometry, editable assets, and diverse layout and furnishing configurations. A pipeline for aligned multimodal and sequential data, linking rendered observations to camera calibration, trajectories, geometry, object annotations, and scene-state records. Controlled data-generation workflows that separate camera variation from scene variation, supporting reproducible comparisons for spatial perception and generation. Related Work Indoor 3D Datasets and Simulation Environments Captured indoor datasets connect visual observations with reconstructed geometry. ScanNet++ provides high-fidelity scans, registered imagery, and semantic annotations~ scannetpp , while Replica and HM3D supply reconstructed indoor environments for visual and embodied research~ replica,hm3d . Synthetic resources expose additional structure: Structured3D pairs rendered observations with structural annotations~ structured3d , 3D-FRONT provides furnished layouts and textured assets~ front , and Hypersim associates photorealistic imagery with dense geometric and semantic supervision~ hypersim . ProcTHOR supports embodied interaction in procedurally generated environments~ procthor , while Aria Synthetic Environments provides synthetic egocentric observations with camera trajectories and structured scene annotations~ ase . These resources emphasize captured appearance, structural understanding, furnished assets, or interactive simulation. For studying controlled spatial changes, recorded views and fixed observation sequences alone provide limited access to matched camera and object variations: observing the same route before and after a chosen edit requires editable geometry and coordinated state records. Spatial Foundry organizes 5,280 furnished residential configurations around paired 2D floor plans and 3D environments, with perspective and panoramic RGB, metric depth, meshes, point clouds, instance annotations, and trajectory--video correspondences. Its scope connects layout-conditioned generation and static perception to sequential observation within the same residential assets. Editable scenes allow camera paths and object configurations to be varied independently, yielding task-specific pairs with explicit geometric and state references. Controllable Generation and Spatial World Models Camera-conditioned generation and interactive world models aim to predict observations under specified motion or actions. RealEstate10K supplies video frames with camera trajectories recovered through SLAM and bundle adjustment~ realestate . CameraCtrl introduces explicit camera-pose conditioning for video diffusion, and CameraCtrl II extends camera-controlled generation to dynamic scene exploration~ cameractrl,cameractrlii . Recurrent world models learn compact predictive environment representations~ worldmodels ; Genie learns action-controllable environments from unlabeled video through a latent action model~ genie . Atlas combines visual and geometric inputs in a shared spatial context for camera-controlled generation, reconstruction, and simulation~ atlas . VSI-Bench evaluates visual-spatial reasoning from sequential video observations~ vsibench . These approaches make camera control, persistent context, and interaction central to visual generation. Their supervision also highlights a data requirement: recovered camera trajectories describe viewpoint changes, whereas latent actions learned from video do not directly specify metric object transforms. Relating a visual change to a particular camera motion or object edit requires corresponding geometric and state records. Spatial Foundry supplies these references through calibrated observations, paired camera trajectories and videos, persistent instance identities, and recorded scene edits. Holding the scene fixed provides camera-conditioned sequences; holding the camera path fixed provides before-and-after edit pairs. Multiple cameras can observe the same state sequence, extending this supervision to cross-view consistency, revisitation, and shared world modeling. Dataset Overview Residential Environments The collection contains 5,280 furnished residential 3D scene configurations. Each configuration combines an architectural layout, structural geometry, and a particular arrangement of furniture and objects. The scenes are generated from U.S. residential design priors, GPT-6 floor-plan definitions, and Infinigen-based Blender assembly. Human review checks room connectivity, passage clearance, and stair access. Variation in room combinations, circulation paths, functional templates, and furnishing arrangements produces diverse US-style residential environments. Multiple furnishing configurations can share a layout, providing variation in both architectural structure and interior contents. The source assets retain explicit geometry and object transforms. Distances and object dimensions use meters. Floor plans describe the arrangement of rooms and structural boundaries; meshes represent surfaces; point clouds provide sampled geometry.
